title: Payment confirmation endpoint is unauthenticated and never binds the Peach result to the transaction id or amount — lets an attacker mark any transaction PAID (money loss)
description: POST /api/transactions/:id/verify-result has NO @UseGuards (unlike every other transaction route which is ClerkGuard/ClerkOrTokenGuard). It takes the transaction id from the URL and an attacker-controlled `resourcePath` from the body. verifyResult() loads the transaction by id, calls peach.verifyPayment(resourcePath), and on result.isSuccess calls markPaid(tx.id, ...). Critically, neither verifyResult nor markPaid ever compares the Peach result's `merchantTransactionId` to the path :id, nor compares result.amount to tx.buyerTotal. PeachPaymentResult carries both merchantTransactionId and amount (peach.service.ts 110-118) but they are discarded. So a successful payment result for ANY checkout can be replayed against ANY transaction id, and any amount passes. Attack: create a cheap R1 listing, pay it legitimately, capture your own success resourcePath from the Peach redirect, then POST it to /transactions/<victimOrOwnExpensiveTxId>/verify-result. The target transaction flips to paymentStatus HELD + listing SOLD with no real payment for that amount; for a PRIVATE_ARRANGE transaction markPaid->maybeImmediatePayout RELEASES funds to the seller instantly (service 978, 992-1053). The webhook path at least binds by merchantTransactionId (service 306-307) but still skips the amount check; the verify-result path binds by neither.
evidence: controller: `@Post(':id/verify-result')` with no guard, `verifyResult(@Param('id') id, @Body('resourcePath') resourcePath) { return this.txService.verifyResult(id, resourcePath); }`. service verifyResult: `const result = await this.peach.verifyPayment(resourcePath); if (result.isSuccess) { await this.markPaid(tx.id, result.paymentId, result.resultCode, tx.listing); return { success: true }; }` — result.merchantTransactionId and result.amount are never checked against tx. peach.verifyPayment builds the URL straight from the caller-supplied path: `const url = `${this.baseUrl}${resourcePath}?entityId=...``.
recommendation: Add server-side binding in verifyResult/markPaid: after peach.verifyPayment, reject unless result.merchantTransactionId === transactionId AND result.amount === tx.buyerTotal (allow only exact-cents match). Treat any mismatch as a hard failure + admin alert. Additionally guard the route with ClerkGuard and verify the caller is the transaction's buyer; the Peach redirect lands on an authenticated page so a Clerk session is available. Do not rely on isSuccess alone.

verdict.reasoning: Verified the full path. (1) UNAUTHENTICATED: controller `transactions.controller.ts:91-97` POST :id/verify-result has NO @UseGuards while every sibling route uses ClerkGuard/ClerkOrTokenGuard. The only global guard is ThrottlerGuard (app.module.ts:92) — rate limiting, not auth. main.ts adds only a ValidationPipe (which doesn't touch the raw @Body('resourcePath')). Frontend caller frontend/app/checkout/complete/page.tsx:24-28 sends no Authorization header / no credentials, confirming the endpoint runs anonymously even in the legit flow — an attacker reproduces it with curl. (2) NO BINDING: verifyResult (transactions.service.ts:264-287) loads tx by the URL :id, calls peach.verifyPayment(resourcePath), and on result.isSuccess calls markPaid(tx.id,...). peach.service.ts:114-116 populates result.merchantTransactionId and result.amount, but a grep of the whole service shows they are NEVER compared to transactionId or tx.buyerTotal. merchantTransactionId appears only in the webhook path (301-307) as a lookup key; the verify-result path binds by neither id nor amount. (3) IMPACT: markPaid (940-955) sets paymentStatus HELD + listing SOLD; maybeImmediatePayout (992-1027) flips PRIVATE_ARRANGE txs to RELEASED and increments seller totalSales — real fund release. The PRIVATE_ARRANGE consent stamp is set at checkout by the buyer (create, 196-199), so a victim's own private-arrange tx already satisfies the defence-in-depth check. EXPLOIT: attacker pays a real R1 listing, captures their genuine success resourcePath (Peach returns isSuccess true), then POSTs {resourcePath} to /transactions/<expensive-or-victim-txId>/verify-result; isSuccess is the sole gate, so the target tx is marked paid with no payment for that amount. Nuances that do NOT defeat it for launch: the paidAt idempotency check (272) only requires the target be unpaid (normal pending state); verifyPayment throws when Peach is unconfigured (96-98) but production is configured. Possible friction only on Peach's side (resourcePath single-use/TTL), but the app enforces nothing. Finding is accurate on facts, call path, and impact.

title: Admin JWT secret falls back to a hardcoded public string with no startup validation — admin takeover if JWT_ADMIN_SECRET is ever unset in prod
lines: admin-jwt.guard 16; admin-auth.service 31; ask-gg.module 27; reloading.module 29; main.ts 16-78 (no env validation)
description: Both the admin JWT signer (AdminAuthService.login) and verifier (AdminJwtGuard) use `process.env.JWT_ADMIN_SECRET || 'dev-admin-secret-change-in-prod'`. The literal appears in 4 files. There is no env-validation at boot (main.ts/AppModule register no ConfigModule schema and no assertion), so if the prod .env is missing/empties this var, the app starts normally and signs+verifies admin sessions with a secret that is committed to the repo. Anyone could forge a JWT `{sub, email, role:'SUPERADMIN'}` and pass AdminJwtGuard on EVERY /admin/* route. This is compounded by the fact that admin pages are NOT server-gated (frontend/middleware.ts marks `/admin(.*)` public and bypasses the coming-soon gate; the only real boundary is this backend JWT). The operator's CLAUDE.md (line 199) lists JWT_ADMIN_SECRET as a required prod var, so in a correctly-provisioned environment the fallback is inert — hence HIGH not CRITICAL — but a single misconfigured deploy silently downgrades the entire admin surface to a known secret with zero signal.
evidence: admin-jwt.guard.ts: `secret: process.env.JWT_ADMIN_SECRET || 'dev-admin-secret-change-in-prod'`. admin-auth.service.ts signs with the same fallback. SuperadminGuard only reads role off the JWT payload (`admin?.role !== 'SUPERADMIN'`), so a forged token with role SUPERADMIN clears it for create/role-change/deactivate admin endpoints.
recommendation: Fail closed: at bootstrap (main.ts) throw if process.env.JWT_ADMIN_SECRET is unset or equals the dev fallback when NODE_ENV==='production'. Remove the hardcoded fallback entirely (or gate it behind NODE_ENV!=='production'). Centralise the secret read so it can't drift across the 4 modules. Consider re-deriving the admin role from the DB in SuperadminGuard (the create-admin comment already claims the service re-checks, but the guard itself trusts the JWT).

verdict.reasoning:
VERIFIED REAL and correctly rated HIGH. Every factual claim checks out against the code.

(1) Signer and verifier both use the committed fallback: admin-auth.service.ts:31 signs and admin-jwt.guard.ts:16 verifies with `process.env.JWT_ADMIN_SECRET || 'dev-admin-secret-change-in-prod'`. (2) The literal genuinely spreads across 4 files — ask-gg.module.ts:27 and reloading.module.ts:29 also JwtModule.register() with it for live admin controllers (AskGgKbAdminController, ReloadingAdminController). (3) No env validation exists: main.ts (1-78) does no assertion; app.module.ts registers no ConfigModule/Joi schema; a grep across backend/src for ConfigModule/Joi/validationSchema returns only an unrelated comment. backend/.env.example:20 ships `JWT_ADMIN_SECRET=` empty, and an empty string is falsy so it triggers the `||` fallback — so a missing/empty var lets the app boot silently signing+verifying with the public secret, zero signal. (4) Admin pages are NOT server-gated: frontend/middleware.ts:17 marks `/admin(.*)` public, line 52 makes it a coming-soon bypass, and lines 60-66 explicitly state there is no middleware admin gate (auth is client-side localStorage JWT). The backend AdminJwtGuard is the only real boundary.

Blast radius confirmed: every admin controller is class-level @UseGuards(AdminJwtGuard). A forged token clears it on catastrophic endpoints that have NO secondary check — POST /admin/transactions/:id/refund (real Peach refunds, admin.controller.ts:310), /release (304), /resolve-dispute-release (324), GET /admin/users/:id/dossier and /transactions/:id/dossier (full PII incl. real names, 237/299), PATCH /admin/users/:id + /bulk-ban (242/253), /admin/listings/:id/delete (193). That is money movement + cross-user PII exfiltration + mass bans = CRITICAL-class capability gated solely by a forgeable token.

One nuance: the finding's evidence line overclaims that a forged SUPERADMIN token clears create/role-change/deactivate. Those 3 endpoints (admin.service.ts createAdmin:1160, updateAdminRole:1236, deactivateAdmin:1261) DO re-fetch the actor by `sub` from the DB and re-check role==='SUPERADMIN', so a forged token whose sub doesn't match a real superadmin row is blocked there (defence-in-depth, also noted in the controller comment at 384-386). This does not rescue the finding — those are 3 of dozens of endpoints and the refund/PII endpoints are wide open — but it means the specific evidence sentence is slightly inaccurate.

Rating: HIGH is correct, not CRITICAL. CLAUDE.md:199 lists JWT_ADMIN_SECRET as a required prod var, so a correctly-provisioned deploy makes the fallback inert. This is a latent fail-open requiring a misconfigured deploy to trigger — but when triggered it is silent and total. That matches HIGH (incident likely on misconfig) rather than CRITICAL (active live breach). The recommendation (fail-closed bootstrap assertion when NODE_ENV==='production', remove the hardcoded fallback, centralise the secret read) is sound.

title: GET /users/me returns the seller's full bank account number/branch over a 24h URL-bearer CHECKOUT token
category: Authentication & Access Control / PII exposure via token scope
description: GET /users/me is guarded by ClerkOrTokenGuard, which accepts a CHECKOUT action token via ?t=<token> and resolves it to the token's authorisedUserId (the buyer). The handler selects and returns the full record including bankAccountNumber, bankBranchCode, bankAccountHolder, bankAccountType, addrLat/Lng. The CHECKOUT token is minted with a 24h TTL and embedded in an SMS link (offers.service notifyBuyerOfAccept) that points at /checkout/<id>?t=<token>; the checkout page then calls /users/me with that token. Because the token == the credential and lives in a URL (SMS history, browser history, referrer, shoulder-surf), anyone who obtains the link can read the user's banking quartet, not just their saved address. It is the user's OWN data (not a cross-user leak), so severity is MEDIUM, but a bearer-in-URL token should expose the minimum needed for checkout (name + delivery address), never full banking credentials. The CHECKOUT token is also explicitly not consumed (multi-request flow), so it stays replayable for the full 24h.
evidence: ClerkOrTokenGuard: on a CHECKOUT token it sets `request.clerkUserId = user.clerkId` for resolved.authorisedUserId and returns true. users.controller me() select includes `bankAccountNumber: true, bankBranchCode: true, bankAccountHolder: true, bankAccountType: true`. The same select has no branch on req.viaActionToken to trim sensitive fields.
recommendation: When the request arrived via an action token (req.viaActionToken === true, already stamped by the guard), return a reduced projection from /users/me that omits all bank* fields (and ideally exact addrLat/Lng), exposing only what the checkout form needs. Keep the full projection for Clerk-session requests only.

verdict.reasoning:
VERIFIED REAL, but the finding's TITLE is factually wrong. Traced the full path. GET /users/me (backend/src/users/users.controller.ts:51-99) selects bankAccountNumber/bankBranchCode/bankAccountHolder/bankAccountType (lines 91-94) and is guarded by ClerkOrTokenGuard (line 52). The guard (backend/src/auth/clerk-or-token.guard.ts:84-94) accepts a CHECKOUT token via ?t=, resolves it to the authorised user's clerkId, stamps request.viaActionToken=true, and does NOT consume it (comment lines 32-35; consume() only runs on transaction creation per action-tokens.service.ts:158-188). The CHECKOUT token has a 24h TTL (offers.service.ts:18,437), is SMS'd as /a/<token> (offers.service.ts:452), which 302-redirects to /checkout/[listingId]?t=<token> (frontend/app/a/[token]/page.tsx:18,92-93), and the checkout form calls GET /users/me?t=<token> via authedRequest (frontend/app/checkout/[listingId]/checkout-form.tsx:90-108,194). The Me type deserializes the bank fields (frontend/lib/types.ts:136-139), so they are returned in the JSON body. I confirmed the finding's central claim: viaActionToken IS used to harden POST /transactions (transactions.controller.ts:78) but is NOT referenced in users.controller.ts, so there is no branch trimming the /users/me projection for token-auth requests. So a replayable 24h URL-bearer token returns a plaintext bank account number + branch + holder in a GET response — if the token leaks (SMS forward, referrer, shared device), it is harvestable for the full window.

CORRECTIONS to the finding: (1) The TITLE claims it returns 'the SELLER's' bank details — FALSE. authorisedUserId is offer.buyerId (offers.service.ts:436), so /users/me returns the TOKEN-HOLDER's OWN record. It exposes the buyer's own banking data, and only when that buyer is also a seller who completed the AVS banking modal (schema.prisma:291-301 — bank fields are null for pure buyers). The finding's own Description correctly says 'user's OWN data (not a cross-user leak),' contradicting its title. (2) The recommendation to also hide addrLat/addrLng is wrong — the checkout LockerPicker needs them (checkout-form.tsx:211-212,257-258,859-860). Only the bank* fields are genuine over-exposure.

Net: real over-scoped-projection / PII-via-token-scope bug; the fix (omit bank* fields when req.viaActionToken) is correct and easy. Not a cross-user leak and not money loss, so not CRITICAL/HIGH. MEDIUM as claimed.

title: Admin refund marks transaction REFUNDED and emails buyer "refund issued" but NEVER calls Peach — money never returns to the buyer
category: Payment correctness / money loss / legal exposure
description: refundTransaction() is the admin's primary refund button (POST /api/admin/transactions/:id/refund, admin.controller.ts:310-318) and the only buyer-favourable resolution for a DISPUTED order. It flips paymentStatus to 'REFUNDED', writes an audit row, fires notifications.refundIssuedBuyer({...buyerTotal...}) telling the buyer they were refunded, and posts a Zoho credit note — but it does NOT call peach.refundPayment(). The admin module never even imports PeachService (grep of backend/src/admin for 'peach' returns only peachCheckoutId/peachPaymentId search fields). Contrast the seller-reject path (transactions.service.ts:478-497) and the dispatch-SLA auto-refund (dispatch-sla.service.ts:128-147), which both correctly call peach.refundPayment before stamping REFUNDED. So a buyer who wins a dispute, or any manual admin refund, is told 'Your refund has been issued' while the funds remain captured at Peach. The accounting also drifts: Zoho gets a credit note for a refund that never happened.
recommendation: Call peach.refundPayment(tx.peachPaymentId, tx.buyerTotal) BEFORE flipping status, exactly as rejectTransaction/autoRefundStale do: only set REFUNDED + notify the buyer + post the credit note if the gateway refund succeeds; on failure raise an urgent AdminAlert and surface an error to the admin. Inject PeachService into AdminService/AdminModule.

verdict.reasoning:
VERIFIED REAL. Traced the full path and every contrast claim holds.

1) admin.service.ts refundTransaction() (lines 989-1054): updates paymentStatus to 'REFUNDED' (996-1004), auto-resolves the BUYER_DISPUTE_RAISED alert (1008-1015), writes a TRANSACTION_REFUND audit row (1019-1029), calls notifications.refundIssuedBuyer({...buyerTotal...}) (1031-1039), and posts a Zoho credit note via zohoBooks.createCommissionCreditNote (1051). There is NO peach.refundPayment call in the method.

2) AdminService cannot even call Peach: its constructor (lines 20-29) injects only prisma, notifications, listings, audit, zohoBooks. Grep of backend/src/admin for peach/refundPayment/PeachService returns only a health-check URL, a dossier comment, two search fields (peachCheckoutId/peachPaymentId, lines 545-546), and a bank-verification comment (946) — zero refund calls.

3) The notification really tells the buyer the money is back: notifications.service.ts:1029 title 'Refund issued', and 1038-1039 body 'a refund of {amount} ... has been issued. Please allow 5-10 business days for it to appear on your statement.' Refund destination row says 'Original payment card' (1047). So the buyer is explicitly told funds were returned to their card.

4) Both reference paths confirm the correct pattern and that Peach refunds are real money movements: transactions.service.ts:478-497 fires peach.refundPayment FIRST, raises an urgent SALE_REJECT_REFUND_FAILED alert and throws on failure, and only stamps REFUNDED after success. dispatch-sla.service.ts:128-147 does the same (DISPATCH_SLA_REFUND_FAILED). peach.service.ts:219-257 shows refundPayment is a live POST to /v1/payments/{id} with paymentType:'RF' — a genuine gateway refund.

5) Ruled out a side channel: no Prisma $use middleware (none in backend/src/prisma), no @OnEvent/EventEmitter listener on TRANSACTION_REFUND or refund_issued, and refundTransaction is only invoked from admin.controller.ts:317 (POST /:id/refund). The TRANSACTION_REFUND audit row and refund_issued notification are purely informational. featured.service.ts:854 separately DOES call peach.refundPayment for its own flow, underscoring that the omission is specific to the admin transaction refund.

Net effect in production (Peach configured, funds captured): the admin's primary buyer-favourable dispute resolution stamps REFUNDED, clears the dispute alert, emails the buyer that their card was refunded, and books a Zoho credit note — while the captured funds remain at Peach and are never returned. Money loss to the buyer, false 'refunded' communication, silent dispute closure, and accounting drift, with no failure alert because the gateway is never contacted.

One caveat that does not reduce severity: when Peach is unconfigured, refundPayment returns a MOCK_REFUND success (peach.service.ts:223-228), so in dev/sandbox no path moves money. In production this defect is the unique gap. The severity rating is correct.

title: Peach webhook signature is computed over re-stringified JSON, not the raw body — verification can never succeed; turning the secret on silently drops every real payment, leaving it off accepts forgeries
description: PaymentsWebhookController.peachWebhook computes `const rawBody = JSON.stringify(body)` from the ALREADY-parsed JSON and passes that to verifyWebhookSignature (peach.service.ts:298-322), which HMAC-SHA256s it against PEACH_WEBHOOK_SECRET. Peach signs the exact bytes it sent; re-serialising the parsed object will not reproduce them (key order, whitespace, number/escape formatting all differ), so the digest will never match. Result: the moment PEACH_WEBHOOK_SECRET is configured for production, verifyWebhookSignature returns false for every legitimate webhook and the controller logs 'signature invalid — dropping' and returns 200 without processing — payments that complete only via webhook (buyer closed the tab before the result page ran) never get marked HELD/SOLD, funds sit captured with the order stuck. While the secret is unset, verifyWebhookSignature fails OPEN (returns true, peach.service.ts:300-302), so the endpoint accepts unauthenticated bodies. There is no configuration in which verification both enforces and lets real traffic through. main.ts already enables rawBody (rawBody: true, line 18) so req.rawBody is available and unused.
recommendation: Verify against the actual raw bytes: read req.rawBody (Buffer) — wire it via @Req() and pass req.rawBody.toString('utf8') (or the Buffer) to the HMAC. Confirm Peach's real header name + signing scheme and FAIL CLOSED in production (treat missing secret as a hard error rather than allow-through). Add an integration test that feeds a captured raw Peach payload + signature.

verdict.reasoning:
The technical defect is REAL and confirmed. transactions.controller.ts:301 does `const rawBody = JSON.stringify(body)` from the already-parsed body, then HMAC-SHA256s it (peach.service.ts:298-322). Re-serialized JSON cannot reproduce the exact bytes Peach signed (key order/whitespace/number formatting), so verification will fail for legitimate webhooks once a secret is set. Fail-open is also confirmed: peach.service.ts:300-302 returns true when PEACH_WEBHOOK_SECRET is unset, so today the endpoint accepts unauthenticated bodies. The codebase proves the correct pattern exists and rawBody is available: users/webhooks.controller.ts:40-54 reads req.rawBody (Buffer) for the Clerk webhook, and main.ts:18 sets `rawBody: true`. So the dual-bind (off=accepts forgeries, on=drops real webhooks) is accurate, and the recommended fix (use req.rawBody, fail closed) is sound.

HOWEVER the CRITICAL severity is OVERSTATED. The finding's core impact claim — payments only complete via webhook so funds get stuck — is wrong about the primary flow. The webhook is a REDUNDANT fallback. The primary confirmation path is verifyResult (transactions.service.ts:264), invoked by the result page (frontend/app/checkout/complete/page.tsx:24 → controller :92), which performs an INDEPENDENT server-to-server authenticated GET to Peach (peach.service.ts:95-118, Bearer token) using the resourcePath from the redirect. That path never touches webhook signature verification, and markPaid is idempotent (paidAt guards at lines 272/314). So with the secret unset (current config) real payments confirm fine; the actual exposure is (a) an unauthenticated webhook endpoint whose handler only calls the idempotent, transaction-id-keyed markPaid or revertListing (forgery requires guessing a cuid and yields limited effect), and (b) a config trap: naively enabling the secret would silently kill the webhook fallback. Both warrant a pre-launch fix but do not constitute guaranteed money-loss/stuck-funds today. Net: real, must-fix, but MEDIUM not CRITICAL.

title: No payment-amount verification in markPaid — a transaction can be marked fully paid for an amount that does not match buyerTotal (and forged via the fail-open webhook)
description: Both completion paths (handlePeachWebhook and verifyResult) only check result.isSuccess and then call markPaid, which sets paymentStatus=HELD, listing=SOLD. Neither ever compares result.amount (parsed in peach.service.ts:114 / 276) against tx.buyerTotal. So a success result for the wrong amount (e.g. a partial/zero authorisation, or a forged webhook body) still flips the order to fully paid and SOLD, and downstream payout releases the full sellerPayout. This is exploitable in combination with the fail-open webhook (finding above): the webhook endpoint is public (no guard) and the merchantTransactionId is exposed in shopperResultUrl (/checkout/complete?transactionId=...). An attacker who knows a transaction id can POST {merchantTransactionId, 'result.code':'000.000.000', amount:'0.00'} and the order is marked paid for free. peachPaymentId has no @unique constraint in schema.prisma (line 721, only @@index at 878), so nothing at the DB layer blocks reuse/forgery either.
recommendation: In markPaid (and before it in both callers), require result.amount === tx.buyerTotal (allow only an explicit, logged tolerance of 0). On mismatch, do not mark paid — log + raise an AdminAlert. Combine with raw-body signature enforcement so forged webhooks are rejected before parsing.

verdict.reasoning: Verified the full exploit chain against the actual code. CORE CLAIM CONFIRMED: markPaid (backend/src/payments/transactions.service.ts:926-955) flips paymentStatus=HELD + listing SOLD with no comparison against tx.buyerTotal; both callers gate only on result.isSuccess (verifyResult line 276-277, handlePeachWebhook line 319-320) and never read result.amount. EXPLOITABILITY CONFIRMED: (1) PaymentsWebhookController.peachWebhook (transactions.controller.ts:284-310) has no @UseGuards; the only global guard is ThrottlerGuard (app.module.ts:92), no global auth guard. (2) verifyWebhookSignature returns true when PEACH_WEBHOOK_SECRET is unset (peach.service.ts:300-302), and that var is absent from every .env in the repo; CLAUDE.md:1629 confirms fail-open. (3) Even if the secret were set, the controller signs JSON.stringify(body) (line 301) not the raw bytes Peach signed (req.rawBody is available since main.ts:18 sets rawBody:true) — so signature enforcement is structurally non-functional; the code comment at 297-300 admits this. (4) parseWebhookPayload (peach.service.ts:270-281) reads merchantTransactionId/result.code/amount straight from attacker body; SUCCESS_PATTERN /^(000\.000\.|...)/ matches the forged 000.000.000. (5) Transaction.id is cuid() (schema:690) and is exposed in the buyer's own URL /checkout/complete?transactionId=${tx.id} (transactions.service.ts:219), so a buyer can mark their own order paid without paying. (6) For PRIVATE_ARRANGE, markPaid -> maybeImmediatePayout (line 978, 992-1027) immediately sets paymentStatus=RELEASED and reveals contact PII with no seller action and no amount check. (7) peachPaymentId has no @unique (schema:721, only @@index at 878). Minor inaccuracies in the finding that do not change severity: the 299-325 line cite is handlePeachWebhook not markPaid (markPaid is 926-982); and the verifyResult path is actually less forgeable because it calls the real Peach API for amount, so the missing check there only affects partial-authorisation edge cases — the webhook is the genuinely forgeable vector, which the finding correctly identifies. Net: an unauthenticated POST can mark any known transaction fully paid and, for PRIVATE_ARRANGE, release real funds.

title: Money-state transitions guard with read-then-write instead of atomic conditional updates — concurrent webhook+result-page (or double clicks) can double-process / double-release
description: verifyResult (checks tx.paidAt at 272), handlePeachWebhook (checks tx.paidAt at 314), and confirmDelivery (checks paymentStatus!=='HELD' and confirmedDeliveryAt at 772-773) all read the guard field first and then later perform a plain prisma.update with no WHERE precondition on that field. Because verifyResult (called from the result page, unguarded POST :id/verify-result) and the webhook can fire near-simultaneously — and confirm-delivery can be double-clicked — two callers can both pass the guard and both run markPaid / both run the release $transaction. markPaid double-firing re-sends sale notifications and can run maybeImmediatePayout twice; confirmDelivery double-firing increments seller.totalSales twice and emits two PAYOUT_RELEASED events. There is no DB-level idempotency backstop (peachPaymentId is not @unique). The action-token consume() path is correctly atomic (updateMany WHERE usedAt:null, action-tokens.service.ts:175-188) — the same pattern is needed here.
recommendation: Gate each transition with an atomic conditional updateMany and act only when count===1: e.g. updateMany({ where: { id, paidAt: null }, data: {...} }) for markPaid; updateMany({ where: { id, paymentStatus: 'HELD', confirmedDeliveryAt: null }, data: {...} }) for release. Move the totalSales increment into the same guarded transaction. Optionally add @unique on peachPaymentId as defence-in-depth.

verdict.reasoning:
VERIFIED REAL, severity correct at HIGH (with one overstated phrase). I traced every cited path and the surrounding guards/throttler/schema.

The read-then-write pattern is confirmed in all three methods:
- verifyResult (transactions.service.ts:272) checks `if (tx.paidAt) return {alreadyProcessed}` then calls markPaid with no precondition.
- handlePeachWebhook (line 314) does the same `if (tx.paidAt)` check then markPaid.
- confirmDelivery (lines 772-773) checks `paymentStatus !== 'HELD'` and `confirmedDeliveryAt`, then runs a $transaction (lines 793-808) whose updates use `where: { id }` only.
markPaid (940-955) updates `where: { id: txId }` with NO `paidAt: null` guard; it then fires maybeImmediatePayout (which increments seller.totalSales + emits PAYOUT_RELEASED, lines 1023-1025) and sendSaleNotifications. confirmDelivery increments seller.totalSales with no precondition (lines 804-807).

No mitigating layer exists:
- verify-result (controller line 91-97) has NO guard — unauthenticated POST, freely repeatable.
- The only rate limiter is a single per-IP ThrottlerGuard bucket of 60/min (app.module.ts:55,92). It does NOT serialize the decisive race: the Peach server-to-server webhook (Peach's IP) vs the buyer browser's result-page POST (browser IP) are DIFFERENT IPs, so the throttler gives zero mutual exclusion; and 60/min trivially permits a confirm-delivery double-click.
- No advisory locks / SELECT FOR UPDATE / serializable isolation anywhere (grep for pg_advisory|FOR UPDATE|isolationLevel|Serializable returned nothing).
- No DB backstop: peachPaymentId is `String?` with only `@@index([peachPaymentId])` (schema lines 721, 878), NOT @unique.
The webhook+result-page double-fire is the NORMAL Peach payment flow on every transaction, so this is a hot-path race, not an exotic edge case. Crucially, the codebase already uses the exact correct fix elsewhere: action-tokens.service.ts:175-188 does `updateMany WHERE usedAt:null` and acts only when count!==0 — so the recommendation is proven-applicable.

One correction to the prior write-up: it overstates the impact as "double-release funds." These code paths do NOT call any payout/disbursement API (payout is a separate manual/Zoho step; Peach is the source of truth for actual money), so there is no automated double-disbursement of cash. The real, concrete harm is data-integrity corruption — double-incrementing seller.totalSales (a PUBLIC seller-reputation metric), duplicate sale/SMS notifications, double-minting the TRANSACTION_ACCEPT token, and two PAYOUT_RELEASED timeline rows (these would NOT be deduped by the TrackingEvent @@unique([transactionId,status,occurredAt]) because the two requests compute different `now`/occurredAt values). That keeps it below CRITICAL (no money loss / PII leak) but well above MEDIUM (normal-flow, payment-capture hot path, corrupts a public metric, fix pattern already in-repo). HIGH is the right rating.

title: Admin refundTransaction has no paymentStatus precondition — can refund an already-RELEASED payout or refund the same order twice, re-notifying buyer and re-posting Zoho credit notes
description: Unlike releaseTransaction (guards paymentStatus==='PENDING_ADMIN_VERIFICATION', line 935) and resolveDisputeRelease (guards 'DISPUTED', line 1076), refundTransaction performs no status check before flipping to REFUNDED. It will happily run on a transaction already in RELEASED (clawing back a completed payout in the ledger while the seller already got notified of payout), on one already REFUNDED (double refund — and once finding #1 is fixed to actually call Peach, this becomes a real double money-out), or DISPUTED/HELD. Each call re-fires refundIssuedBuyer and re-invokes zohoBooks.createCommissionCreditNote (which is idempotent on zohoCreditNoteId, but the notification + audit are not). This is the kind of one-click money mutation that needs a strict precondition.
recommendation: Reject unless paymentStatus is in a refundable set (e.g. HELD or DISPUTED). Use an atomic guarded updateMany({ where: { id, paymentStatus: { in: ['HELD','DISPUTED'] } } }) and only notify/credit-note/Peach-refund when count===1, so concurrent or repeat clicks can't double-act.

verdict.reasoning:
VERIFIED REAL but OVERSTATED. The core structural claim holds: admin.service.ts refundTransaction (lines 989-1054) has no paymentStatus precondition, while both siblings do — releaseTransaction guards 'PENDING_ADMIN_VERIFICATION' (line 935) and resolveDisputeRelease guards 'DISPUTED' (line 1076). The update at 996-1004 unconditionally flips any state to REFUNDED. Genuine present-day harm: an admin can refund an already-RELEASED tx (seller already paid out + totalSales incremented at line 984) or re-refund a REFUNDED one, corrupting ledger state and firing a false 'Refund issued' email to a buyer not actually being refunded — refundIssuedBuyer (notifications.service.ts:1014) is NOT idempotent: it calls notification.create (raw create, line 406), send() email (line 1052) every call. So duplicate inbox rows + duplicate/false buyer emails are real (SMS at 1060 has a fixed dedupe key 'refund-${txId}' so it may dedupe; email does not). Audit is also conditional on a note being present (line 1019 `if (note && note.trim())`), so a no-note refund mutates state unaudited.

HOWEVER the severity is overstated for two concrete reasons. (1) NOT a public exploit: the controller @Post(':id/refund') is admin-gated via @CurrentAdmin() (admin.controller.ts:310-318), so this is an operator footgun, not an unauthenticated breach — rules out CRITICAL and weakens the 'one-click money mutation' framing toward 'one-click by a trusted admin'. (2) The 'real double money-out' claim is speculative: refundTransaction does NOT call Peach at all today — there is no peach.refundPayment in this method. The actual Peach refund lives in transactions.service.ts rejectSale (line 479), which is separately state-guarded (line 464 blocks if already accepted). The audit explicitly hangs the money-loss escalation on a hypothetical future fix to its own 'finding #1', i.e. it is conditional, not present reality. Zoho is idempotent (zoho-books.service.ts:709 `if (tx.zohoCreditNoteId) return;`), which the audit conceded. Net: a legitimate financial-record-drift + false-customer-notification defect, and the recommended atomic guarded updateMany({ where: { id, paymentStatus: { in: ['HELD','DISPUTED'] } } }) is the correct fix — but with no money movement and admin-only access, the impact is MEDIUM, not HIGH.

title: Minimum-commission floor silently erases the Top Seller discount and can make commission 100% of the sale on small-ticket items
description: calculateCommission subtracts the Top Seller 0.5% discount, then if the rounded result is below MIN_COMMISSION_CENTS (R30) it returns Math.min(MIN_COMMISSION_CENTS, priceZarCents). Two issues: (1) the Top Seller discount — described as LOCKED per CLAUDE.md — is silently discarded on any sale where banded commission lands under R30, so Top Sellers get no discount on small sales (both tiers pay the same R30 floor). (2) For a sale priced below R30 (e.g. a R10 accessory, priceZarCents=1000) the clamp makes commission = min(3000,1000) = 1000, i.e. 100% of the sale price; with seller-absorbs-fee (passFeeToBuyer=false) sellerPayout = 1000 - 1000 - processingFee, clamped to 0 (breakdown line 126) — the seller nets nothing. There's no minimum-sale-price gate preventing this.
recommendation: Decide the intended interaction: either apply the Top Seller discount to the floor too (e.g. floor*(1-discount)) so the tier still benefits, and/or enforce a minimum listing price so commission can never approach 100% of a tiny sale. At minimum document/flag in the Sell form that the R30 floor overrides the Top Seller discount on small sales.

verdict.reasoning:
Both code facts in the finding are accurate and the bad path is reachable. fee.calculator.ts:59-72 matches verbatim. The minimum settled price is only @Min(100) = R1.00: CreateListingDto.price (create-listing.dto.ts:31), offerAmount (create-offer.dto.ts:8) and counterAmount (counter-offer.dto.ts:5) are all @Min(100); listings.service.ts:127 only checks price truthiness, so there is no higher floor. Claim 2 is real: for a R10 sale (1000 cents) banded commission = 1000*0.09 = 90, which is < MIN_COMMISSION_CENTS (3000), so calculateCommission returns Math.min(3000,1000)=1000 = 100% of price; with passFeeToBuyer=false, sellerPayout = 1000-1000-processingFee, clamped to 0 at fee.calculator.ts:126, so the seller nets R0. Claim 1 is real: any sale whose banded commission lands under R30 returns the R30 floor for BOTH tiers, so the Top Seller 0.5% discount is discarded (e.g. R300 sale: Top Seller 2700-150=2550 < 3000 -> R30; non-Top-Seller 2700 < 3000 -> R30; identical).

However the severity is overstated. (a) The Sell form already discloses this: PriceBreakdown in frontend/app/listings/new/page.tsx:2368-2456 detects hitMinimum and renders "Platform commission (R30 minimum)" plus a live "Your payout" line and a "Minimum platform fee: R30 per sale" bullet, so the seller sees their (near-)R0 payout BEFORE listing and can decline — the finding's own primary recommendation ("document/flag in the Sell form") is already implemented. The "silently" framing is therefore inaccurate for the payout/floor. (b) This is a fee-math/UX edge case confined to sub-~R350 sales; it is no money loss to the platform, no security or data issue, and the seller is not deceived about their payout. The only genuinely undisclosed aspect is the Top-Seller-discount-erasure interaction (the frontend calcCommissionCents at lines 56-72 has no isTopSeller branch and never shows the discount anywhere, so a Top Seller sees the same R30 they will actually pay). Real but minor.

title: Offer-based checkout doesn't re-check listing availability and races on the offer→transaction unique link, allowing duplicate reservations/checkouts
description: In create(), the offer branch validates only offer.status==='ACCEPTED' and TAKE_A_SHOT type; it deliberately skips the listing.status==='ACTIVE' check that the BUY_NOW branch enforces (lines 82-88). So an accepted offer can be taken to checkout even if the listing already moved to PAYMENT_PENDING/SOLD via another path, reserving it again (listing.update to PAYMENT_PENDING at 168-171) and creating a Peach checkout. Additionally, two concurrent checkout calls for the same accepted offer both pass the status read, both create Transaction rows and both create Peach checkout sessions; only at the final offer.update({status:'CONVERTED', transactionId}) does the @unique on Offer.transactionId (schema.prisma:1154) trip for the loser — but by then two payable Peach sessions and a duplicate reservation exist, and the buyer could pay both.
recommendation: For the offer branch, also require the listing to be ACTIVE (or at least not already PAYMENT_PENDING/SOLD/COMPLETED). Atomically claim the offer at the start with updateMany({ where: { id, status: 'ACCEPTED' }, data: { status: 'CONVERTING' } }) and proceed only when count===1, so only one checkout can ever be created per accepted offer.

verdict.reasoning:
VERIFIED REAL, with one mechanism claim in the finding being incorrect.

Confirmed true:
1. backend/src/payments/transactions.service.ts:79-89 — the offer branch checks only rawOffer.status==='ACCEPTED', offer ownership, and listingType==='TAKE_A_SHOT'. It deliberately skips the `if (listing.status !== 'ACTIVE')` guard that the else/BUY_NOW branch enforces at lines 83-85.
2. Accepting an offer never changes listing status. In backend/src/offers/offers.service.ts, accept() (124-145), acceptCounter() (215-234), and the auto-accept path in submit() (100-109) leave listing.status untouched; the listing stays ACTIVE. And @@unique([listingId, buyerId]) (schema.prisma:1159) only limits one offer per buyer per listing, so two DIFFERENT buyers can each hold an ACCEPTED offer on the same TAKE_A_SHOT listing.
3. No concurrency control on POST /transactions. transactions.controller.ts:68-69 has only @UseGuards(ClerkOrTokenGuard) — no @Throttle. The only limiter is the global APP_GUARD ThrottlerGuard at 60/min/user (app.module.ts:54-92), which does NOT stop 2 near-simultaneous requests.
4. Two concurrent create() calls for the same accepted offer both pass the status read, both set listing to PAYMENT_PENDING (168-171), both create Transaction rows (174-201), and both create payable Peach checkout sessions (222-228). The Transaction model has NO unique/partial index on listingId (schema.prisma:689-744), so the DB does not block two live transactions per listing.
5. Payment is genuinely double-payable: verifyResult (264-272) and handlePeachWebhook (306-317) are keyed on the individual tx.id (merchantTransactionId) and guard idempotency only via per-transaction tx.paidAt. markPaid (940-955) sets listing to SOLD but there is NO listing-already-SOLD check rejecting the second payment — so both transactions reach HELD (or RELEASED immediately if PRIVATE_ARRANGE, 992-1027). Result: buyer charged twice for one item, requiring a manual Peach refund; or two distinct buyers each pay for one item (second buyer's funds held with no goods).

Finding got WRONG: the claim that "the @unique on Offer.transactionId (schema.prisma:1154) trips for the loser." In the same-offer race both create() calls run offer.update WHERE id = offerRecord.id (246-249) — they update the SAME row, so setting transactionId twice does not violate a unique constraint (which only forbids two different rows sharing a value). Both updates succeed; the offer just ends up pointing at the last tx. So there is no partial protection — the issue is slightly worse than described, and the stated unique-constraint safety net does not exist.

Net: genuinely exploitable double-sell / double-charge with zero mitigating guard on a regulated firearms-marketplace money path. The recommended fix (require listing ACTIVE in the offer branch + atomic claim via updateMany({where:{id,status:'ACCEPTED'},data:{status:'CONVERTING'}}) and proceed only when count===1, plus a partial unique index on active transactions per listing) is correct.

title: Peach payment webhook accepts forged 'payment succeeded' events — fail-open signature check + no out-of-band verification = free orders / payout fraud
description: The Peach webhook POST /api/payments/webhook/peach is the endpoint that flips a Transaction to paid (paymentStatus HELD) and the Listing to SOLD, which starts the seller-payout/dispatch flow. It has NO auth guard (only @HttpCode(200)). Its only protection is verifyWebhookSignature(), which FAILS OPEN: if process.env.PEACH_WEBHOOK_SECRET is unset it returns true and processes the body unauthenticated. I confirmed the live backend/.env contains PEACH_ENTITY_ID, PEACH_ACCESS_TOKEN and PEACH_BASE_URL but NOT PEACH_WEBHOOK_SECRET — so the check is currently fail-open in production. The handler trusts the request body entirely: parseWebhookPayload reads merchantTransactionId (which is our own Transaction.id, exposed to the buyer at checkout) and the success code from body['result.code']; markPaid() never calls Peach to confirm the payment and never re-validates the amount against the transaction. So an unauthenticated attacker can POST {"merchantTransactionId":"<known-tx-id>","result.code":"000.000.000","amount":"..."} and the order is marked paid without any real payment. Secondary defect: even if the secret WERE set, the controller computes the HMAC over JSON.stringify(@Body()) (a re-serialized parse of the body, transactions.controller.ts line 301) instead of the true raw bytes Peach signed — main.ts enables rawBody:true but this route ignores it — so enabling the secret would reject every legitimate webhook (key-order/whitespace/unicode differences) while today every forged webhook is accepted.
evidence: peach.service.ts:298-302 `verifyWebhookSignature(rawBody, providedSignature){ const secret = process.env.PEACH_WEBHOOK_SECRET; if (!secret) { return true; // dev / not configured — allow through }`. transactions.controller.ts:301 `const rawBody = JSON.stringify(body);` then :302 `const valid = this.txService.verifyPeachWebhook(rawBody, signature);`. peach.service.ts:270-280 parseWebhookPayload reads merchantTransactionId/result.code straight from body; :279 `isSuccess: SUCCESS_PATTERN.test(resultCode)`. transactions.service.ts:319-320 `if (result.isSuccess) { await this.markPaid(tx.id, result.paymentId, result.resultCode, tx.listing);` — markPaid (926-955) sets paymentStatus HELD + listing SOLD with no amount check and no callback to Peach. Live .env grep returned PEACH_ENTITY_ID/PEACH_ACCESS_TOKEN/PEACH_BASE_URL only — PEACH_WEBHOOK_SECRET absent.
recommendation: Before launch: (1) make the check fail-CLOSED — if PEACH_WEBHOOK_SECRET is unset in production, reject/log, never process; (2) set the real PEACH_WEBHOOK_SECRET and verify HMAC over req.rawBody (already available via rawBody:true) NOT JSON.stringify(body); (3) regardless of signature, treat the webhook as a trigger only and confirm status out-of-band by calling Peach's payment-status API with the stored paymentId, and assert the returned amount/currency equals the Transaction before markPaid; (4) add a unique idempotency guard on peachPaymentId.

verdict.reasoning: Traced the full path and every specific claim holds. (1) PaymentsWebhookController.peachWebhook (transactions.controller.ts:284-310) is registered (payments.module.ts:27) and carries ONLY @HttpCode(200) — no ClerkGuard/ClerkOrTokenGuard, unlike every other money-touching route in the same file. (2) verifyWebhookSignature (peach.service.ts:298-302) returns true when PEACH_WEBHOOK_SECRET is unset — fail-open. (3) backend/.env confirms only PEACH_ENTITY_ID, PEACH_ACCESS_TOKEN, PEACH_BASE_URL — PEACH_WEBHOOK_SECRET is absent, so the check currently accepts everything. (4) parseWebhookPayload (peach.service.ts:270-281) reads merchantTransactionId and result.code straight from the attacker-controlled body; isSuccess is just SUCCESS_PATTERN.test(resultCode). (5) handlePeachWebhook (transactions.service.ts:299-325) finds the tx by the supplied id and, on isSuccess, calls markPaid with NO callback to Peach and NO amount/currency check. (6) markPaid (transactions.service.ts:926-955) sets paymentStatus HELD + paidAt and flips the listing to SOLD; for PRIVATE_ARRANGE it then RELEASES funds immediately and reveals both parties' contact PII (maybeImmediatePayout, 992-1047). (7) The buyer/attacker knows the exact merchantTransactionId because create() returns transactionId: tx.id (transactions.service.ts:254) and embeds it in the result URL (line 219). So an unauthenticated POST of {"merchantTransactionId":"<own-tx-id>","result.code":"000.000.000"} marks a real order paid with no payment. Mitigations I checked and ruled out: the global ThrottlerGuard (app.module.ts:54-92, 60/min) only rate-limits and does not authenticate — one forged request per tx suffices; the tx.paidAt idempotency guard (line 314) only blocks reprocessing, not the initial forge; peachPaymentId is String? with @@index but NOT @unique (schema.prisma:721,878). A correct out-of-band path DOES exist (verifyResult -> peach.verifyPayment, 264-287), but it is a separate authenticated-ish path and does not protect the webhook — it merely proves the team knows how to verify and didn't here. Secondary defect also confirmed: main.ts:18 enables rawBody:true but the controller computes the HMAC over JSON.stringify(body) (transactions.controller.ts:301), not req.rawBody, so enabling the secret would likely reject legitimate Peach webhooks (key-order/whitespace). Net: unauthenticated forging of paid orders and immediate-payout fraud — money loss + cross-user PII reveal.

title: Ask-GG accepts arbitrary client-supplied image URLs and forwards them to the Anthropic API as fetchable image sources (SSRF / content-injection, no host allowlist)
description: POST /api/ask-gg/messages accepts imageUrls: string[] directly from the authenticated client. The only validation is 'is a non-empty string' and a per-tier count cap — there is NO check that the URL is a Cloudinary URL (the intended source from POST /ask-gg/uploads). These URLs are persisted on the message and later sent to Anthropic as image content blocks of type 'url' ({ type:'image', source:{ type:'url', url } }), which causes Anthropic's servers to fetch the attacker-chosen URL. This is a server-side-request-forgery via the upstream provider plus a cost/abuse vector: any signed-in user can make the platform's Claude calls fetch and ingest arbitrary remote content (private image hosts, tracking/canary URLs, oversized payloads to inflate token cost). Because the value is stored and replayed on every subsequent turn of the conversation, it is durable. I confirmed no allowlist exists anywhere in the ask-gg module (grep for cloudinary/new URL/allowlist returned nothing).
evidence: ask-gg.service.ts:95-97 `const imageUrls = (input.imageUrls ?? []).filter((u) => typeof u === 'string' && u.length > 0);` — no host/scheme check. ask-gg-claude.service.ts:363-366 `const imageBlocks = urls.map((url) => ({ type: 'image' as const, source: { type: 'url' as const, url } }));`. ask-gg.controller.ts:64 body type `imageUrls?: string[]` passed straight to askGg.sendMessage. Grep for `cloudinary|new URL(|allowlist` in ask-gg/ → no matches.
recommendation: Validate every entry of imageUrls with new URL(u): require https and hostname ending in res.cloudinary.com (or your exact Cloudinary delivery host); reject anything else with 400. Prefer to ignore client URLs entirely and instead reference the Cloudinary public_ids returned by /ask-gg/uploads so the client can never inject a foreign URL.

verdict.reasoning:
The core technical claim is verified. POST /api/ask-gg/messages (ask-gg.controller.ts:56-68) types the body as an inline interface { imageUrls?: string[] } and passes it straight to sendMessage. There is NO DTO class, so the global ValidationPipe({ whitelist: true }) in main.ts:31-37 is a no-op for this body (whitelist only validates class-validator-decorated classes; an inline TS interface erases at compile time). In ask-gg.service.ts:95-97 the only check is `typeof u === 'string' && u.length > 0` — no scheme/host allowlist. Grep for cloudinary|res.cloudinary|new URL|allowlist|isCloudinary in backend/src/ask-gg returns only comments and the CloudinaryService import; no server-side enforcement that the URL is a Cloudinary URL — that contract lives only in the frontend upload flow. The strings are persisted on the message (service.ts:156-163) and rebuilt into Claude history on every turn (service.ts:168-177), then sent to Anthropic as fetchable image sources `{ type:'image', source:{ type:'url', url } }` (ask-gg-claude.service.ts:363-366). So it is durable and replayed, exactly as described.

However the HIGH rating is overstated. This is NOT classic SSRF against the platform's own infrastructure: the fetch egresses from Anthropic's servers, not the Gun Galore VPS, so an attacker cannot reach 169.254.169.254 metadata, localhost, or the Vultr private network — the property that normally makes SSRF critical does not apply. Realistic harms are bounded: (1) cost/token-inflation abuse is capped by the per-tier photo cap of <=10/message (maxPhotosPerRequest), the per-IP throttle of 30 msg/min (controller:55), and per-user quotas (FREE 5/30d, MEMBER 20/hr, PRO 60/hr in ask-gg-quota.service.ts); (2) request-laundering / canary-token pinging via Anthropic IPs; (3) arbitrary remote image content-injection — Anthropic itself enforces image type/size limits, capping payload abuse. Auth is required (ClerkGuard, controller:43), so not anonymous. It is a genuine input-validation hardening gap that should be fixed pre-launch (validate https + Cloudinary host, or reference public_ids), but it does not breach the platform's own trust boundary and the cost vector is already multiply throttled — MEDIUM, not HIGH.

title: Express 'trust proxy' is never set, so the per-IP throttler keys every request to the nginx upstream IP — rate limits do not isolate users or attackers
description: @nestjs/throttler's default tracker uses req.ip. The app is deployed behind nginx on the Vultr VPS but main.ts never calls app.set('trust proxy', ...) (grep for trust proxy across backend/src returns nothing). With trust proxy off, Express reports req.ip as the nginx upstream address (e.g. 127.0.0.1) for ALL traffic, so every client shares ONE throttler bucket. Consequence: the documented per-route limits (auth/KYC/ask-gg/actions/range-estimator) cannot distinguish an attacker from legitimate users — a single abuser fills the shared bucket (denying everyone) and, conversely, the limits provide no per-attacker isolation for brute-force/cost-abuse. This undermines every @Throttle in the codebase, including the cost-DoS guards on the Anthropic-backed endpoints. (Note: the action-tokens controller's own reqIp() does read X-Forwarded-For, but it is used only for audit logging of consumedFromIp, not for throttling.)
evidence: main.ts has no `trust proxy` call anywhere (only setGlobalPrefix, useGlobalPipes, enableCors). Grep `trust proxy|trustProxy|set('trust` across backend/src → No matches found. app.module.ts:54-55 ThrottlerModule.forRoot([{ name:'default', ttl:60_000, limit:60 }]) with default tracker (req.ip). Default ThrottlerGuard.getTracker returns req.ip.
recommendation: In main.ts set the trust-proxy hop count to match nginx, e.g. app.set('trust proxy', 1) (use a fixed number of hops, not 'true', to prevent XFF spoofing past your own proxy). Verify req.ip then reflects the real client. Consider a custom getTracker that uses the Clerk user id for authenticated routes so abuse is bounded per account, not per shared IP.

verdict.reasoning:
VERIFIED REAL. I traced the full path:

1. backend/src/main.ts (lines 16-78): bootstrap calls only setGlobalPrefix, useGlobalPipes, enableCors, body parsers, listen. NO app.set('trust proxy', ...). Grep across all of backend/src for `app.set|trust|trustProxy|getHttpAdapter().getInstance()` returns nothing relevant — Express trust proxy is left at its default of false.

2. backend/src/app.module.ts:54-56 registers ThrottlerModule.forRoot([{ name:'default', ttl:60_000, limit:60 }]) with the stock ThrottlerGuard as APP_GUARD (line 92). There is exactly ONE forRoot, no custom getTracker / generateKey / skipIf anywhere in the codebase.

3. The installed package confirms the default tracker: backend/node_modules/@nestjs/throttler/dist/throttler.guard.js:141-143 `async getTracker(req){ return req.ip; }`. So every bucket keys on req.ip.

4. With trust proxy=false behind nginx, req.ip = the immediate TCP peer = nginx. CLAUDE.md:153 documents "Nginx + PM2" hosting and main.ts:74-76 listens on localhost:${PORT}, so nginx proxies over loopback and req.ip collapses to 127.0.0.1 for ALL clients → one shared throttler bucket globally.

5. Independent corroboration that nginx forwards the real client header but the throttler ignores it: action-tokens.controller.ts:587-593 reqIp() explicitly parses req.headers['x-forwarded-for'] (and is used only for audit consumedFromIp, exactly as the finding states), proving XFF is present yet unused by the rate limiter.

6. The undermined @Throttle decorators guard genuine abuse surfaces: SMS action-token consumption (action-tokens.controller.ts:112-288, limits 6-10/min — token brute-force/replay defense-in-depth), Anthropic-cost endpoints (ask-gg.controller.ts:55/87/132, range-estimator.controller.ts:39 — cost DoS), offers (5/min), KYC, public user lookups. All now share a single bucket.

Net effect: a single source at 60/min trips the global default bucket for every user (shared-bucket DoS), and per-attacker isolation on paid AI endpoints is lost. The finding's recommendation (set a FIXED hop count `trust proxy`, 1, not `true`, to avoid XFF spoofing) is correct. One nuance worth noting for calibration: action tokens are cryptographic single-use values, so per-IP throttling was never the sole anti-guess defense — but it's still nullified defense-in-depth, and the shared-bucket denial + loss of cost-control are real. No money loss / data leak / PII exposure, so not CRITICAL.

title: GET /actions/:token (unauthenticated SMS-link resolver) is @SkipThrottle and the brute-force lockout never increments on this path
description: The token here is the sole auth credential for unauthenticated offer/auction/dispatch/checkout actions. The resolve endpoint carries @SkipThrottle() (no rate limit at all) and resolve() does not call markInvalid on a miss — so the per-token invalidAttempts lockout (MAX 5) is only ever incremented by the POST handlers via runAction, never by GET resolves. The mitigating factor is genuine: tokens are 128-bit CSPRNG (randomBytes(16) base64url), so blind enumeration is infeasible and this is not a practical breach. But combined with the trust-proxy defect above (the POST throttles are also weakened) the only remaining brute-force barrier is the per-token counter, which an attacker probing via the unthrottled GET can sidestep for reconnaissance, and an unthrottled GET is also a free amplification/DoS surface (each call does several DB reads + a service call for auction state).
evidence: action-tokens.controller.ts:73-75 `@Get(':token') @SkipThrottle() async resolve(...)`. action-tokens.service.ts:126-130 on not-found it throws NotFoundException with NO markInvalid call; markInvalid (202-212) is only invoked from runAction (247) on the POST paths. Token entropy: TOKEN_BYTES=16 (line 50), generateTokenString uses crypto.randomBytes (267-272).
recommendation: Remove @SkipThrottle on GET /actions/:token and apply a modest @Throttle (e.g. 30/min) so the resolver is bounded once trust-proxy is fixed; keep the 64-char length pre-check. Optionally rate-limit per-token-prefix to blunt enumeration amplification.

verdict.reasoning:
Facts verified in C:\dev\gun-galore (the OneDrive tree is a stale copy — I confirmed against the real repo). The cited code is accurate: action-tokens.controller.ts:73-74 `@Get(':token') @SkipThrottle()`; service resolve() (119-156) throws NotFoundException on a miss (126-130) with no markInvalid; markInvalid is only called from runAction (247) on POST paths; tokens are 128-bit CSPRNG (TOKEN_BYTES=16, randomBytes base64url, 267-272). I also confirmed trust proxy is NOT set in main.ts (no app.set('trust proxy')), so the global ThrottlerGuard (app.module.ts:54-55, single 60/min bucket, default getTracker=req.ip) does collapse to nginx's 127.0.0.1 behind the proxy — the 'trust-proxy defect above' the finding leans on is real, but it is a SEPARATE finding.

However the finding's CORE mechanic is wrong. (1) Adding markInvalid to the GET miss path would be a no-op: markInvalid (203-211) does update where {token} and SILENTLY swallows the throw for a non-existent row, so it never increments on misses regardless of caller. (2) The per-token invalidAttempts lockout (MAX 5, checked at 131) is by design a defense against cross-purpose probing of an ALREADY-MINTED token via the POST handlers — it was never an enumeration control, so 'an attacker probing via the unthrottled GET can sidestep it for reconnaissance' describes bypassing a control that doesn't apply on that axis. (3) With 128-bit tokens blind enumeration is infeasible (the finding concedes this), and resolve() has a length>64 pre-check (120) gating the DB hit.

The only genuine residual is a modest hardening gap: an unauthenticated, fully unthrottled GET doing 1-3 indexed point-lookups per call (and getAuctionState adds 2 more for AUCTION_BID, auctions.service.ts:62-101) is a free DoS-amplification surface, made worse by the unset trust proxy meaning no effective per-IP ceiling anywhere. That is real but minor (bounded by nginx-level limits, no money/data/privacy impact, no plausible auth bypass). Recommendation to swap @SkipThrottle for a modest @Throttle is reasonable. Net: factually accurate observations, but the stated brute-force/reconnaissance mechanism is a false positive; what's left is LOW-severity hardening, not MEDIUM.

title: Anonymous, cost-bearing AI endpoint (range-estimator) is throttled only per-IP and authorized by a client-rotatable device header — cost-DoS exposure
description: POST /api/hunt-ballistics/estimate-range is fully anonymous (only an X-Device-Id header, which the caller supplies and can rotate at will) and every call makes a paid Anthropic vision request (~$0.01 Sonnet, up to ~$0.05 on Opus fallback per the controller comment). The sole guard is @Throttle 10/min, which is per-IP — and per finding #3 the per-IP tracker is broken behind nginx (no trust proxy), so the limit is either a single shared global bucket or otherwise misattributed. An attacker rotating IPs (or exploiting the shared-bucket misconfig) can drive sustained Anthropic spend with no account and no payment. The device id is validated only for length >= 8, not throttled on.
evidence: range-estimator.controller.ts:39 `@Throttle({ default: { limit: 10, ttl: 60_000 } })`; :47-48 auth is `@Headers('x-device-id') deviceId`; :61-65 only check `if (!deviceId || deviceId.length < 8)`. Class comment lines 30-31: 'each call hits the Anthropic API and costs real money (~$0.01 Sonnet, ~$0.05 if Opus fallback fires)'.
recommendation: Add a per-device-id throttle (and/or a global daily spend ceiling / circuit-breaker) in addition to per-IP, fix trust proxy so the per-IP limit actually works, and consider requiring a lightweight signed app-attestation token rather than a free-text device id for this paid endpoint.

verdict.reasoning:
Verified end-to-end. The endpoint and its protections are exactly as described, with one correction to the exploit framing.

CONFIRMED FACTS:
1. Anonymous + paid: range-estimator.controller.ts:35-65 — POST /api/hunt-ballistics/estimate-range has no auth. The only APP_GUARD in app.module.ts:92 is ThrottlerGuard (no global Clerk/AuthGuard), and hunt-ballistics.module.ts:24 comment states "no guard at this level." Auth is only @Headers('x-device-id') with a length>=8 check (controller :61). Every call reaches RangeEstimatorClaudeService.estimate() which makes a real Anthropic vision call (range-estimator-claude.service.ts:450 Sonnet, :465 Opus fallback when confidence < 0.7). Sends the full base64 image (:516), so per-call cost is dominated by image input tokens and can exceed the ~$0.01 comment.
2. Trust-proxy IS broken: main.ts is a NestExpressApplication (line 17) with NO app.set('trust proxy', …) anywhere. @nestjs/throttler ^6.5.0 (package.json) default getTracker() returns req.ip; with trust proxy off, Express ignores X-Forwarded-For and req.ip is the socket peer — which behind nginx proxy_pass-to-localhost is 127.0.0.1 for every request. So @Throttle({default:{limit:10,ttl:60_000}}) (controller :39) collapses to ONE shared global 10/min bucket, not per-IP. No custom tracker reads X-Forwarded-For (grep found only an unrelated logging use in action-tokens.controller.ts:589).
3. No spend ceiling / circuit-breaker: grep for daily/monthly spend, budget, circuit-breaker, cost ceiling found nothing in backend/src. Cost is computed and logged only (claude.service estimateCostUsd / service.ts:118).

CORRECTION TO THE FINDING'S EXPLOIT MECHANISM: the finding says an attacker can "rotate IPs (or device ids) to drive sustained spend." Because the bucket is accidentally GLOBAL, rotating IPs/devices does NOT raise throughput — everyone shares the same 10/min bucket, so total system-wide spend is capped (~10 calls/min → roughly $150–$290/day Sonnet-only, ~$720/day Opus-worst-case). So this is bounded, not an unbounded cost-DoS. The free-text device id provides no throttling key, but the per-IP defect here makes the limit STRICTER globally rather than wide-open.

NET: still a real, valid issue — an anonymous paid AI endpoint with (a) no per-identity throttle, (b) a misconfigured proxy trust that turns the rate limit into a single app-wide bucket (which also lets one abuser DoS the feature for all legitimate Hunt Ballistics users), and (c) no spend ceiling/circuit-breaker. The recommendations (fix trust proxy, add per-device throttle + global daily ceiling/circuit-breaker, app-attestation) are correct. Severity MEDIUM is right: real but bounded spend, easy feature-DoS, no data/security breach, no user money loss, not launch-blocking.

title: Dealer-verification upload omits the content-type/size ParseFilePipe that every other upload uses
description: POST /api/:id/dealer-verification (FileFieldsInterceptor for saps534/stockRegister/firearmSerial) declares @UploadedFiles() with NO ParseFilePipe — unlike the KYC, listings, raffles, ask-gg and range-estimator uploads which all attach MaxFileSizeValidator + FileTypeValidator. Only a multer fileSize limit (10MB) is enforced; content-type is unvalidated at the controller. Real-world impact is contained because the endpoint is ClerkGuard-protected and seller-scoped, and the buffers are handed to Cloudinary.uploadImage (resource_type image) which rejects non-images server-side — so a malicious non-image is bounced downstream rather than stored. Still worth aligning for defence-in-depth and consistent error messaging.
evidence: transactions.controller.ts:137-148 FileFieldsInterceptor with only `{ limits: { fileSize: 10*1024*1024 } }`; :153 `@UploadedFiles() files: {...}` — no ParseFilePipe/validators. Contrast users.controller.ts:323-330 and ask-gg.controller.ts:97-105 which wrap @UploadedFile(s) in ParseFilePipe with FileTypeValidator(/image\/(jpeg|png|webp).../).
recommendation: Wrap the three fields with the same FileTypeValidator(/^image\/(jpeg|png|webp)$/) + MaxFileSizeValidator pattern used elsewhere (or validate file.mimetype in uploadAndScore before the Cloudinary call) so non-image payloads are rejected at the edge with a clear 400.

verdict.reasoning:
Every factual claim in the finding is verified against the code, and the severity (LOW) is correctly rated and not overstated.

CONFIRMED FACTS:
- backend/src/payments/transactions.controller.ts:150-158: uploadDealerVerification declares `@UploadedFiles() files: {...}` with NO ParseFilePipe. The FileFieldsInterceptor at :138-148 enforces ONLY `{ limits: { fileSize: 10 * 1024 * 1024 } }` — no content-type validation at the edge.
- The inconsistency is real: 5 sibling controllers wrap uploads in ParseFilePipe + FileTypeValidator — users/KYC (users.controller.ts:323-330, regex image/(jpeg|png|webp)|application/pdf), ask-gg (ask-gg.controller.ts:97-105), plus listings, raffles, and range-estimator (all matched on ParseFilePipe).

DOWNSTREAM MITIGATION IS REAL (so impact is contained, as the finding states):
- The three file buffers are passed ONLY to CloudinaryService.uploadImage (dealer-verification.service.ts:169-171) and nowhere else — no disk write, no local buffer parsing, no shell.
- cloudinary.service.ts:33 sets `resource_type: 'image'`, so Cloudinary rejects a non-image server-side; the reject handler at :40 throws, propagating an error rather than storing/serving anything malicious.
- The endpoint is authenticated (@UseGuards(ClerkGuard), :136) and seller-scoped in the service (dealer-verification.service.ts:147-148: `tx.seller.clerkId !== sellerClerkId` throws), plus gated to firearm DEALER_TRANSFER transactions only (:150-157). Not an unauthenticated or cross-user surface.
- Size IS bounded (10MB multer limit), so there is no unbounded-upload angle; only content-type validation is missing at the controller edge.

VERDICT: The finding accurately describes a genuine defence-in-depth / consistency gap and honestly self-characterises the real-world impact as contained by the Cloudinary `resource_type: image` rejection. There is no security breach, money loss, data leak, or broken core flow. LOW is the correct severity. Recommendation (align the three fields with the same FileTypeValidator pattern, or validate file.mimetype before the Cloudinary call) is sound. Real but minor — keep at LOW.

title: Prod schema is applied via `prisma db push --accept-data-loss` on every deploy; migration history is abandoned and badly drifted from schema.prisma
description: The documented deploy procedure runs `npx prisma db push --accept-data-loss` against production Postgres (CLAUDE.md:76). `db push` does NOT use the migrations folder — it diffs schema.prisma directly against the live DB and applies whatever DDL it computes, with `--accept-data-loss` pre-authorising any destructive step (DROP COLUMN, DROP TABLE, type narrowing, NOT NULL additions) with zero prompt and no migration file to review. The migrations directory is now massively divergent from the schema: there are NO migrations for Notification, FeaturedSlot/FeaturedAuction/FeaturedSlotBid, ActionToken, Subscription/SubscriptionCharge, AskGg* (5 models), PushSubscription, or WatchedListing — all of which exist in schema.prisma and in prod. Conversely the add_raffles migration (20260518162012/migration.sql:13-21) creates Raffle columns `isFirearm` and `marginPercent` that no longer exist in the current Raffle model, proving the two have silently diverged. This means: (a) there is no reviewable record of what DDL actually ran in prod, (b) `prisma migrate status` is meaningless, (c) prod and any fresh-from-migrations DB are structurally different, and (d) a single mistaken schema edit (rename/remove a column on Transaction or User) becomes irreversible silent data loss on the next deploy because `--accept-data-loss` won't stop it.
evidence: CLAUDE.md:76 `npx prisma db push --accept-data-loss  # tsvector GENERATED cols get re-created by onModuleInit`. migrations/ ends at 20260518162012_add_raffles + two unrelated ballistics migrations; grep for Notification|FeaturedSlot|ActionToken|Subscription|AskGg|PushSubscription|WatchedListing across migrations/ returns 'No files found'. add_raffles/migration.sql:21 still defines `"marginPercent" DOUBLE PRECISION NOT NULL` which is absent from the current Raffle model.
recommendation: Stop using `db push --accept-data-loss` for prod. Baseline the current prod schema with `prisma migrate diff` to generate one catch-up migration, commit it, then switch the deploy to `prisma migrate deploy` (which only applies committed, reviewed migrations and never silently drops data). Keep the tsvector GENERATED columns as a hand-written SQL step inside a migration (or via onModuleInit, see separate finding) so they survive. At minimum, drop `--accept-data-loss` so a destructive diff aborts the deploy instead of executing.

verdict.reasoning: All factual claims verified true. (1) DEPLOY MECHANISM: CLAUDE.md:76 literally runs `npx prisma db push --accept-data-loss` as the prod schema step; a repo-wide grep shows `prisma migrate deploy` appears NOWHERE — `db push` is the only schema-application path. (2) DRIFT PROVEN: add_raffles/migration.sql:18,20 create Raffle columns `isFirearm` and `marginPercent DOUBLE PRECISION NOT NULL`, but the current Raffle model (schema.prisma:1263+) has neither marginPercent nor commissionPercent (it moved to an itemCostCents pricing model and also dropped endTime/skillQuestion/skillAnswer). (3) MISSING MIGRATIONS: a search across all 13 migration.sql files for Notification/FeaturedSlot/ActionToken/Subscription/AskGg/PushSubscription/WatchedListing returns NO matches, yet all exist in schema.prisma (lines 450,1213,1244,1612,1863,2029,2065,2093-2180). Git log confirms commits 4ce5d2e (featured/subscriptions) and a2e14d9 (Ask GG) edited schema.prisma but never touched the migrations dir; only the two ballistics commits added migrations afterward. (4) The risk is acknowledged in-tree: schema.prisma:2259 and ask-gg-kb.service.ts:22 reference `db push` dropping columns under --accept-data-loss. SEVERITY DOWNGRADE rationale: the --accept-data-loss flag is not gratuitous — it exists for three Postgres tsvector GENERATED columns (AskGgKbEntry.searchTsv, HuntPdfPage.textTsv, ReloadingManualPage.textTsv) that Prisma can't model and tries to DROP each push; onModuleInit re-creates them and Postgres re-derives them from source text, so those specific drops are genuinely lossless. The financial/user tables (User:207, Transaction:689, Offer:1137, Bid:1169) carry no such columns and marketplace search uses Meilisearch, not tsvector — so routine deploys are NOT actively destroying money/user data today. This is a latent landmine (no reviewable DDL, migrate status meaningless, no rollback, silent irreversible loss the moment anyone renames/removes a populated column) rather than an in-progress breach. That is squarely HIGH ('an incident is likely'), not present-tense CRITICAL ('money/data loss' happening now). The recommendation is sound.

title: Clerk `user.deleted` webhook hard-deletes the User row; cascade wipes Subscription + SubscriptionCharge billing history (SARS/POPIA retention) and integrity depends on incidental Restrict FKs
description: The Clerk webhook handler calls `usersService.deleteByClerkId(data.id)` → `prisma.user.deleteMany({ where: { clerkId } })`, a HARD delete of the user row driven by an external event (any Clerk-side account deletion, or anyone who can forge a verified webhook). Whether this destroys retained financial records depends entirely on which child relations happen to be declared Cascade vs Restrict — there is no soft-delete and no explicit retention guard. The relations that DO cascade from User include `Subscription` (schema.prisma:2032) and, transitively, `SubscriptionCharge` (2068) — i.e. the recurring-billing charge ledger (amountCents, peachPaymentId, status SUCCEEDED/REFUNDED). For a user who subscribed to Ask GG but never listed/transacted/bid, the delete SUCCEEDS and silently erases their entire subscription payment history, which is exactly the kind of financial record SARS requires retained for 5 years. AskGgConversation/Message/Usage (cost/spend audit) are also cascade-wiped. For users WITH a Listing/Transaction/Bid/Offer/Rating, the delete instead throws a Prisma P2003 FK violation (those relations default to Restrict) — and webhooks.controller.ts:82 has no try/catch, so the webhook 500s and Clerk retries forever. So the same code path is either an unhandled crash-loop or silent financial-record destruction, depending only on incidental relation config.
evidence: users.service.ts:152 `await this.prisma.user.deleteMany({ where: { clerkId } });`. webhooks.controller.ts:82 `await this.usersService.deleteByClerkId(data.id);` (no error handling). schema.prisma:2032 Subscription.user `onDelete: Cascade`; 2068 SubscriptionCharge.subscription `onDelete: Cascade` → User delete cascades to charge ledger.
recommendation: Never hard-delete a User that has any financial footprint. On `user.deleted`, anonymise/soft-delete instead: set isBanned/a deletedAt flag, null out PII (firstName/lastName/phone/email/idNumberEncrypted), and KEEP Transaction, Subscription, SubscriptionCharge, and AdminAuditEvent rows. Change Subscription/SubscriptionCharge off `onDelete: Cascade` from User (use Restrict or SetNull) so billing history can never be cascade-erased. Wrap the webhook call in try/catch so a delete that's correctly blocked by Restrict doesn't crash-loop Clerk retries.

verdict.reasoning:
Verified against the actual code. The defect is REAL but the CRITICAL rating is OVERSTATED because its headline scenario is not yet reachable.

CONFIRMED FACTS:
- webhooks.controller.ts:81-83 calls deleteByClerkId on `user.deleted` with NO try/catch; users.service.ts:152 is a raw hard delete `prisma.user.deleteMany({ where: { clerkId } })`. grep confirms this is the ONLY caller (no admin/internal path).
- Cascade chain is real: Subscription.user onDelete: Cascade (schema.prisma:2032) -> SubscriptionCharge.subscription onDelete: Cascade (2068); also AskGgConversation/Message/Usage onDelete: Cascade (2096/2122/2183).
- Restrict-by-default is real: Transaction.buyer/seller (696/698), Listing.seller (526), Rating.rater/rated (1113/1115), Offer.buyer (1142), Bid.bidder (1174) all declare the User relation with NO onDelete, so Prisma defaults to Restrict. A user with any marketplace footprint throws P2003; with no try/catch the handler 500s and svix retries. The bifurcated behavior (silent-wipe vs crash-loop) is accurately described.
- The schema HAS isBanned/bannedAt (User:281-282), so the recommended anonymise/soft-delete is viable.

WHY OVERSTATED (the load-bearing correction): The CRITICAL claim rests on silent destruction of the SubscriptionCharge billing ledger (a SARS-retained financial record). But there is ZERO code in backend/src that ever creates a Subscription or SubscriptionCharge row: grep for `subscriptionCharge`/`SubscriptionCharge` = no files; grep for `subscription.create|upsert|update`/`prisma.subscription` = no matches; there is no subscriptions module/controller; the admin module references neither `Subscription` nor `subscriptionTier`. Schema comments confirm the billing rail is unbuilt ("when Peach recurring billing lands...", User.peachCustomerId "NULL until the subscription billing rail goes live - operator-side blocker"). So the charge ledger is always EMPTY today; the financial-record-loss cannot occur in the current codebase. It is a genuine LATENT landmine that activates the day subscriptions ship.

Other minor overstatements: the data that IS actively cascade-wiped is AskGg chat history + usage/cost telemetry (Ask GG is live), which is not a SARS financial record. "Anyone who can forge a verified webhook" requires possession of CLERK_WEBHOOK_SECRET (svix HMAC verified at controller.ts:48-54), not an open endpoint. AdminAuditEvent (schema:1033) references AdminUser, not the marketplace User, and resourceId is free-text with no FK, so it is NOT cascade-affected - the "keep AdminAuditEvent" recommendation is moot.

NET: The live, reachable bug today is the unhandled P2003 crash-loop / failed-cleanup for any user with a marketplace footprint, plus an architecturally real but currently inert cascade onto financial tables. Real and worth fixing before launch (and the schema FK change is the right pre-emptive fix), but it is not a present money/data-loss CRITICAL. Rating HIGH.

title: Three runtime-added tsvector GENERATED columns + GIN indexes are dropped by every `db push --accept-data-loss` deploy and only re-created on next backend boot — search outage window + boot-order fragility
description: Three FTS artifacts are created OUTSIDE Prisma via $executeRawUnsafe in onModuleInit: AskGgKbEntry.searchTsv + AskGgKbEntry_searchTsv_idx, ReloadingManualPage.textTsv + its GIN index, and HuntPdfPage.textTsv + its GIN index. None are declared in schema.prisma, so on every deploy `prisma db push --accept-data-loss` computes them as 'extra' and DROPs them (accept-data-loss authorises the drop silently). They are only re-added when the NestJS process restarts and the relevant module's onModuleInit runs. The data itself survives (GENERATED ALWAYS columns repopulate from source text), so this is not permanent data loss — but: (1) between `prisma db push` (CLAUDE.md:76) and `pm2 reload gungalore-backend` (:79) the columns/indexes do not exist, so any FTS query in that window throws (the search code does raw `... @@ websearch_to_tsquery` against a now-missing column); (2) each onModuleInit swallows failures and only logs a warning (ask-gg-kb.service.ts:52-58), so if the DDL ever fails the app boots 'healthy' with search permanently degraded to a silent LIKE fallback and no alert; (3) re-creating a GIN index over a large ReloadingManualPage/HuntPdfPage corpus on every boot adds avoidable restart latency. The audit brief also referenced AskGgUsage.bulletLookupCount as a fourth drifted column — that column does not exist anywhere in the schema or codebase (grep returns no matches), so only these three tsvector artifacts are actually at risk.
