evidence: ask-gg-kb.service.ts:38-50 `ALTER TABLE "AskGgKbEntry" ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS "searchTsv" tsvector GENERATED ALWAYS AS (...) STORED;` then `CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS "AskGgKbEntry_searchTsv_idx" ... USING GIN`. schema.prisma:2252-2263 explicitly documents the drop-on-push behaviour and calls it 'safe'. ask-gg-kb.service.ts:52-58 catch only warns; query at :114-117 uses the column unconditionally.
recommendation: Move these tsvector columns + GIN indexes into a committed SQL migration (raw SQL is fully supported in a Prisma migration file) so `migrate deploy` creates them transactionally and `db push` never sees them as droppable — eliminating both the outage window and the boot-order dependency. If they must stay in onModuleInit, gate the deploy so the backend is reloaded BEFORE the app serves traffic, and surface a hard alert (not a swallowed warning) when the DDL fails so a silent LIKE-fallback degradation is caught.

verdict.reasoning:
VERIFIED REAL, but OVERSTATED at HIGH — correct level is MEDIUM.

Mechanism confirmed end-to-end:
1. The three tsvector GENERATED columns + GIN indexes are declared NOWHERE in committed schema/migrations. In schema.prisma `searchTsv`/`textTsv` appear only inside explanatory comments (lines 2252-2263, 2354-2359). Grep for tsvector|GENERATED ALWAYS|textTsv across all 14 migration dirs returns ZERO matches. They are created solely in onModuleInit: ask-gg-kb.service.ts:38-50, reloading.service.ts:72-80, hunt-pdf.service.ts:48-56.
2. Production deploy uses `npx prisma db push --accept-data-loss` (CLAUDE.md:76, with the literal comment "tsvector GENERATED cols get re-created by onModuleInit"), NOT `migrate deploy`. db push diffs live DB vs schema and silently drops the undeclared columns + dependent GIN indexes.
3. Re-creation only happens at next process boot (onModuleInit), which runs at `pm2 reload` (CLAUDE.md:79) AFTER db push (76) + generate (77) + npm run build (78). The window spans the whole backend build (tens of seconds+). CLAUDE.md:33-38 confirms pm2 reload is graceful (old worker keeps serving), so the OLD process services search queries against now-dropped columns for the entire window.
4. onModuleInit catches swallow DDL failures with only logger.warn (ask-gg-kb:52-58, reloading:84-92, hunt-pdf:58-64) — a failed DDL boots 'healthy' with search broken.

Where the finding is WRONG/overstated:
- Claim (2) 'silently degraded to a LIKE fallback' is FALSE. There is NO LIKE fallback anywhere. searchVerified (ask-gg-kb:100-123) and both searchPages use the tsvector column unconditionally in raw SQL; a missing column THROWS, not degrades. (The comment at ask-gg-kb:54 lies — code has no LIKE path.)
- Blast radius is narrow and transient: affected surfaces are Ask GG KB search-as-you-type, the Ask GG reloading-manual AI tool, and Hunt Ballistics iOS info-centre search — none are core marketplace/money/auth flows. The reloading-tool path is fully resilient: the outer catch in ask-gg-claude.service.ts:737-748 converts the thrown error into an is_error tool_result, so Claude just answers 'no data' (no 500). Only /ask-gg/kb/search (ask-gg.controller.ts:211) and /info-centre/search (hunt-pdf.controller.ts:46) raise raw 500s, and only during a controlled, infrequent deploy window, and only if a user searches in that minute.
- No data loss (GENERATED cols repopulate instantly from source text), no money/security/compliance impact.

This is genuine architectural fragility and the recommendation (move DDL into a committed migration) is correct, but 'a core flow is broken or an incident is likely' (HIGH) overstates a transient, self-healing, deploy-only degradation of auxiliary search surfaces. That is MEDIUM. The finding also correctly notes the phantom AskGgUsage.bulletLookupCount column does not exist.

title: User.phone has no unique constraint or index; uniqueness is enforced only by a racy app-code check, and phone routes security-sensitive SMS action tokens
description: `User.phone` is declared `phone String?` (schema.prisma:217) with no @unique and no @@index. Uniqueness is enforced only in application code: users.service.ts:445 does `findFirst({ where: { phone: trimmedPhone, id: { not: user.id } } })` and throws if a match exists. The code comment (440-443) explicitly acknowledges the DB constraint is missing ('Phone @unique isn't enforced at the DB level yet'). Two problems: (1) it is a check-then-act race with no surrounding transaction or unique index, so two concurrent phone-change/verify requests can both pass the check and persist the same number — there is no DB backstop; (2) it's a sequential scan per phone change (no index). This matters beyond cleanliness because phone is the addressing key for the ActionToken SMS flow (the /a/<token> pages that let a user accept an offer, pay, or raise a bid WITHOUT a Clerk session — schema.prisma:1831-1906). Two accounts sharing a phone number means action-link SMS and OTPs can be delivered to / associated with the wrong human, undermining the trust model of session-less mutating actions.
evidence: schema.prisma:217 `phone String?` (no @unique/@@index — confirmed against the full User model where only clerkId/email/username/kycIdHash/peachCustomerId are unique). users.service.ts:440-446 comment 'Phone @unique isn't enforced at the DB level yet ... so we enforce in app code' + non-transactional findFirst guard.
recommendation: After de-duplicating the known test-account collision, add a partial unique index on phone (e.g. unique where phone IS NOT NULL and phoneVerified = true, so unverified placeholders don't collide) plus a plain index for lookups. The DB constraint closes the TOCTOU race that the app-code check cannot.

verdict.reasoning:
The schema/code facts are accurate but the security thesis that drives the severity is wrong, so the finding is real-but-overstated.

VERIFIED FACTS (true): schema.prisma:214 `phone String?` has no @unique/@@index (confirmed; the only @unique fields on User are clerkId/email/username/kycIdHash + bank/peach ids). No migration adds a phone index (grep of backend/prisma/migrations shows only plain `"phone" TEXT`). users.service.ts:445-453 is a non-transactional findFirst check-then-act, and the comment at 440-443 admits the DB constraint is absent. So a TOCTOU race in that one method is technically possible.

THE CENTRAL CLAIM IS FALSE — phone does NOT route ActionToken authorisation. In action-tokens.service.ts:84-99 mint() stores `authorisedUserId` (a User.id FK), and resolve()/runAction() (119-257) run the action AS that fixed authorisedUserId. Phone is never used to resolve who a token authorises. Callers bind the token to the transaction's own party FK: transactions.service.ts:1113-1119 mints with `authorisedUserId: tx.sellerId`, and the SMS goes to `tx.seller.phone` (1140) / `tx.buyer.phone` — i.e. the specific party record, never a phone lookup. offers.service.ts:393-447 follows the same pattern. Therefore two accounts sharing a phone CANNOT misroute authorisation: a token minted for User A's offer/transaction only ever authorises that one action as User A, regardless of who else has the same number. A phone collision is purely a delivery artifact (an SMS landing on a shared SIM), not a capability escalation. The seller OTP flow is also safe: requestPhoneChange (462-466) sends the OTP to the number being CLAIMED and verifies it against the claimer's own row, so you must control the SIM — a collision can't intercept another user's OTP.

ADDITIONALLY, the 'race' framing understates and slightly mis-describes the real situation: uniqueness isn't merely racy, it's mostly unenforced. completeProfile (256-262) and saveBuyerPhone (297-301) write `phone` with NO dedup check at all, and upsertFromClerk (136/145) writes it from Clerk unchecked. PATCH /me is correctly fenced (ProfileUpdate excludes phone; controller whitelist users.controller.ts:219-232 omits it). So duplicates can be created single-threadedly through normal endpoints, not just via a concurrency race.

NET IMPACT: worst case is duplicate phone rows causing SMS/notification delivery ambiguity to a shared handset and dirty analytics/anti-fraud signal — a data-hygiene/UX issue. No cross-user data leak, no money loss, no auth bypass. A partial unique index is still a reasonable hardening, but the MEDIUM rating is driven by an incorrect security model.

title: `isFirearm` / `requiresLicence` (SAPS-regulated routing) live on both Category and Listing with no DB-level coupling — a wrong/stale flag silently allows illegal shipping methods
description: Whether an item is legally a firearm — which forces DEALER_TRANSFER and forbids Pudo/TCG courier per SAPS — is stored redundantly as `Category.isFirearm`/`requiresLicence` (494-500) AND denormalised onto `Listing.isFirearm` (538), with `Listing.shippingMethods` (584) being a free-form enum array defaulting to `[]`. There is no DB constraint or generated linkage keeping Listing.isFirearm in sync with its Category, and no constraint preventing a firearm listing from carrying PUDO/TCG in shippingMethods. The schema comment at 578-585 says ListingsService.create/update enforce the firearm→DEALER_TRANSFER rule in application code only. Because the denormalised boolean is a point-in-time snapshot, a Category re-classification (or a listing created/edited through any path that doesn't re-run the exact guard) can leave a regulated firearm with isFirearm=false and courier shipping enabled — a compliance breach with no database backstop. The default `shippingMethods @default([])` also lets a row exist with zero shipping methods, which the comment says should be impossible.
evidence: schema.prisma:538 `isFirearm Boolean @default(false)` on Listing duplicates Category.isFirearm (494). schema.prisma:584 `shippingMethods ShippingMethod[] @default([])` — no CHECK tying firearm listings to DEALER_TRANSFER; enforcement is described as service-layer only (578-585).
recommendation: Treat the firearm/shipping coupling as an invariant, not a convention: add a Postgres CHECK (via a raw-SQL migration) that rejects rows where isFirearm = true AND shippingMethods overlaps {PUDO, TCG} or does not contain DEALER_TRANSFER, and reject empty shippingMethods on ACTIVE listings. Derive Listing.isFirearm from the Category at write time in one shared code path and add a periodic consistency check that flags listings whose isFirearm disagrees with their category.

verdict.reasoning:
VERIFIED REAL, and slightly under-rated. The denormalization gap is genuine and the impact is NOT contained downstream.

Single source of truth: Listing.isFirearm is set from the category in exactly ONE place — listings.service.ts:380 `isFirearm: category.isFirearm` inside create(). There is no updateMany/reconciliation/backfill job anywhere (tasks/ has none; grep found only create()). So the snapshot is permanent once written.

Trigger path A (admin, as the finding claims): AdminCategoriesService.update() (admin-categories.service.ts:119) flips Category.isFirearm and updates ONLY the Category row — no back-fill of the listings tied to it. A non-firearm→firearm reclassification (realistic at launch while categories are being corrected) leaves every existing listing with isFirearm=false and its courier shippingMethods intact.

Trigger path B (the finding MISSED this — it's worse, seller-reachable): UpdateListingDto extends PartialType(CreateListingDto) (update-listing.dto.ts:4), so it includes categoryId. ListingsService.update() (listings.service.ts:730-737) writes the new categoryId via the `...dto` spread but NEVER recomputes isFirearm, and its firearm guard (line 712-720) checks the STALE `listing.isFirearm`, not the new category. A seller can PATCH /listings/:id moving their own listing into a firearm category while keeping shippingMethods:['PUDO'] — guard is skipped because old isFirearm=false. The endpoint is live (listings.controller.ts:113-121, ClerkGuard only); no /[id]/edit UI exists but the API is directly callable.

Impact is real because downstream trusts the snapshot, not the category: TransactionsService.create → validateShipping(listing.isFirearm, listing.shippingMethods, dto.shippingMethod) (transactions.service.ts:94-97; logic at 1223-1242) classifies firearm-vs-not purely from listing.isFirearm. With a stale false, validateShipping(false, ['PUDO'], 'PUDO') passes and a real firearm ships via Pudo locker — a SAPS-compliance breach. quoteForListing also only blocks when listing.isFirearm is true (shipping.service.ts:128), so a stale-false firearm gets a courier quote too.

Empty-array sub-claim also confirmed: shippingMethods @default([]) (schema:584) + the `if (dto.shippingMethods && ...)` guards (listings.service.ts:238, 712) mean a firearm can be created/updated with shippingMethods=[] by omitting the field; quoteForListing line 144 skips the seller-offered check when length===0.

What tempers it: the happy-path create() is correct (server-derives isFirearm, enforces DEALER_TRANSFER when methods are supplied), and the DTO has no isFirearm field so a seller can't directly inject it. The bug only fires on an admin reclass of existing rows or a crafted categoryId PATCH — not the default flow, and no current UI drives either.

Recommendation in the finding (Postgres CHECK invariant + single shared derivation path + periodic consistency check + back-fill on category flip) is the correct fix; minimally, update() must re-derive isFirearm whenever categoryId changes and re-run the DEALER_TRANSFER guard against the NEW category, and AdminCategoriesService.update() must updateMany the affected listings.

title: Offer-based checkout never re-checks listing status — TAKE_A_SHOT items can be sold to multiple buyers (double-sell / double-charge)
description: In TransactionsService.create(), the offer-checkout branch validates the offer status but completely skips the listing-availability check. The non-offer (BUY_NOW) branch at lines 82-89 guards `if (listing.status !== 'ACTIVE') throw 'Listing is no longer available'`, but the offer branch (lines 75-81) only checks `rawOffer.status === 'ACCEPTED'` and `listing.listingType === 'TAKE_A_SHOT'` — it never looks at listing.status. A single TAKE_A_SHOT listing can hold one offer PER buyer (schema @@unique([listingId, buyerId]) at schema.prisma:1159, so many buyers each get their own offer). Nothing rejects the other offers when one is accepted or when the listing sells: OffersService.accept()/auto-accept (offers.service.ts:100-118, 124-145) only mutate the single offer, and markPaid() (transactions.service.ts:951-954) sets the listing SOLD without touching sibling offers. So Buyer A pays (listing → PAYMENT_PENDING → SOLD), and Buyer B — who also holds an ACCEPTED (or auto-accepted) offer — can still call create() with their offerId. The offer branch passes (status ACCEPTED), line 168-171 unconditionally flips the listing back to PAYMENT_PENDING, a second Peach checkout is created, and Buyer B is charged for an item already sold to Buyer A.
evidence: Offer branch with no status guard: `if (dto.offerId) { const rawOffer = ...; if (rawOffer.status !== 'ACCEPTED') throw...; if (listing.listingType !== 'TAKE_A_SHOT') throw...; offerRecord = rawOffer; } else { if (listing.status !== 'ACTIVE') throw new BadRequestException('Listing is no longer available'); ... }` — the ACTIVE check lives only in the else. Then unconditionally: `await this.prisma.listing.update({ where: { id: listing.id }, data: { status: ListingStatus.PAYMENT_PENDING } });`. Auto-accept makes this worse: OffersService.submit() sets status ACCEPTED for every buyer who clears autoAcceptThreshold (offers.service.ts:87-109) with no reservation, so N buyers can each hold a payable ACCEPTED offer simultaneously.
recommendation: In the offer branch, also require `listing.status === 'ACTIVE'` (reject if PAYMENT_PENDING/SOLD/etc.). Make the reservation atomic: replace the blind `listing.update(... PAYMENT_PENDING)` with a conditional `updateMany({ where: { id, status: 'ACTIVE' }, data: { status: 'PAYMENT_PENDING' } })` and abort if count===0. When an offer is accepted (and at markPaid), mass-reject/expire the other open offers on that listing (`offer.updateMany({ where: { listingId, status: { in: [PENDING, COUNTERED, ACCEPTED] }, id: { not: acceptedId } }, data: { status: REJECTED } })`).

verdict.reasoning: Verified the full path; the finding is accurate. (1) transactions.service.ts:75-81 — the offer branch checks only rawOffer.status==='ACCEPTED', buyerId ownership, and listingType==='TAKE_A_SHOT'; it never reads listing.status. The `listing.status === 'ACTIVE'` guard exists ONLY in the else/BUY_NOW branch (line 83-85). (2) Reservation at 168-171 is an unconditional `listing.update({ data: { status: PAYMENT_PENDING } })` — not a conditional updateMany on status==='ACTIVE', and not wrapped in a read+reserve transaction, so it blindly overwrites SOLD→PAYMENT_PENDING and also races. (3) Multiple buyers really can hold ACCEPTED offers at once: schema.prisma:1159 `@@unique([listingId, buyerId])` = one offer PER buyer, and offers.service.ts:87-109 auto-accept sets status ACCEPTED for every buyer who clears autoAcceptThreshold with no reservation; seller accept() (124-145) and acceptCounter() (215-234) each mutate only the single offer. (4) Nothing rejects sibling offers on sale: markPaid (transactions.service.ts:951-954) flips listing→SOLD without touching other offers; create() only marks the ONE converting offer CONVERTED (246-249). The sole offer.updateMany (offers.service.ts:345) is the TTL expireStale cron, unrelated. (5) No idempotency stops a second create: paidAt checks (272, 314) guard a given transaction in verifyResult/webhook, not a second checkout for a different buyer; the controller (transactions.controller.ts:68-86) only adds a token/listingId match check, no listing-status gate. Exploit: Buyer A pays (listing SOLD, A's offer CONVERTED), Buyer B still holds ACCEPTED → POST /transactions with B's offerId passes the offer branch, listing is blindly set PAYMENT_PENDING, a second Peach checkout is created, B is charged for an item already sold. With auto-accept on, two above-threshold buyers trivially both hold ACCEPTED offers, so this is reachable in normal use, not a contrived race (and a genuine TOCTOU race exists even otherwise). Guaranteed double-charge + refund/dispute liability with real money movement on a regulated SA firearms marketplace. The recommended fix (require listing.status==='ACTIVE' in the offer branch, conditional updateMany reservation aborting on count===0, and mass-reject sibling open offers on accept/markPaid) is correct.

title: raffleWinner.userId can be null for a postal winner — winner notification, claim, and dispatch silently break
description: Postal (CPA Section 36 free-entry) tickets are created with NO buyerId (createPostalEntry, lines 783-792 set only postalEntryId). They are eligible for the draw (runDraw selects status in ['CONFIRMED','POSTAL'] at line 863-864). When a POSTAL ticket wins, RaffleWinner.userId is written as null (line 924-932, userId: w.userId where w.userId = candidate.buyerId = null). Downstream every winner path is keyed on userId: winner-#1 notification only fires `if (w1?.userId)` (line 954) so a postal winner gets NO win email; the backup-promotion cron only emails/promotes `if (next?.userId)` and otherwise jumps straight to EXPIRED_UNCLAIMED (line 995-1013), so if the primary winner is postal the backups are never told; claimPrize() compares `winner.userId !== user.id` (line 1036) so a postal winner can never claim through the app. The postal entrant's name/phone/email live on the PostalEntry row, which the winner pipeline never reads. Net effect: a legitimate free-entry winner is invisible to the system and the prize silently lapses — a direct fairness/compliance failure for the route that exists specifically to make the competition legal.
evidence: runDraw winner insert: `userId: w.userId` where userId originates from `candidate.buyerId` (null for postal). Notify guard: `if (w1?.userId) { const user = await tx.user.findUnique({ where: { id: w1.userId } }); ... }`. expireClaims promotion: `if (next?.userId) { ... raffleBackupPromoted ... } else { ...status: 'EXPIRED_UNCLAIMED' }`. Postal tickets created without buyerId: `tx.ticket.create({ data: { raffleId, ticketNumber, referenceCode, status: 'POSTAL', postalEntryId: entry.id } })`.
recommendation: When a winner has no userId, resolve contact details from the linked PostalEntry (join Ticket.postalEntryId → PostalEntry.{firstName,email,phone}) and either notify the operator to contact the postal winner manually or raise an AdminAlert so the prize isn't silently forfeited. At minimum, do not let a null-userId primary winner skip backup promotion / mark EXPIRED_UNCLAIMED without an operator alert.

verdict.reasoning:
VERIFIED REAL but the severity is OVERSTATED. I traced every claimed path.

CONFIRMED TRUE:
- Schema: RaffleWinner.userId is nullable (schema.prisma:1452, comment "null for postal winner"). Postal tickets created with only postalEntryId, no buyerId (raffles.service.ts:784-792).
- Postal tickets ARE draw-eligible (runDraw status in ['CONFIRMED','POSTAL'], line 864) and the winner row is written with userId=candidate.buyerId=null (lines 905/912/927). The CPA Section 36 free-entry route is publicly advertised on every competition page (free-entry-button.tsx), so postal winners are genuinely reachable.
- Win notification IS gated on `if (w1?.userId)` (line 954) -> postal winner gets NO automated win email. TRUE.
- claimPrize requires `winner.userId !== user.id` (line 1036) -> postal winner can never self-claim in-app. TRUE.
- expireClaims promotes backup only `if (next?.userId)` (line 995) else silently sets status 'EXPIRED_UNCLAIMED' (line 1011) with no operator alert. So a POSTAL backup is skipped and the raffle silently expires; no AdminAlert is raised anywhere in runDraw/expireClaims (grep: zero AdminAlert refs). TRUE and the most damaging sub-claim.
- markWinnerPrizeDispatched dispatch notification gated on `if (winner.userId && winner.user)` (line 1350) -> no dispatch notice to postal winner; and the frontend "Mark as dispatched" button only renders when dispatchState==='PENDING', which requires claimState==='CLAIMED' (page.tsx:252-256) -- unreachable for a postal winner. TRUE.

OVERSTATED / WRONG:
- The finding's headline "invisible to the system / prize silently lapses" is too strong. The operator dossier getWinnersForAdmin returns the winner row regardless of userId, and the frontend WinnerCard explicitly handles the null-user case: it shows the winning ticketId, an "Awaiting claim" state, and the message "Postal entry -- contact details live on the postal-entries page" (page.tsx:282, 350-353). The command-center "rafflesNewlyDrawn" card also counts it (admin-command-center.service.ts:168-175). So a postal win IS visible to a monitoring operator for the duration of the claim window.

UNDERSTATED (one part is actually worse than described):
- That on-screen pointer is a dead end: the admin postal-entries page is a write-only create form with NO list/search (postal-entries/page.tsx), and there is NO GET endpoint for postal entries anywhere (raffles.controller.ts only has @Post('postal-entries'); admin.controller.ts has zero postal refs). So even a diligent operator cannot recover the winner's name/phone/email through the UI -- only via direct DB query on Ticket.postalEntryId -> PostalEntry.

NET: A real compliance/business-logic gap -- the legally-mandated free-entry winner cannot be notified, cannot claim, cannot be dispatched, and (as a backup) is silently skipped, all through the normal product flow. But because the win is visible in the dossier as a persistent awaiting-claim to-do, a manual DB-backed fulfillment path exists, postal entrants are statistically rare vs. paid, and the multi-day claim window gives the operator time, this is a degraded/edge-case defect rather than a launch-blocking, incident-likely HIGH. Recommend MEDIUM. The two concrete fixes worth prioritizing: (1) in expireClaims, do not skip a null-userId backup / do not silently mark EXPIRED_UNCLAIMED without raising an operator alert; (2) make getWinnersForAdmin join Ticket.postalEntryId -> PostalEntry so the dossier shows the postal entrant's contact details (and/or give the postal-entries page a real list view), since the current "see the postal-entries page" pointer leads nowhere.

title: Skill-question answer is hard-coded to 'C' for every raffle — defeats the CPA competition-vs-lottery gate
description: South African raffles are run as 'competitions' (requiring a skill/knowledge element) to avoid being an unlawful lottery. The correct answer is a single global constant CORRECT_ANSWER = 'C' applied to EVERY raffle (line 49), and createPendingTickets rejects only when `dto.answer !== CORRECT_ANSWER` (line 634). Because the answer is always 'C' regardless of the actual question, the 'skill' gate is trivially bypassable (any entrant who has ever entered once, or who reads this constant's behaviour, always answers C) and provides no genuine element of skill. If the lawful-competition defence depends on the question being a real knowledge test, a uniform always-C answer undermines that defence. The code comment frames it as an operator convenience, but it is a legal-correctness risk worth surfacing for sign-off before launch rather than an implementation nit.
evidence: `// The correct answer is ALWAYS option C — operator decision so we don't have to track per-raffle correctness in admin UX. const CORRECT_ANSWER: 'A' | 'B' | 'C' | 'D' = 'C';` and `if (dto.answer !== CORRECT_ANSWER) { throw new BadRequestException('Incorrect answer to the question'); }`. No per-raffle correctAnswer column exists in the Raffle model.
recommendation: Store the correct answer per raffle (a Raffle.correctAnswer column, set at create, never exposed via publicSelect) and validate against it. If the operator genuinely wants a fixed answer, get explicit legal sign-off and document it, but do not hard-code one answer across all competitions.

verdict.reasoning:
VERIFIED REAL — code evidence is accurate. backend/src/raffles/raffles.service.ts:49 defines a single global `const CORRECT_ANSWER = 'C'` and line 634 rejects only `dto.answer !== CORRECT_ANSWER`, applied to EVERY raffle. The Raffle model (backend/prisma/schema.prisma:1263-1310) has `question` + `optionA`-`optionD` but NO per-raffle correct-answer column; schema.prisma:1309 explicitly comments "optionC ... ALWAYS the correct answer (hardcoded)". The CPA game-of-skill gate is therefore structurally trivial — and worse than the finding states: the frontend (frontend/app/competitions/[id]/enter-panel.tsx:232) renders options in fixed ['A','B','C','D'] order with literal letter labels, so the correct answer is always the same third radio labelled "C". This is a legitimate legal-correctness concern (lottery-vs-competition defence) worth operator/legal sign-off, exactly as framed.

The finding's leak sub-claim is already mitigated and the finding acknowledges it: publicSelect() (lines 112-139) exposes question+options but no answer, and the answer isn't a DB column, so it cannot leak via API. Not overstated there.

HOWEVER the finding OMITS a major severity-reducing fact: raffle ticket PAYMENT is not wired up in production. The enter panel hard-throws outside dev (enter-panel.tsx:169-173 "Raffle payment integration is being finalised"), and the only ticket-confirm route is `tickets/dev-confirm`, which is disabled in prod (raffles.controller.ts:144-145 throws "Dev confirm is disabled in production"). No Peach webhook path exists for raffle tickets (zero matches in backend/src/payments for raffle/confirmTickets). So at launch no member of the public can actually pay for and hold a competition ticket — the weak skill gate is currently unexploitable for money. The design flaw is real and baked into the schema, and will go live the instant the payment flow is finished, so it remains a genuine pre-launch sign-off item, but it is not currently an active HIGH incident.

Downgrading HIGH -> MEDIUM: real, correctly-diagnosed compliance/legal design flaw, but exploitability is gated by an unfinished (prod-disabled) payment flow. Recommendation in the finding (per-raffle Raffle.correctAnswer column never exposed via publicSelect, set at create, or explicit legal sign-off for a fixed answer) is sound and should be actioned before competitions go live.

title: Ticket.ticketNumber has no uniqueness constraint and is allocated by counting outside/inside mixed scopes — concurrent buyers can collide
description: ticketNumber is described as 'sequential within a raffle' but the schema has no @@unique([raffleId, ticketNumber]) (only referenceCode is globally unique). All three allocators assign it by reading a count/max and adding an offset: createPendingTickets counts inside its tx (raffles.service.ts:654-668), createPostalEntry counts inside its tx (775-792), and autoEnterSubscribers reads max once then increments locally (309-326). Under PostgreSQL's default READ COMMITTED isolation, two concurrent ticket purchases on the same raffle both read the same count and create tickets with identical ticketNumbers — there is no DB constraint to stop it. This corrupts the human-facing ticket numbering (PDFs, postal forms, audit) and can make two physically-distinct tickets share a 'ticket number' shown to buyers, undermining trust in the draw even though referenceCode stays unique.
evidence: Schema: `ticketNumber Int // sequential within a raffle (1, 2, 3, …)` with only `referenceCode String @unique` and indexes `@@index([raffleId, status])`, `@@index([buyerId])` — no compound unique on (raffleId, ticketNumber). Allocation reads then writes without a serializing lock: `const counted = await tx.ticket.count({...}); for (...) tx.ticket.create({ data: { ticketNumber: counted + i + 1, ... } })`.
recommendation: Add `@@unique([raffleId, ticketNumber])` and allocate via an atomic counter on the Raffle row (e.g. a nextTicketNumber column incremented with `{ increment: n }` returning the new value) or wrap allocation in a SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on the raffle, so concurrent buyers can never mint the same number.

verdict.reasoning: Verified REAL and correctly rated MEDIUM. (1) No DB uniqueness on (raffleId, ticketNumber): schema.prisma:1410-1442 has only referenceCode @unique; migration 20260518162012_add_raffles/migration.sql:146-152 creates only Ticket_referenceCode_key (UNIQUE) plus non-unique raffleId_status and buyerId indexes; no later migration adds the compound unique. (2) All three allocators read-then-write without serialization: createPendingTickets (raffles.service.ts:653-678) does tx.ticket.count then create(ticketNumber: counted+i+1) — and its comment at :650-652 falsely claims this is atomic; createPostalEntry (:778-794) same pattern; autoEnterSubscribers (:309-326) reads max once then increments locally. (3) Isolation is default READ COMMITTED — PrismaService (prisma.service.ts) sets no isolationLevel, and grep for isolationLevel/Serializable/RepeatableRead across backend/src and FOR UPDATE/pg_advisory/SET TRANSACTION in the raffles module both return nothing. Under READ COMMITTED two concurrent buyers both read the same committed count and insert identical ticketNumbers; nothing stops them. (4) The buy endpoint is per-user concurrent: POST /raffles/:id/tickets -> createPendingTickets via ClerkGuard (raffles.controller.ts:110-117). Severity is correctly MEDIUM (not higher): runDraw (:857-933) selects by array index and dedupes by ticket.id, never ticketNumber, and referenceCode stays globally unique, so the draw/winner-identity/money are unaffected. Impact is confined to corrupted human-facing sequential numbering, which IS shown to buyers (getMyTickets/:66, :427; subscriber view :449) and used on PDFs/postal/audit — a data-integrity/trust defect on a regulated draw. Note: the recommended @@unique alone would turn silent collisions into P2002 insert failures on the buy path, so the atomic-counter/FOR UPDATE half of the fix is required too.

title: Raffle oversell pre-check runs outside the transaction — concurrent buyers can exceed targetTicketCount
description: createPendingTickets reads `raffle.ticketsSoldPaid + raffle.ticketsSoldPostal` from the raffle row fetched BEFORE the transaction (line 640, raffle loaded at 625) and rejects oversell against that stale snapshot. The transaction that actually reserves the tickets (653-686) re-counts existing tickets but never re-validates the count against targetTicketCount. Two buyers requesting the last few tickets concurrently both pass the pre-check and both reserve, so total sold can exceed the target. Because the sold-out → CLOSED_AWAITING_DRAW trigger keys on `>= targetTicketCount`, oversell isn't fatal to the draw, but it means more tickets sold than the prize value backs, and the 'X remaining' UX is wrong. Tickets are non-refundable, so an over-sold buyer has paid for a ticket that should never have been offered.
evidence: Pre-check on stale data: `const totalSold = raffle.ticketsSoldPaid + raffle.ticketsSoldPostal; if (totalSold + dto.quantity > raffle.targetTicketCount) { ... throw }` — raffle was loaded with `findUnique` before `this.prisma.$transaction(...)`, and the inner tx only does `tx.ticket.count(...)` for numbering, with no target re-check before `tx.ticket.create`.
recommendation: Move the oversell check inside the transaction and re-read the live counts there (or use the atomic raffle counter), aborting if `liveSold + quantity > targetTicketCount`.

verdict.reasoning: Verified REAL by reading the full path. In raffles.service.ts, `raffle` is loaded via findUnique at line 625 BEFORE the transaction, and the oversell guard at lines 640-648 checks `raffle.ticketsSoldPaid + raffle.ticketsSoldPostal + dto.quantity > raffle.targetTicketCount` against that stale snapshot. The transaction (653-686) uses `tx.ticket.count(...)` (line 654) ONLY to number tickets (counted + i + 1, line 667) and never re-checks targetTicketCount before tx.ticket.create. I confirmed no mitigation lives elsewhere: (1) no isolationLevel is set on any $transaction in the codebase (grep = 0 matches), so it runs at Postgres default READ COMMITTED, which does not prevent this race; (2) the tx takes no row lock — no SELECT FOR UPDATE and no early tx.raffle.update on the raffle; (3) crucially the Ticket model (schema.prisma 1400-1443) has NO unique constraint on (raffleId, ticketNumber) — only @@index([raffleId,status]) (non-unique) and referenceCode @unique (a random value) — so concurrent txns reading the same count both commit, with no DB rollback to backstop the oversell (and they even produce duplicate ticket numbers); (4) the buy endpoint POST /:id/tickets (controller 110-117) has no @Throttle override, inheriting the global 60 req/min/IP bucket, wide enough to fire concurrent requests. The same uncounted pattern repeats in createPostalEntry (778-787) but that's admin-driven. Severity MEDIUM is correct, not higher: the window is narrow (the inner count includes PENDING_PAYMENT, so it only races at the last-few-tickets boundary when requests interleave between the pre-check and the count), quantity is capped at 100 (DTO line 9), and oversell is NOT fatal to the draw because the sold-out trigger keys on >= targetTicketCount (732, 812). The real harm matches the finding: targetTicketCount = ceil(itemValueCents/ticketPriceCents) (line 183) is the exact prize-cost coverage line, tickets are non-refundable (617-619), and the 'X remaining' UX (646) becomes wrong — a financial/UX-correctness defect, not money loss or legal exposure.

title: Auto-accepted offers are never reserved and competing offers are never invalidated — sellers can over-commit one item
description: When a listing has autoAcceptThreshold set, every buyer whose offer meets it gets status ACCEPTED immediately (lines 87-109) with no listing reservation and no effect on other offers. Likewise manual accept()/reject() mutate only the single offer. There is no path anywhere that, on acceptance, rejects the other open offers on the same listing or marks the listing reserved. The result is N simultaneously-payable ACCEPTED offers from N buyers on one item. This is the upstream enabler of the CRITICAL double-sell finding, but is worth fixing independently: even with a listing-status guard at checkout, the first buyer to pay wins and every other accepted buyer hits a confusing 'no longer available' at the very end after believing their offer was accepted.
evidence: Auto-accept: `const autoAccept = listing.autoAcceptThreshold !== null && dto.offerAmount >= listing.autoAcceptThreshold; ... status: autoAccept ? OfferStatus.ACCEPTED : OfferStatus.PENDING`. accept(): single `prisma.offer.update({ where: { id: offerId }, data: { status: ACCEPTED, ... } })` with no sibling-offer handling and no listing reservation.
recommendation: On any accept (manual or auto), reject the other open offers on that listing and/or move the listing to a reserved state, so only one accepted offer is payable at a time.

verdict.reasoning:
Verified against the actual code paths; the finding is accurate.

(1) Auto-accept makes every qualifying offer payable: offers.service.ts:87-118 computes autoAccept purely from `dto.offerAmount >= listing.autoAcceptThreshold` and creates the offer with `status: ACCEPTED` (line 106), with no listing reservation and no effect on sibling offers. submit() only blocks a *re-offer by the same buyer* (lines 62-67, via the `@@unique([listingId, buyerId])` key) and only checks `listing.status === 'ACTIVE'` (line 55) — which auto-accept never changes — so N different buyers can each hold an ACCEPTED offer on one listing.

(2) Manual accept() (offers.service.ts:130-144) and counter() do a single `offer.update`, no sibling rejection, no reservation.

(3) No mitigating path exists anywhere in backend/src: the only `offer.updateMany` is the TTL `expireStale` cron (line 345); the only REJECTED writes are single-offer (lines 158, 247). Schema (schema.prisma:1159) confirms uniqueness is per-buyer, not per-accepted-offer, and there is no DB constraint limiting active transactions per listing.

(4) The downstream symptom is reachable and is money loss, not just bad UX: in transactions.service.ts:73-89 the offer-checkout branch checks only `rawOffer.status === 'ACCEPTED'` and does NOT check `listing.status` (that guard is only in the BUY_NOW `else` branch). Reservation at lines 167-171 is an unconditional `listing.update`, not a conditional `updateMany({where:{status:ACTIVE}})`, so two concurrent accepted buyers are not serialized. markPaid (lines 926-955) then runs for both — both buyers' funds end up HELD with one item.

Note: comment at offers.service.ts:142 references `TransactionsService.payOffer`, which does not exist (the real path is TransactionsService.create with dto.offerId) — stale comment, not a functional issue.

Severity: the finder deliberately scoped this as the upstream enabler at MEDIUM and split off the money-loss as a separate CRITICAL double-sell finding. As an independent business-logic defect MEDIUM is fair, so I keep MEDIUM — while flagging that the boundary to its CRITICAL sibling is thin because the missing listing-status check in the offer-checkout path turns this enabler directly into double-payment. The recommended fix (reject siblings and/or reserve the listing on accept) is correct and should be paired with an atomic listing-status guard in transactions.service.create for the offer path.

title: pollCreditBalances writes a CreditSnapshot per result but its threshold dedup updates can be lost on partial failure, and Anthropic spend uses balance<=threshold semantics
description: Two issues in the 15-min credit-poll cron. (1) Semantics bug acknowledged in-code: for Anthropic the 'balance' is 24h SPEND (higher = worse), but checkCreditThreshold applies the same `balance <= threshold` rule used for remaining-credit services (lines 434-437, 458). This means a SPEND spike (balance rising above the threshold) will NEVER fire an alert — the operator gets no warning exactly when Anthropic cost is running away. The comment tells the operator to set negative thresholds, which is non-obvious and easy to get wrong; a misconfiguration silently disables the alert. (2) The alarm/warn dedup writes lastAlarmAlertAt/lastWarnAlertAt only after fanOutCreditAlert resolves; fanOut is best-effort and swallows per-admin send failures, so the timestamp is written even if every SMS/email failed, suppressing the next 6h of alerts after a fully-failed dispatch.
evidence: `if (threshold.alarmThreshold != null && balance <= threshold.alarmThreshold) { ... await this.fanOutCreditAlert(...); await this.prisma.creditThreshold.update({ ..., data: { lastAlarmAlertAt: now } }); }` and the comment: `for that service the "balance" is SPEND (USD over 24h) not balance-remaining ... For now we apply the same balance <= threshold rule — the operator should set Anthropic's thresholds to NEGATIVE numbers`.
recommendation: Add a direction/comparator to CreditThreshold (e.g. 'below' vs 'above') and apply `>=` for spend-style services. Only stamp lastAlarmAlertAt/lastWarnAlertAt when fanOutCreditAlert reports at least one successful send.

verdict.reasoning:
Both sub-claims are factually verified against the code.

(1) Inverted Anthropic semantics — REAL, and actually slightly worse than the finding states. admin-credits.service.ts:442 returns balance=sumSpend for Anthropic (24h USD spend; higher=worse), confirmed by the explicit comment at lines 366-372 "balance here is INVERTED ... it's SPEND_USD over the last 24h, NOT money remaining." tasks.service.ts:436 and :458 apply the uniform `balance <= alarmThreshold`/`<= warnThreshold` rule, so a spend SPIKE (e.g. 500 vs threshold 100 → `500 <= 100` is false) never fires — alerts only trigger when spend is LOW, which is backwards. The same inverted comparison is duplicated in countServicesBelowAlarm() at admin-credits.service.ts:890-894, so the admin dashboard "creditsBelowAlarm" counter is also wrong for Anthropic. The documented workaround (set NEGATIVE thresholds, tasks.service.ts:415-418) is non-functional: spend is always >= 0, so `spend <= -100` can never be true — a negative threshold permanently disables the alert rather than inverting it. So the in-code mitigation the comment offers does not work.

(2) Dedup-on-failure — REAL. fanOutCreditAlert (tasks.service.ts:483-553) try/catches each admin send (:543) and never throws; the lastAlarmAlertAt/lastWarnAlertAt updates at :450-453 and :471-474 run unconditionally after it resolves, so a fully-failed dispatch still stamps the 6h dedup and suppresses retries.

Mitigating factors that cap real-world impact: no CreditThreshold rows are seeded anywhere (no seed.ts; grep found no Anthropic threshold creation), and checkCreditThreshold returns early when !threshold || !threshold.enabled (tasks.service.ts:428). So by default Anthropic has NO threshold and no alert is even expected — the operator must opt in manually, and the comment explicitly says to leave it unset and use the trend chart. This is an internal cost-monitoring cron for the operator's own Anthropic bill: not user-facing, no money-between-users, no data leak, no legal exposure. The live /admin/credits trend chart still shows spend. The dedup-on-failure case only bites if both SMS and email are down for every superadmin, and the next poll is 15 min away, so at most one 6h internal-alert window is lost.

Net: genuinely a business-logic bug (and the suggested negative-threshold workaround is itself broken), but for launch readiness it is a polish-grade internal-ops issue, not MEDIUM. Recommendation stands: add a direction/comparator column and only stamp the dedup timestamp when at least one send succeeds.

title: Subscriber raffle auto-enter dedup check runs outside its transaction — re-entrancy can double-issue free tickets
description: autoEnterSubscribers computes the already-issued set with a findMany OUTSIDE the $transaction (lines 298-303), then issues tickets inside the transaction. There is no @@unique([raffleId, buyerId]) on Ticket, so the 'idempotent' guarantee relies entirely on that pre-read. The method is invoked from create() and open(), and the comment advertises it as 'safe to re-run on open()'. If it is ever invoked twice with overlapping execution (e.g. an admin double-submits open, a retried request, or a future caller), both passes read the same empty existing-set and both issue a free CONFIRMED ticket to the same subscriber, doubling that user's odds in a fairness-sensitive draw and double-incrementing ticketsSoldPaid. runSubscriberRaffleDraws also flips status to CLOSED_AWAITING_DRAW then immediately draws, so any stray concurrent auto-enter near draw time is unguarded by status.
evidence: `const existing = await this.prisma.ticket.findMany({ where: { raffleId, buyerId: { in: subscribers.map((s) => s.id) } }, select: { buyerId: true } }); const existingIds = new Set(existing.map((t) => t.buyerId)); const toIssue = subscribers.filter((s) => !existingIds.has(s.id)); ... await this.prisma.$transaction(async (tx) => { ... for (const s of toIssue) { await tx.ticket.create({ data: { raffleId, buyerId: s.id, ... status: 'CONFIRMED', amountCents: 0 } }); } ... })` — existence check is not inside the tx and no unique constraint backs it.
recommendation: Add a unique constraint preventing two free subscriber tickets for the same (raffleId, buyerId) — or move the existing-ticket check inside the transaction with appropriate locking — so concurrent or retried auto-enter cannot double-issue.

verdict.reasoning:
The factual core is correct: schema.prisma (Ticket model, lines 1400-1443) has NO @@unique([raffleId, buyerId]) — only @@index([raffleId,status]), @@index([buyerId]), and referenceCode @unique (random per ticket, irrelevant to dedup). The dedup pre-read (raffles.service.ts 298-303) runs OUTSIDE the $transaction (opened at line 306), so idempotency rests entirely on a non-atomic, non-locked read. That much is real.

However the finding overstates reachability and severity:

1) create() path (line 246) is structurally immune. The raffleId is generated fresh inside create() at line 194; no other code can hold that ID at the instant auto-enter runs. A double-submitted create() yields two DIFFERENT raffles (distinct IDs + referenceNumbers via allocateForRaffle), not duplicate tickets on one raffle. It cannot collide with itself or with open().

2) open() path (line 522) is guarded by `if (raffle.status !== 'DRAFT') throw BadRequestException` (line 501) before the status flip to ACTIVE (line 504). To double-issue, two open() calls must both read DRAFT before either writes ACTIVE — a genuine TOCTOU window, but sub-millisecond and only reachable by a trusted operator double-firing the SAME DRAFT raffle. Realistic operator double-clicks are seconds apart; the second hits BadRequestException.

3) Both callers sit on @Controller('admin/raffles') @UseGuards(AdminJwtGuard) (controller lines 152-153). The only actors are authenticated operators, NOT end users — this is not a public attack surface.

4) The finding's claim that "stray concurrent auto-enter near draw time is unguarded by status" is incorrect. autoEnterSubscribers is invoked ONLY from create() and open() — there is no cron/recurring caller (verified by grepping all callers). runSubscriberRaffleDraws (462-491) flips ACTIVE→CLOSED_AWAITING_DRAW then draws, but nothing re-runs auto-enter at draw time, and by then the raffle is long past DRAFT so open() can't re-trigger. The described scenario has no triggering code path.

5) Impact if it ever fired: one duplicate FREE CONFIRMED ticket (amountCents: 0) and a double-increment of ticketsSoldPaid for a single subscriber — a minor odds skew in a free promotional draw. No money loss, no data leak, no legal/compliance exposure; operator-correctable.

Net: a legitimate defensive-hardening item (adding @@unique([raffleId,buyerId]) is cheap and would fully close it), but the exploit windows are near-zero, operator-only, and the worst case is a free duplicate ticket. MEDIUM is too high.

title: Auction Buy Now does not reserve the listing or create the transaction — concurrent Buy-Now + first bid can both proceed
description: AuctionsService.buyNow() validates `bidCount === 0` and returns a checkoutAmount, but performs NO state change — it neither reserves the listing nor records intent. The actual reservation only happens later when the buyer reaches TransactionsService.create()/markPaid. Between buyNow() returning and the buyer completing Peach checkout, another user can place the first bid (placeBid only rejects Buy Now via getAuctionState exposing buyNowPrice once bidCount>0, but placeBid itself has no Buy-Now lock). The buy-now buyer's later checkout goes through the BUY_NOW path which does require listing ACTIVE, so the worst case is the buy-now buyer being rejected at the end after committing — but the inverse race (two buy-now buyers, or buy-now vs bid) is decided only by who hits markPaid first, with no early reservation. This is a weaker sibling of the offer double-sell: state is only made consistent at payment, not at intent.
evidence: `async buyNow(...) { ... if (listing.bidCount > 0) throw ...; if (!listing.buyNowPrice) throw ...; return { checkoutAmount: listing.buyNowPrice, listingId: listing.id }; }` — comment explicitly: `We don't create the Transaction here ... we just flag the listing so the checkout page knows to use buyNowPrice`, but no flag/lock is actually written.
recommendation: Either reserve the listing (atomic conditional update to PAYMENT_PENDING / a short-lived BUY_NOW hold) when buyNow() is invoked, or accept the late-rejection behaviour but ensure the checkout path for buy-now performs an atomic ACTIVE→PAYMENT_PENDING transition so two buyers cannot both reach markPaid.

verdict.reasoning:
The finding correctly observes that AuctionsService.buyNow() (backend/src/auctions/auctions.service.ts:548-587) writes no state — it only validates and returns {checkoutAmount, listingId}. But its central claim — a MEDIUM concurrency race where "two buy-now buyers, or buy-now vs bid, [is] decided only by who hits markPaid first" — is FALSE, because no auction Buy-Now buyer can ever reach markPaid. I traced the full path:

1. Frontend handleBuyNow() (frontend/app/listings/[id]/auction-panel.tsx:294-314) calls POST /auctions/:id/buy-now, then on success does router.push(`/checkout/${listingId}`) at line 309.
2. The checkout page server-renders a hard guard: frontend/app/checkout/[listingId]/page.tsx:34 — `if (listing.listingType !== 'BUY_NOW') return notFound();`. An AUCTION listing's listingType is 'AUCTION' (distinct Prisma enum value, schema.prisma:42-45; frontend type lib/types.ts:1), so the buyer hits a 404 and never sees a checkout form.
3. Even if that were bypassed, the only checkout-creating endpoint is POST /transactions → TransactionsService.create(), which for any non-offer checkout enforces listing.listingType === 'BUY_NOW' at transactions.service.ts:86-87 ("Only BUY_NOW listings support direct checkout"). buildPayload() (checkout-form.tsx:402-452) never sends offerId, so the offer branch can't apply either.

So the atomic ACTIVE→PAYMENT_PENDING reservation the finding worries is "only made consistent at payment" is in fact present for the real BUY_NOW path (transactions.service.ts:168-171) with rollback on Peach failure (231-235) and idempotent webhook/verify guards on tx.paidAt (272, 314). The described double-sell race for auction Buy-Now cannot occur because the second half of the flow does not exist.

The real defect is more severe than reported: the auction Buy-Now feature is entirely non-functional. A buyer who clicks "Buy Now" on a zero-bid auction is routed to a 404 and can never complete the purchase. That is a broken core flow (HIGH), not a MEDIUM concurrency race. The finding identified the right code smell (buyNow writes no state) but drew the wrong consequence; the specific business-logic-correctness race it asserts is a FALSE_POSITIVE as written. I am flagging finalSeverity HIGH because the underlying code region is genuinely broken and launch-relevant, but the finding's described vulnerability (concurrent buy-now/bid double-proceed via markPaid) is not real.

title: pickModBig rejection-sampling fallback applies modulo bias on the second draw
description: The draw index picker uses rejection sampling to avoid modulo bias, but the fallback branch (when the first 48-bit value lands in the biased tail) re-hashes once and then unconditionally returns `v2 % N` without re-checking the acceptance bound. For raffles where N does not divide 2^48 evenly, the fallback path reintroduces a tiny modulo bias toward low indices. The probability of hitting the fallback at all is (2^48 mod N)/2^48 — astronomically small for realistic ticket counts — so the practical fairness impact is negligible, but for a draw whose entire selling point is verifiable fairness, a provably-unbiased loop is cheap insurance and avoids an awkward question if the algorithm is ever audited.
evidence: `if (value < acceptUpTo) return value % N; const next = createHash('sha256').update(bytes).digest(); let v2 = 0; for (let i = 0; i < 6; i += 1) v2 = v2 * 256 + next[i]; return v2 % N;` — the second value is returned with `% N` even if it also exceeds acceptUpTo.
recommendation: Loop the rejection sampling (re-hash and re-test against acceptUpTo) until a value below the bound is found, rather than returning a single re-hashed value with `% N`.

verdict.reasoning:
Verified against backend/src/raffles/raffles.service.ts:1418-1428. The code matches the finding verbatim: pickModBig accepts the first 48-bit draw only when `value < acceptUpTo` (line 1423), but the fallback (lines 1424-1427) re-hashes once and returns `v2 % N` with NO re-test against acceptUpTo. So for any N that does not divide 2^48 evenly, the fallback path does reintroduce a modulo bias toward low indices. The bug is genuine, not a false positive.

However, the practical impact is even smaller than 'LOW' suggests, for two compounding reasons: (1) P(reaching the fallback) = (2^48 mod N)/2^48; with realistic ticket counts N (eligible.length at line 893, plausibly <=10^6 even for a huge raffle) this is < 10^6/2.8e14 ≈ 3.5e-9. (2) The bias WITHIN the fallback is the same tail fraction ≈3.5e-9. The excess probability for any given low index is the product ≈1e-17 — far below the entropy non-uniformity of SHA-256 itself and entirely unobservable. 

Caller context (runDraw, lines 857-916) also shows a larger, already-accepted source of non-uniformity: the linear-probe collision handling for backup winners (lines 896-900, `probe = (idx+1) % N`) skews toward indices following a used ticket far more than the modulo tail ever could. So a 'provably unbiased loop' here is cosmetic. The finder correctly self-rated it negligible. It is a real correctness-hygiene nit worth a one-line fix (loop the rejection sampling) but has zero money/fairness/legal impact; it sits at the very bottom of LOW.

title: Stale frontend comment claims seller real names are still shipped in the listing payload (no leak, but misleading)
description: The listing detail page correctly renders username only, and the backend public endpoints (listings.service.ts findById line 657-664 and browse line 626-642) explicitly DO NOT select firstName/lastName, so there is no real-name leak — the username-only compliance rule is upheld. However, the frontend comment asserts 'firstName/lastName are still in the payload for internal flows ... but the listing surface is username-only', which is factually wrong for this endpoint (those fields are not in the payload) and could mislead a future developer into believing it is safe to render them, or into thinking the data is present when it is not. Worth correcting to prevent a future accidental leak introduced on the back of a false assumption.
evidence: Frontend: `/* Platform policy: public listings show the seller's username, never their real name. firstName/lastName are still in the payload for internal flows (KYC, order chips) but the listing surface is username-only. */`. Backend findById select: `seller: { select: { id: true, clerkId: true, // firstName/lastName are explicitly NOT selected here ... username: true, ... } }`.
recommendation: Update the comment to state that the public listing payload does not include firstName/lastName at all (they are only fetched in admin/KYC/own-data contexts), so nobody is tempted to render fields that aren't there or to add them back.

verdict.reasoning: Traced the full path. Frontend page frontend/app/listings/[id]/page.tsx fetches GET /listings/${id} (line 55) and renders only listing.seller.username (line 489). That route maps to ListingsController @Get(':id') -> findById (listings.controller.ts:58-62). The findById seller select (listings.service.ts:657-677) does NOT include firstName/lastName — confirmed by Grep: those two tokens appear in this service ONLY inside comments (lines 629, 630, 661), never in a select. Browse select (lines 626-642) also omits them. So the compliance claim is upheld: no real-name leak, username-only rule intact. The frontend comment (lines 484-487) is genuinely inaccurate for THIS payload: it states 'firstName/lastName are still in the payload for internal flows (KYC, order chips)' — but those fields are not in the listing payload at all; the comment conflates 'exists on the User model elsewhere' with 'present in this object.' A future dev could be misled into rendering listing.seller.firstName (would be undefined) or re-adding it to the select on a false 'it's already here' assumption. That said, the risk is bounded: the same code path carries two CORRECT, explicit guardrail comments (backend lines 629-632 and 661-663: 'explicitly NOT selected here — listing detail must not leak the seller's real identity'), so a dev adding the field would hit a contradicting warning at the select site. Real documentation-hygiene issue, no security/compliance impact, correctly rated LOW.

title: Declined card payment is shown to the buyer as "Payment successful"
description: The payment-result page decides success purely from the HTTP status (`if (res.ok)`), ignoring the `success` field in the response body. The backend `verifyResult` (backend/src/payments/transactions.service.ts:274-287) returns HTTP 200 with `{ success: false, resultCode }` when Peach reports the card was DECLINED — it only throws (→ HTTP 400) when the verify call itself errors. So a genuinely declined payment returns 200, the frontend treats it as `res.ok`, sets status `'ok'`, renders "Payment successful", and redirects the buyer to `/transactions/{id}` as if they bought the item. Meanwhile the backend has already reverted the listing to ACTIVE (revertListing). The buyer walks away believing they paid; they did not.
evidence: Frontend: `if (res.ok) { setStatus('ok'); setTimeout(() => router.replace(`/transactions/${transactionId}`), 1500); } else { setStatus('failed'); }`. Backend verifyResult: `if (result.isSuccess) { await this.markPaid(...); return { success: true }; } await this.revertListing(tx.listingId); return { success: false, resultCode: result.resultCode };` — the decline branch returns normally (HTTP 200).
recommendation: Parse the JSON body and gate on `success === true`, not just `res.ok`. Treat `{ success: false }` as a failed payment (show the failure UI). Only `success === true` should redirect to the order page.

verdict.reasoning:
VERIFIED REAL. Traced the full path; no mitigation exists anywhere.

1) Peach decline does NOT throw. peach.service.ts:95-119 — verifyPayment GETs the resourcePath; a declined card returns Peach HTTP 200 with a non-success result.code, so res.ok is true (line 105) and it returns normally with isSuccess:false (line 117, SUCCESS_PATTERN fails on decline codes e.g. 800.100.*).

2) verifyResult returns normally on decline. transactions.service.ts:280-282 — `await this.revertListing(tx.listingId); return { success: false, resultCode }` with no exception. revertListing (1086-1091) flips the listing back to ACTIVE.

3) Controller returns 2xx. transactions.controller.ts:91-97 — plain @Post, no guard, no @HttpCode, returns the service object directly. main.ts (read in full) registers only ValidationPipe + CORS; Grep across backend/src found NO global interceptor or exception filter. So a normally-returned {success:false} serializes with a 2xx status → frontend res.ok === true.

4) Frontend gates on res.ok only. checkout/complete/page.tsx:30-35 — ignores the success field, sets status 'ok', renders "Payment successful" (line 67), redirects to /transactions/{id} (line 32).

5) The order page reinforces the false success. schema.prisma:719 `paymentStatus PaymentStatus @default(HELD)` means the row is HELD from creation (create() never sets it; transactions.service.ts:174-201) and a decline never changes it. transactions/[id]/page.tsx:859 therefore renders the "Payment held" badge and line 884 shows "You paid R…". No failure UI fires for this state (rejected/REFUNDED banners require rejectedAt, which a decline never sets), and the only honest chip (line 463) is hidden because it gates on tx.paidAt (null after a decline).

Net: a buyer whose card was genuinely declined sees "Payment successful," lands on an order page saying "Payment held," while the listing silently returns to sale and no funds were captured. The webhook path (handlePeachWebhook) is separate and does not repair the buyer's UI. The recommended fix (parse JSON, gate on success === true) is correct.

Severity: the rubric reserves CRITICAL for money loss / data loss / data leak / clear legal exposure. Here no money moves (card declined) and there is no cross-user data exposure, so it falls short of that bar. It is a broken core checkout-result flow that will mislead buyers on the first declined card (disputes, confusion-driven chargebacks, trust + plausible SA consumer-protection exposure on a regulated payments product) — top-of-band HIGH. The prior CRITICAL is mildly overstated.

title: "Your card was not charged" is a false guarantee when verification errors out
description: On the `failed` branch the page tells the buyer "Your card was not charged. Please try again or contact support." But `failed` is reached whenever `verify-result` is non-OK or the fetch throws — including the case where the backend's `verifyResult` throws `BadRequestException('Payment verification failed')` because Peach was unreachable/timed out (transactions.service.ts:283-286). In that path the payment status is UNKNOWN: the card may well have been charged at Peach and only the result-page confirmation failed (the separate Peach webhook handler, handlePeachWebhook, exists precisely because the result page is unreliable and will markPaid independently). Asserting the card was not charged can drive the buyer to retry and double-pay, or to dispute a charge support can't immediately explain.
evidence:
`

Your card was not charged. Please try again or contact support.

` shown for all non-success outcomes, while backend verifyResult catch block throws on Peach errors: `this.logger.error('Peach verify failed', err); throw new BadRequestException('Payment verification failed');`
recommendation: Distinguish a confirmed decline (`success:false`) from an unknown/verification-error state. For the unknown state, use neutral copy like "We couldn't confirm your payment yet — do NOT retry; check your order status in a few minutes or contact support" instead of guaranteeing no charge.

verdict.reasoning: Verified end-to-end and the mechanism holds. frontend/app/checkout/complete/page.tsx:30-38 keys the result purely on res.ok and collapses BOTH the non-OK HTTP branch (line 34) and the fetch catch (line 37) into a single `failed` state, which unconditionally renders "Your card was not charged. Please try again or contact support." (lines 86-88) plus a "Try again" button (89-95). backend transactions.service.ts:274-286 throws BadRequestException('Payment verification failed') (HTTP 400) whenever peach.verifyPayment throws — and peach.service.ts:105-108 throws on any non-2xx/network error of the verify GET. So a Peach verify-call timeout or 5xx that occurs AFTER the card was actually charged at Peach produces the false "not charged" message. The charge is independent of our verify call: the notificationUrl webhook is registered at checkout creation (peach.service.ts:70) and PaymentsWebhookController.peachWebhook (transactions.controller.ts:284-310) -> handlePeachWebhook -> markPaid (service:319-320) will later mark the tx HELD. The webhook's very existence confirms the result page is non-authoritative. main.ts has no exception filter/interceptor that would alter these status codes, so the path is real, not mitigated. Consequence: a definite false guarantee about money on a regulated SA financial platform, with the retry CTA inviting double-pay and the false claim driving disputes. I am downgrading HIGH to MEDIUM: it requires a gateway verify-time error coincident with a successful charge (edge case, not the happy path) and does not auto-move money (retry needs the user to re-enter card details), so it is not a broken core flow or an at-launch likely incident — but it is a genuine, easily-fixed correctness/trust bug. Recommendation as written is sound: distinguish confirmed decline (success:false) from unknown/verification-error and use neutral "we couldn't confirm your payment yet — do not retry, check order status / contact support" copy, suppressing the retry button in the unknown state. Side observation in the same component (not the assigned finding): res.ok-only logic means a genuine card DECLINE returns HTTP 200 {success:false} (service:281) and would incorrectly render "Payment successful" and redirect — a separate bug in the opposite direction.

title: Peach widget result URL falls back to a relative path (NEXT_PUBLIC_FRONTEND_URL never set)
description: Both checkout forms build the Peach COPYandPAY widget's post-payment `action` (shopperResultUrl) as `${process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_FRONTEND_URL ?? ''}/checkout/complete?...`. `NEXT_PUBLIC_FRONTEND_URL` is not defined in `.env.example` or `.env.local`, so in practice it resolves to an empty string and the action becomes a relative URL `/checkout/complete?...`. Peach expects an absolute shopperResultUrl; a relative value is fragile across the widget's redirect/iframe context and an operator following .env.example has no hint this var exists. Same code path duplicated in the offer checkout form (offer-checkout-form.tsx:174).
evidence: `action={`${process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_FRONTEND_URL ?? ''}/checkout/complete?transactionId=${checkout.transactionId}`}` — and `grep NEXT_PUBLIC_FRONTEND_URL .env.example .env.local` returns nothing.
recommendation: Add NEXT_PUBLIC_FRONTEND_URL to .env.example (and the prod env) with the public https origin, or derive an absolute origin client-side via window.location.origin as a fallback. Verify the Peach return flow end-to-end against a real transaction.

verdict.reasoning:
VERIFIED REAL, severity correctly rated MEDIUM, but the finding's impact analysis is incomplete (it missed a backend safety net).

Confirmed mechanical claims:
- Both checkout forms build the COPYandPAY widget action as a relative URL when the env var is unset: frontend/app/checkout/[listingId]/checkout-form.tsx:589 and frontend/app/checkout/offer/[offerId]/offer-checkout-form.tsx:174 both contain action={`${process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_FRONTEND_URL ?? ''}/checkout/complete?transactionId=...`}.
- NEXT_PUBLIC_FRONTEND_URL is genuinely undefined: not in frontend/.env.example (lines 8-18 list NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL and Clerk vars only), not in frontend/.env.local (which DOES exist, 1133 bytes — minor correction to the finding's wording — but has no such var), and next.config.mjs has no `env` block injecting it. Next.js inlines process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_FRONTEND_URL at build time, so unset → undefined → ?? '' → '' → relative path. Across the whole repo, FRONTEND_URL/NEXT_PUBLIC_FRONTEND_URL appears only in BACKEND files/scripts, never in any frontend config or deploy doc.
- The redirect target page /checkout/complete/page.tsx exists (Bash ls + Grep confirm; Glob's ** missed it due to the bracketed sibling dirs) and reads resourcePath from the Peach-appended query string to POST /transactions/:id/verify-result.

Nuance the finding MISSED (reduces blast radius, justifies MEDIUM not higher): the backend ALREADY supplies a correct absolute shopperResultUrl when creating the Peach checkout — transactions.service.ts:219 builds `${frontendUrl}/checkout/complete?...` and peach.service.ts:69 sends it as 'shopperResultUrl' to /v1/checkouts; frontendUrl comes from process.env.FRONTEND_URL with a request protocol+host fallback (transactions.controller.ts:83-84). So the checkout-level redirect URL is correct regardless of the broken frontend action. In OPPWA COPYandPAY the form `action` can override that checkout-level value, so a relative action is still genuinely fragile (after the on-by-default 3DS redirect — CLAUDE.md:480 — Peach needs an absolute URL to return the browser; a relative path could resolve against oppwa.com and strand a paying buyer). But whether the widget honors the form action over the checkout-level URL, and whether its client-side JS pre-resolves the relative action against the gungalore origin (which would make it work), is implementation-dependent — hence medium confidence on real-world breakage.

Net: a real, undocumented pre-launch config gap on the live payment-return path that an operator following .env.example would miss; not money-loss (charge still verifies via resourcePath/webhook and the backend URL is correct), so not CRITICAL/HIGH. The recommendation (add the var to .env.example + prod, or fall back to window.location.origin client-side) is correct and cheap.

title: Offer checkout charges item-price only with no live shipping quote, unlike standard checkout
description: The standard checkout form fetches a live shipping quote and blocks Pay until `quoteState.kind === 'ready'`, showing a full item+shipping+processing breakdown. The offer checkout form does neither: `isReady()` for PUDO only requires a selected locker (no quote), the button always reads `Pay {settledAmount}` (the agreed item price, no shipping line), and there is no order-summary breakdown. Since the backend recomputes the real total server-side, the buyer can be charged a different amount than the `settledAmount` shown (if shipping is added), or shipping silently isn't billed for offer purchases — either way it's an undisclosed price discrepancy on a money path.
evidence: offer-checkout-form: `function isReady() { if (method === 'PUDO') return !!selectedLocker; ... }` and button label `{submitting ? 'Setting up payment…' : `Pay ${formatPrice(settledAmount)}`}` — no quoteState, no previewBreakdown, no shipping line. Compare checkout-form.tsx:463-465 which requires `quoteState.kind === 'ready'`.
recommendation: Mirror the standard checkout: fetch the shipping quote for PUDO/TCG, show the item+shipping+processing breakdown, and make the Pay button reflect the true total the buyer will be charged.

verdict.reasoning:
The core observation is real but the finding is overstated and its severity is too high. VERIFIED against the actual code:

REAL part: For a non-firearm TAKE_A_SHOT offer, the offer checkout form (frontend/app/checkout/offer/[offerId]/offer-checkout-form.tsx) differs from the standard form. isReady() (lines 91-105) gates PUDO only on a selected locker (no quote), there is no live shipping quote, no itemized order summary, and the Pay button (line 275) reads `Pay ${formatPrice(settledAmount)}` — the item price only. The backend DOES add shipping: transactions.service.ts:119-151 re-fetches a live PUDO/TCG quote server-side for BOTH offer and direct checkout (no offer-specific skip), fee.calculator.ts:113-115 computes buyerTotal = listingPrice + shippingCost + processingFee, and line 226 charges Peach amountZarCents: buyerTotal. So the buyer's card is charged settledAmount + shipping + processing while the button shows only settledAmount. The button understatement is genuine.

OVERSTATED / WRONG: (1) The finding's "or shipping silently isn't billed for offer purchases" branch is false — shipping is unambiguously billed server-side. (2) The bigger correction: the buyer is NOT charged a different amount silently. handleProceed() swaps to the confirmation screen (offer-checkout-form.tsx:131-154) which renders the true "Total charged" = formatPrice(checkout.breakdown.buyerTotal) (shipping+processing included; backend returns buyerTotal at transactions.service.ts:257) on the SAME screen as the Peach card-entry widget (lines 170-178). The card form only appears there, so the buyer sees the real higher total BEFORE entering card details and before any charge. It is a two-step button-then-confirm, not a silent overcharge — no money loss, no undisclosed final price at point of payment.

Net: a real disclosure/UX inconsistency (misleading Pay-button label + missing live quote and shipping line item that the standard checkout has), but mitigated by the pre-charge confirmation screen showing the correct total. Not a financial-correctness breach. (Separately, I noticed offer page hardcodes isFirearm={false} — a firearm TAKE_A_SHOT would render PUDO/TCG and be backend-rejected — but that is a different latent bug, not this finding.)

title: /ask-gg is not a public route, so signed-out users are bounced to sign-in and never see the in-page SignInRequiredCard
description: The Ask GG page is designed as a marketing/acquisition surface: when `isLoaded && !isSignedIn` it renders a rich `SignInRequiredCard` with the tier-perks comparison table and a sign-in CTA (frontend/app/ask-gg/page.tsx:210, 376, 1810). But `/ask-gg` is absent from `isPublicRoute` in the middleware, so a signed-out visitor is redirected to `/sign-in` before the page ever renders. The carefully-built signed-out hero is effectively dead code, and a curious prospect tapping an Ask-GG link is dropped on a bare sign-in form instead of the value pitch.
evidence: isPublicRoute list contains `/`, `/listings(.*)`, `/competitions(.*)`, `/sellers(.*)` etc. but no `/ask-gg`. Middleware then does `const { userId } = await auth(); if (!userId) { ... return NextResponse.redirect(signInUrl); }`. The page's `showSignInCard = isLoaded && !isSignedIn` branch can therefore never be reached.
recommendation: Either add `/ask-gg` to the public-route matcher so the SignInRequiredCard renders for signed-out users (the backend chat endpoint stays Clerk-guarded regardless), or delete the dead signed-out UI if the gate is intentional.

verdict.reasoning:
VERIFIED REAL; technical claim is fully correct, severity slightly overstated.

Trace confirmed:
- frontend/middleware.ts:4-38 — `isPublicRoute` lists `/`, `/listings(.*)`, `/competitions(.*)`, `/sellers(.*)`, legal pages, etc., but NOT `/ask-gg`.
- middleware.ts:146-151 — the matcher `'/((?!_next|...).*)'` catches `/ask-gg` (it's not a static asset).
- middleware.ts:98 `if (isPublicRoute(request)) return;` is skipped for /ask-gg; the /checkout token bypass (105-110) doesn't apply; so line 117 `const { userId } = await auth();` runs and 118-142 returns `NextResponse.redirect(signInUrl)` for any signed-out visitor.
- frontend/app/ask-gg/page.tsx:1 is `'use client'`, so middleware runs first on the navigation and the page never renders. Therefore page.tsx:210 `const showSignInCard = isLoaded && !isSignedIn;` → :376-377 `<SignInRequiredCard />` → def at :1810 (a full marketing hero with `<TierPerksTable current={null}/>` at :1877 and a `<SignInButton mode="modal">` at :1886) is unreachable for signed-out users = dead code.

Crucially, this is corroborated by the developers' own stated intent, contradicting the middleware:
- components/bottom-tab-bar.tsx:370-373 — "Page itself is open (no auth gate at the route level) so signed-out users see the marketing/upgrade surface; FREE tier sees an upgrade card; MEMBER + PRO get the live chat."
- ask-gg/page.tsx:7-9 — signed-out is the intended state 1.

Reachability confirmed: the `/ask-gg` links are NOT wrapped in a Clerk `<SignedIn>` guard. nav.tsx:131-136 (desktop) renders the link unconditionally; bottom-tab-bar.tsx:367-376 registers the Ask GG tab and the bar self-gates only on `isStandalone` (line 338 `if (!isStandalone) return null;`), not on auth. So signed-out PWA users / desktop nav users / anyone following a shared link can hit /ask-gg and get bounced to a bare /sign-in form (with redirect_url back to /ask-gg).

Not a false positive: no guard/redirect elsewhere rescues it; the backend chat endpoint being Clerk-guarded is irrelevant to the routing/UX claim (page comment :8 already notes the backend stays guarded). The fix (add `/ask-gg` to isPublicRoute) is safe.

Severity correction: This is purely an acquisition-funnel/UX defect plus dead code. No security, money, data-loss, or compliance exposure (the word 'escrow' / real-name rules are not implicated; backend stays auth-guarded). Impact is bounded to one marketing page's signed-out experience. MEDIUM is borderline-defensible given a whole documented signed-out hero is rendered unreachable and a deliberate marketing funnel is defeated, but the most accurate rating is LOW — it degrades polish/edge UX for signed-out visitors on a paid feature rather than breaking a core flow.

title: Buyer's full real name leaked to seller in offer notifications (email/SMS/in-app), violating username-only policy
description: Gun Galore policy (enforced everywhere else) is that other users only ever see @username, never a real name. When a buyer makes an offer, notifySellerOfOffer sets buyerName to the buyer's FULL LEGAL NAME (firstName + lastName) and the offerReceived notification renders it to the seller in the in-app inbox body, the email body, the email preheader AND the SMS. This happens at the offer stage, before any transaction commitment and before any consented contact exchange. The same full-name leak repeats for counter-offer accept/decline (notifications.service.ts:1365, 1375, 1402, 1412, fed from offers.service.ts:526, 547).
evidence: offers.service.ts:409  `buyerName: `${offer.buyer.firstName ?? ''} ${offer.buyer.lastName ?? ''}`.trim() || 'A buyer',`  then notifications.service.ts:1188  ``body: `Hi ${b(d.sellerName)}, ${b(d.buyerName)} has made an offer on your listing ${b(d.listingTitle)}...``` and SMS 1204 ``Gun Galore: ${truncate(d.buyerName, 20)} offered R...``. Contrast offers.service.ts:304 (the in-app received-offers API) which deliberately selects `buyer: { username: true ... }` with the comment 'Buyer identity stays private until checkout completes.' — so the in-app surface is correct but the notification channel leaks the legal name.
recommendation: Replace buyerName in offer/counter notifications with offer.buyer.username (fall back to a generic 'A buyer' if username is null). The seller does not need the buyer's legal name to accept/reject an offer. Mirror the same fix for sellerName where a real name is sent to the other party pre-transaction.

verdict.reasoning:
VERIFIED REAL. Traced the full path in C:\dev\gun-galore.
