The leak: offers.service.ts:409 builds buyerName = `${offer.buyer.firstName} ${offer.buyer.lastName}` and passes it to notifications.service.ts `offerReceived`, which renders the BUYER's real name TO THE SELLER across four channels: in-app body (1178), email body (1188 "Hi {sellerName}, {buyerName} has made an offer..."), email preheader (1194), and SMS (1204). The b() helper (line 289) only HTML-escapes — no redaction; truncate() (2374) just slices. Same leak repeats for counter accept/reject: offers.service.ts:526 -> counterAccepted (in-app 1365, email 1375, preheader 1380) and offers.service.ts:547 -> counterRejected (in-app 1402, email 1412, preheader 1417). All paths are reachable: notifySellerOfOffer fires on offer creation (offers.service.ts:113), the counter notifiers fire at lines 229/250.

Schema confirms severity: User.firstName/lastName (schema.prisma:222-223) are real legal names, populated from the Home Affairs SA ID lookup (schema comment 255-256); username (213) is the "Public-facing handle." So this discloses a buyer's verified legal name to another user.

The platform's own documented boundary is explicit and is being violated: offers.service.ts:286 ("Public-facing — username only, no real name") and 303 ("Buyer identity stays private UNTIL CHECKOUT COMPLETES") select username-only on the in-app API, yet the notification channel sends the legal name at the OFFER stage — pre-checkout, pre-payment. The auction analogue bidPlaced (notifications 1441) correctly omits the bidder identity entirely. Real names ARE legitimately exchanged later (transactions.service.ts:683-685, dealer-verification.service.ts:368/383) but only post-purchase for the SAPS dealer transfer — confirming the pre-checkout disclosure is the anomaly, not intended behaviour. Matches the user's standing rule "Never expose real names to other users."

One correction to the finding: its recommendation also says to fix sellerName "where a real name is sent to the other party pre-transaction." In these offer notifications sellerName is only ever used to greet the seller themselves (own-name salutation) and is never sent to the buyer, so that half is unnecessary. The actionable fix is to swap buyerName -> offer.buyer.username (fallback 'A buyer') at offers.service.ts:409, 526, 547. Mitigating factors that cap this below CRITICAL: only the name leaks (no phone/email/address/ID in these payloads), and it only fires for buyers who have a name on file (pure buyers without KYC fall back to 'A buyer').

title: Other party's real name (and buyer email) returned in transaction API response for all non-PRIVATE_ARRANGE orders
category: Real-name leakage / personal data between users
description: findById() selects firstName, lastName, email and phone for BOTH buyer and seller, then a redaction block tries to strip contact details for non-PRIVATE_ARRANGE orders. The block only blanks the OTHER party's phone (and the seller's email). It never blanks firstName/lastName for either party, and never blanks the buyer's email. As a result, for every ordinary order (e.g. a normal DEALER_TRANSFER firearm sale or a PUDO courier sale) the counterparty's legal first + last name sits in the JSON API response. The order page only renders the full name inside the PRIVATE_ARRANGE-gated UI block, so it is not visible on screen — but any party to the transaction can read the other person's real name (and the buyer's email) straight out of the network response. This contradicts the comment at lines 736-739 which claims the block prevents exactly this leak, and it breaches the platform's own no-real-names policy and POPIA minimisation.
evidence: Lines 744-757: `if (!isPaidPrivateArrange) { if (tx.buyerId !== user.id) tx.buyer.phone = null; if (tx.sellerId !== user.id) { tx.seller.phone = null; (tx.seller as unknown as { email: string | null }).email = null; } }` — firstName, lastName and tx.buyer.email are never cleared. The same firstName/lastName-for-both-parties exposure exists in the order-list endpoint findMany() at lines 685-686.
recommendation: In the non-PRIVATE_ARRANGE branch, also null out the OTHER party's firstName, lastName and email (the buyer's email is currently never stripped). Better: only select username for the counterparty and select real-name/contact fields solely when isPaidPrivateArrange is true, so the personal data never enters the response object at all.

verdict.reasoning:
Verified REAL by tracing the full path. In backend/src/payments/transactions.service.ts:707-726, findById() selects firstName, lastName, email, phone for BOTH buyer and seller. The redaction block at lines 744-757 only nulls the OTHER party's phone (and the seller's email) for non-PRIVATE_ARRANGE orders; it never nulls firstName/lastName for either side and never nulls the buyer's email. The block's own comment (736-739) claims it stops this leak — it does not for names. schema.prisma:255-256 confirms firstName/lastName are the user's LEGAL names populated from the Home Affairs SA ID (KYC) lookup, i.e. exactly the data the no-real-names policy and POPIA minimisation protect.

No serialization strips the fields: transactions.controller.ts:114-118 returns the service result raw, and a repo-wide grep for ClassSerializerInterceptor/useGlobalInterceptors/APP_INTERCEPTOR found NONE. The endpoint is independently client-reachable — ClerkGuard (clerk.guard.ts:36-73) accepts any valid Clerk bearer token, the authorization check (service lines 732-734) only confirms the requester is the buyer or seller of THAT tx (not field-level), and the NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL pattern is used across the frontend, so a party to the transaction can GET /api/transactions/{id} with their own token and read the counterparty's legal name + (for the buyer) email straight from the JSON. The order page (frontend .../transactions/[id]/page.tsx:169,173) renders only username on screen and shows the full name solely inside the PRIVATE_ARRANGE-gated card (206-246), so the leak is in the network payload, not the visible UI — exactly as the finding states. The same firstName/lastName-for-both-parties exposure also exists in findForUser() at lines 685-686, returned raw by findAll (controller 102-109).

Adversarial falsification attempts all failed: no DTO/interceptor field-stripping; names are real KYC identities not usernames; auth is row-level not field-level; SSR does not save it because the API is directly reachable. Finding is accurate and correctly described.

Severity: I keep it HIGH rather than CRITICAL. It is a genuine cross-user personal-data leak that breaches the platform's explicit no-real-names policy, but the blast radius is bounded to the single counterparty in an existing transaction (not public, not arbitrary-user enumeration), and the leaked data is name + email only (no ID number, address, or financial data). Real and correctly rated.

title: Offer-checkout hardcodes isFirearm=false, breaking the mandatory dealer-transfer route for offer-based firearm purchases
category: SAPS dealer-transfer flow / broken core flow
description: When a buyer wins/accepts an offer, the offer-checkout page renders OfferCheckoutForm with isFirearm hardcoded to false, even though offer.listing is available. The form uses isFirearm to choose shipping options: `allowedMethods = isFirearm ? ['DEALER_TRANSFER'] : ['PUDO', 'TCG']` and defaults the method to PUDO. So for an accepted offer on a FIREARM listing the buyer is shown PUDO/TCG courier options and is never offered DEALER_TRANSFER, and the dealer picker never appears. The backend correctly rejects this (validateShippingMethod in transactions.service.ts:1224-1241 throws 'Firearms must ship via DEALER_TRANSFER or PRIVATE_ARRANGE' for a firearm), so it is NOT an illegal-shipment hole — but it means a buyer fills in card details and is rejected at submit, and there is no UI path to complete a legitimate firearm purchase through the offer flow at all. Offer-based firearm sales are effectively broken.
evidence: page.tsx:102 `isFirearm={false}` while offer.listing is fully loaded (the regular checkout at checkout/[listingId]/checkout-form.tsx:114-123 correctly uses listing.isFirearm). offer-checkout-form.tsx:78 `const allowedMethods: ShippingMethod[] = isFirearm ? ['DEALER_TRANSFER'] : ['PUDO', 'TCG'];` and :55 default `useState<ShippingMethod>(isFirearm ? 'DEALER_TRANSFER' : 'PUDO')`.
recommendation: Pass the real value: include isFirearm on the offer DTO (offer.listing already exists server-side) and render `<OfferCheckoutForm ... isFirearm={offer.listing.isFirearm} />`. Ensure the dealer-selection UI is wired into offer-checkout-form the same way it is in the main checkout form.

verdict.reasoning:
VERIFIED REAL, rating correct. Traced the full path.

BUG CONFIRMED: frontend/app/checkout/offer/[offerId]/page.tsx:102 hardcodes isFirearm={false}. The form gates on it: offer-checkout-form.tsx:78 `allowedMethods = isFirearm ? ['DEALER_TRANSFER'] : ['PUDO','TCG']`, :55 default method PUDO, and :196 the method picker only renders `{!isFirearm && ...}`. The DEALER_TRANSFER block (:255 `{method === 'DEALER_TRANSFER' && ...}`) can never render because method is locked to PUDO/TCG. So a firearm offer shows only courier options and has no UI path to dealer transfer.

REACHABILITY CONFIRMED (the make-or-break check): firearm listings CAN be TAKE_A_SHOT — listings.service.ts:127-145 imposes no firearm/TAKE_A_SHOT exclusion (only requires firearms include DEALER_TRANSFER in shippingMethods), and create-listing.dto.ts:29 supports TAKE_A_SHOT for any category. Offers are allowed on any TAKE_A_SHOT listing regardless of isFirearm (offers.service.ts:56-58). Buyers reach /checkout/offer/[offerId] from offer-panel.tsx:61 and my/offers/page.tsx:201. So a firearm + make-an-offer purchase routes here.

NOT A SHIPMENT HOLE (finding states this correctly): transactions.service.ts:94-95 reads listing.isFirearm server-side and validateShipping (1234-1238) throws 'Firearms must ship via DEALER_TRANSFER or PRIVATE_ARRANGE'. Backend is authoritative; no illegal courier shipment of a firearm occurs. (Note: actual method name is validateShipping, not validateShippingMethod, but same lines/behaviour.)

NO ALTERNATIVE WORKING PATH (finding missed this; it strengthens the verdict): the SMS CHECKOUT action-token redirects to /checkout/[listingId]?t=token (action-tokens.controller.ts:582), but that page hard-returns notFound() for any non-BUY_NOW listing (checkout/[listingId]/page.tsx:34), its form never sends offerId, and it relies on listing.price which is null for TAKE_A_SHOT (enforced at listings.service.ts:130-131). So the SMS path is also dead for offer checkouts — /checkout/offer/[offerId] is the ONLY entry point, and it is broken for firearms.

ONE CORRECTION to the finding's premise: isFirearm is NOT currently present in the offer payload. Backend offers.service.ts getById (314-325) selects listing { id, title, autoAcceptThreshold, passFeeToBuyer, seller } — no isFirearm; and the frontend Offer type (lib/types.ts:373-380) omits it. The author's 'offer.listing is fully loaded' is imprecise. The fix therefore requires adding isFirearm to the backend select AND the Offer type, then passing offer.listing.isFirearm. The DealerTransferConsent UI already exists in the offer form (:255-260), so only the method-gating needs fixing, not new dealer UI.

NET EFFECT: a buyer with an accepted offer on a firearm enters card details, picks PUDO (only option), clicks Pay, and is hard-rejected at submit with no way to complete the purchase. Core regulated flow broken, no workaround, but no money loss / data leak / illegal shipment. Matches HIGH ('a core flow is broken'). Only mild mitigant is that it affects the firearm + TAKE_A_SHOT subset, but that is a normal first-class scenario for this platform, not an edge case — HIGH stands.

title: The banned word "escrow" appears in user-facing Terms of Service
lines: 161 (user-facing); also referenced in the file's comment at 11-14
description: Operator policy (and CLAUDE.md line 215: 'The word "escrow" never appears anywhere — not in code, UI') is an absolute ban on the regulated SA financial term 'escrow' in user-facing copy, because Gun Galore is not registered to operate an escrow product. title: No code-level enforcement of competency certificate / possession licence / 18+ age for firearm transactions
lines: User model (no competency/possessionLicence/dateOfBirth fields anywhere in schema); checkout flow frontend/app/checkout/[listingId]/checkout-form.tsx has no attestation gate
description: The Firearms Compliance Policy and Terms require both parties to a firearm transaction to be 18+ and hold a valid SAPS Competency Certificate (and Possession Licence for buyers). However, there is no data model or runtime gate enforcing this. A schema search finds no competency, possessionLicence/possessionLicense, or dateOfBirth/dob field on User (or anywhere). The firearm checkout flow only constrains the shipping method to DEALER_TRANSFER; it does not require the buyer to even tick a 'I hold a valid competency certificate / I am 18+' attestation. Eligibility currently rests entirely on the dealer's manual licence check at handover (firearms-compliance section 5) and on prose in the Terms — there is no platform-side record or checkbox, which weakens the audit trail and means an under-age or non-competent buyer can transact up to the point of dealer handover with no platform friction.
evidence: grep for competency|possessionLicence|dateOfBirth across schema.prisma returns no matching field. grep for competency|attest|licen[cs]e across frontend/app/checkout returns only shipping-method and 'SAPS-licensed dealer' label strings — no eligibility attestation control. The dealer-verification service (backend/src/payments/dealer-verification.service.ts) verifies the post-sale SAPS 534 + stock register photos, not the buyer's pre-purchase competency.
recommendation: At minimum add a mandatory pre-payment attestation gate on firearm checkout (buyer confirms 18+, holds competency + possession licence / pending application) and persist the attestation timestamp on the transaction for the audit trail. Consider capturing competency/licence reference numbers on the User or Transaction so SAPS audit requests can be answered, and so the platform is not relying solely on free-text policy plus the dealer's discretion.

verdict.reasoning:
VERIFIED REAL and correctly rated MEDIUM. The factual claims all hold up under tracing:

1. No User fields for eligibility: User model (schema.prisma:207-336) has kycStatus, kycIdHash (SA ID hash), idNumberEncrypted, etc., but NO competency, possessionLicence, or dateOfBirth/age field. Confirmed.

2. No Transaction attestation field: Transaction (schema.prisma:689-879) persists privateArrangeAcceptedAt (line 792) and post-sale dealer-verification fields (saps534PhotoUrl, dealerVerificationStatus, etc.), but NO buyer competency/age/possession-licence attestation. Confirmed.

3. Checkout has no eligibility gate: I read both consent components. DealerTransferConsent (checkout-form.tsx:1603-1617) only attests "I understand Gun Galore holds my funds until... verified" — funds-held mechanics. PrivateArrangeConsent (1710-1748) only attests to waiving payment protection + contact-detail sharing. Neither mentions 18+, competency, or possession licence. Confirmed.

4. Backend has no buyer-eligibility check: grep across backend/src found only (a) dealer-verification.service.ts matches on the post-sale SAPS 534 "Notification of Change in Possession" form (dealer-completed, post-sale — already acknowledged by the finding), and (b) verifynow.service.ts:151 extracts `dob` from the Home Affairs API response for SELLERS but does NOT persist it (no dob column exists). No buyer competency/age gate anywhere.

5. The platform DOES know which listings are firearms (Category.isFirearm/requiresLicence schema.prisma:496-500; Listing.isFirearm:538), so a targeted gate is technically feasible — rebutting any "infeasible" defense.

6. Both Terms (terms/page.tsx §4 lines 88-92) and Firearms Compliance (firearms-compliance/page.tsx §2 lines 61-73) require 18+ and a valid Competency Certificate, but ONLY as prose policy with no code enforcement.

SEVERITY CORRECTLY CAPPED at MEDIUM (not higher) because the legally-enforced control point exists at the dealer, not the platform. Firearms Compliance §5 (lines 116-117, 124) is explicit: the buyer presents their Competency Certificate, Possession Licence and ID at the dealer's premises, and "The dealer is the responsible party for ensuring the buyer has the right to take possession." §11 (190-209) states GunGalore is NOT a SAPS dealer and explicitly does NOT verify licences. No firearm changes hands until the dealer completes SAPS 271/Section 17 paperwork, and for DEALER_TRANSFER the buyer's funds are held (refundable) until dealer stock-in verification. So an under-age/non-competent buyer is hard-stopped at the dealer with no money loss or illegal possession — the missing checkbox is a defence-in-depth / audit-trail gap, not a money/legal breach. The finding itself is honest: it scopes the issue to "weakens the audit trail" + "no platform friction," rates it MEDIUM, and recommends a pre-payment attestation persisted on the Transaction (mirroring the existing privateArrangeAcceptedAt pattern). That is an accurate and proportionate assessment — not a false positive, not overstated.

title: Dealer-transfer documentation/process mismatch: policy cites SAPS 271 while the verification system is built on SAPS 534, and the promised vetted-dealer directory does not exist
description: Two consistency gaps in the firearm-transfer story. (1) The Firearms Compliance Policy describes the dealer completing 'SAPS 271 / Section 17 forms' (line 117) and the buyer retaining a SAPS 271 (line 164), but the actual dealer-verification code is built entirely around the SAPS 534 'Notification of Change in Ownership / Possession' form (dealer-verification.service.ts:14, 57) plus the FCA Reg 86 stock-register entry. The two documents reference different SAPS forms, so the published process and the implemented process disagree. (2) The policy promises buyers choose a dealer 'from the directory of dealers GunGalore has vetted' (line 113) and lists 'Maintaining the directory of SAPS-licensed dealers' as a core function (line 200), but the verification code comment states 'We don't have a verified-dealer DB lookup anymore. Pass the seller-supplied dealer name so Claude can flag a mismatch' (dealer-verification.service.ts:209-211) — i.e. the dealer is free-text and unvetted. The public legal commitment overstates the actual control.
evidence: firearms-compliance/page.tsx:117 'Dealer completes the SAPS transfer paperwork (SAPS 271 / Section 17 forms...)' vs dealer-verification.service.ts:14 'SAPS 534 form — "Notification of Change in Ownership / Possession"'. firearms-compliance/page.tsx:113 '...from the directory of dealers GunGalore has vetted' vs dealer-verification.service.ts:209 'We don't have a verified-dealer DB lookup anymore.'
recommendation: Reconcile the form references (use the same SAPS form name the workflow actually verifies, or document both stages), and either (a) build the vetted-dealer directory the policy promises, or (b) amend the policy to say the buyer/seller nominate any SAPS-licensed dealer and Gun Galore verifies the resulting paperwork, so the public legal text matches the implemented control.

verdict.reasoning:
Both halves verified against actual code; not a false positive.

PART 1 (SAPS form mismatch) — REAL. Compliance policy frontend/app/(legal)/firearms-compliance/page.tsx:117 says the dealer completes "SAPS 271 / Section 17 forms" and :164 says the buyer retains "SAPS 271 (Possession Acquisition Notification)". But the implemented verification flow is built entirely on SAPS 534: backend/src/payments/dealer-verification.service.ts:14 and :479 ("SAPS 534 form — Notification of Change in Ownership/Possession"), and the SELLER-FACING UI frontend/app/transactions/[id]/dealer-verification/page.tsx:35-36 titles the upload slot "SAPS 534 form" / "Notification of Change in Possession". So two user-facing surfaces disagree on the form for the same transfer step. (The policy's SAPS 522 disposal ref at :153 is consistent and not in dispute; refund-policy :147 "Section 17" is unrelated CPA Section 17.)

PART 2 (vetted-dealer directory does not exist) — REAL. Policy :113 promises the buyer chooses "from the directory of dealers GunGalore has vetted" and :200 lists "Maintaining the directory of SAPS-licensed dealers" as a core function. Actual checkout contradicts this: frontend/app/checkout/[listingId]/checkout-form.tsx:1067-1075 comment "We don't yet have a comprehensive SAPS dealer directory, so instead of forcing the buyer to pick from an incomplete dropdown we let them use any SAPS-licensed dealer of their choice," and :438-441 "no dealerId — buyer picks their own SAPS [dealer]... DealerVerificationService gates payout instead." DealerTransferConsent (:1484) is a consent block, not a picker. CLAUDE.md:236 states "no dealer directory page." A Dealer admin-CRUD model exists (backend/src/admin/admin-dealers.service.ts) whose docstring claims it is "used by checkout," but that is stale — the live checkout does not surface it. dealer-verification.service.ts:158-162 and :209-211 confirm dealer is seller-supplied free-text, not vetted. So the published legal commitment overstates the actual control.

SEVERITY: Agree with LOW. Mitigating: the page is an explicit unpublished draft (lastUpdated "pre-launch · v0.1 draft"), and the real transfer-safety control (Claude-vision verification of genuine SAPS 534 + stock register + funds-held-until-approved) is implemented and sound regardless of the label error. But it is a genuine compliance-text defect that must be fixed before the policy is published: naming the wrong SAPS form and claiming a non-existent "vetted dealer directory" control in a legal document on a regulated SA firearms platform is real consumer-protection/legal exposure.

title: Peach webhook fails OPEN and verifies a re-serialized body it can never match — unauthenticated attacker can mark any transaction PAID without paying
description: The Peach webhook endpoint POST /api/payments/webhook/peach is unauthenticated (no guard) and its only protection — verifyWebhookSignature — fails OPEN. When PEACH_WEBHOOK_SECRET is unset it returns true (peach.service.ts:300-301: `if (!secret) return true;`). Worse, even WITH a secret set it can never validate: the controller signs `JSON.stringify(body)` (transactions.controller.ts:301) — a re-serialized JSON string whose key order/whitespace will not match the raw bytes Peach HMAC-signed, so a real Peach call would be rejected. The controller comment (lines 297-300) admits 'For full security we'd configure a raw-body parser... Live wiring of the raw body is a small follow-up.' This structurally forces the operator to leave the secret unset to avoid breaking real webhooks, locking in the fail-open. handlePeachWebhook (transactions.service.ts:319) then calls markPaid purely on result.isSuccess, flipping the listing to SOLD and paymentStatus to HELD. A buyer (who knows their own cuid transactionId from /transactions/[id]) can POST {merchantTransactionId:'<txid>','result.code':'000.000.000'} and the seller is then instructed to dispatch a firearm with no money received.
evidence: peach.service.ts:300 `if (!secret) { return true; // dev / not configured — allow through }`. controller.ts:301-306 `const rawBody = JSON.stringify(body); const valid = this.txService.verifyPeachWebhook(rawBody, signature); if (!valid) {...return} ` then line 308 `await this.txService.handlePeachWebhook(body);`. transactions.service.ts:319 `if (result.isSuccess) { await this.markPaid(...) }`.
recommendation: Before launch this endpoint MUST fail CLOSED: require PEACH_WEBHOOK_SECRET in prod (refuse to boot or reject all webhooks if missing). Wire the rawBody parser already enabled in main.ts (rawBody:true) and verify the HMAC against the exact raw bytes Peach sends, using the header/scheme Peach actually uses (confirm with Peach docs). Until verified, do not rely on the webhook to release funds — keep markPaid gated only on the server-to-server verifyPayment(resourcePath) call which independently re-queries Peach.

verdict.reasoning:
VERIFIED REAL and correctly rated CRITICAL. Traced the full path:

1. Route is live and unauthenticated. PaymentsWebhookController is registered (payments.module.ts:27); POST /api/payments/webhook/peach (controller.ts:284) has @HttpCode(200) and NO @UseGuards. The only global guard (app.module.ts:92, APP_GUARD) is ThrottlerGuard — a rate limiter (60/min), not auth. One forged request is enough, so throttling doesn't mitigate. No nginx/IP-allowlist config exists anywhere in the repo. CLAUDE.md:755 confirms webhook handlers are intentionally "public routes — no JWT".

2. Fails OPEN. peach.service.ts:300-301 `if (!secret) { return true; }`. PEACH_WEBHOOK_SECRET appears in NO env/deploy file in the repo (only the two source files + CLAUDE.md), so it is almost certainly unset in prod → fail-open is active. CLAUDE.md:1627-1633 documents this exact behavior ("fails open when the secret isn't configured").

3. Even WITH a secret it can't validate. controller.ts:301 hashes `JSON.stringify(body)`, NOT `req.rawBody`, even though main.ts:18 enables `rawBody:true`. A genuine Peach HMAC over raw bytes won't match re-serialized JSON, so enabling the secret would break real webhooks — structurally forcing the operator to leave it off. Self-admitted at controller.ts:297-300. So the system is broken either way.

4. No amount check. parseWebhookPayload (peach.service.ts:270-281) reads attacker-controlled body['result.code'], body.merchantTransactionId, body.amount. handlePeachWebhook (service.ts:319) and markPaid (service.ts:926-957) never compare amount to the stored transaction. markPaid sets paymentStatus='HELD' and listing status='SOLD' (service.ts:944,953).

5. Attacker knows the id. merchantTransactionId == tx.id, which is handed to the buyer in their own result URL `?transactionId=${tx.id}` (service.ts:219,224). So a buyer POSTs {merchantTransactionId:'<own txid>','result.code':'000.000.000'} and the listing flips SOLD/HELD with zero money captured → seller is then driven through accept→dispatch of a regulated firearm.

ESCALATION the finding missed: for PRIVATE_ARRANGE transactions, markPaid calls maybeImmediatePayout (service.ts:978) which flips paymentStatus='RELEASED', increments seller totalSales, and emails BOTH parties' contact PII (service.ts:1015-1047). A forged webhook there desyncs the ledger to RELEASED and leaks personal data between users.

Skeptical counter-checks all fail to save it: idempotency (tx.paidAt, service.ts:314) only blocks replay after the first forged hit; throttler is not auth; no infra allowlist in repo. Minor imprecision in the finding: a forged webhook does not drain real money out of Peach — it desynchronizes the platform's records (marks SOLD/HELD/RELEASED, prompts firearm dispatch, leaks PII) with no captured payment. The legal/financial/PII exposure on a regulated firearms marketplace fully justifies CRITICAL. Recommendation in the finding is sound: fail CLOSED (require secret in prod), verify HMAC against req.rawBody using Peach's real scheme, and gate fund-release on the server-to-server verifyPayment(resourcePath) re-query (peach.service.ts:95) rather than trusting webhook fields.

One unverifiable environmental assumption: whether PEACH_WEBHOOK_SECRET is set on the live VPS .env (not readable here). But point 3 means even a set secret yields a broken/effectively-fail-open state, so the verdict is robust to that unknown.

title: JWT_ADMIN_SECRET falls back to the hardcoded public string 'dev-admin-secret-change-in-prod' — admin auth fully bypassable if the env var is missing
description: Both the admin JWT signer and verifier default to a hardcoded secret committed to the repo: `process.env.JWT_ADMIN_SECRET || 'dev-admin-secret-change-in-prod'`. If JWT_ADMIN_SECRET is unset (or empty) in prod, the verifier accepts tokens signed with this publicly-known string. Any attacker can mint a token `{sub,email,role:'SUPER_ADMIN'}` signed with 'dev-admin-secret-change-in-prod' and pass AdminJwtGuard, gaining full admin access (credits, refunds, user data, competition draws). There is no startup validation that rejects the default — main.ts (1-78) does no env assertions. Note `||` is used (not `??`), so even an accidentally-empty string falls back to the default. The same default appears in at least 4 places, so a single missing var compromises all admin-guarded routes.
evidence: admin-jwt.guard.ts:15-17 `const payload = await this.jwtService.verifyAsync(token, { secret: process.env.JWT_ADMIN_SECRET || 'dev-admin-secret-change-in-prod' });`. admin-auth.service.ts:31 signs with the same fallback.
recommendation: Fail CLOSED on config: read JWT_ADMIN_SECRET once at bootstrap and throw if missing/empty/equal to the dev default in production (NODE_ENV==='production'). Remove the literal fallback from all four files and source the secret from a single config provider. Rotate the secret since the literal is in git history.

verdict.reasoning:
VERIFIED REAL. All four call sites confirmed verbatim using `process.env.JWT_ADMIN_SECRET || 'dev-admin-secret-change-in-prod'`: admin-jwt.guard.ts:16 (verifier), admin-auth.service.ts:31 (signer), ask-gg.module.ts:27, reloading.module.ts:29.

The fallback is unambiguously the OPERATIVE secret, not dead code: AdminModule registers `JwtModule.register({})` with NO secret (admin.module.ts:49), and AdminJwtGuard passes `secret` explicitly to `verifyAsync` (line 15-17). So there is no other secret layer — the inline literal is exactly what verifies tokens. `||` (not `??`) is confirmed, so an empty-string env var also falls through to the default (and main.ts:1-9 calls dotenv with `override:true`, which is documented there to handle shells that export vars as empty strings — a realistic path to an empty value).

No fail-closed guard exists anywhere: main.ts (1-78) does zero env assertions; app.module.ts has no `ConfigModule.forRoot` and no Joi `validationSchema`; the only `process.exit` in the tree is an unrelated test file. So the fail-open is genuinely reachable.

Blast radius confirmed: AdminJwtGuard protects 18 endpoints on admin.controller.ts including `:id/refund` (310), `:id/release` (304), `:id/resolve-dispute-release` (324), credits `balance/refresh` (444), `:id/delete`, `bulk-ban`, `:id/dossier` (user PII), `dealer-verification/override` (342). An attacker who knows the committed string can mint `{sub,email,role:'SUPER_ADMIN'}` and pass the guard — money loss + PII leakage + regulated-platform legal exposure.

NUANCE (not overstated, but important): the catastrophic outcome is CONDITIONAL on JWT_ADMIN_SECRET being unset/empty in prod. CLAUDE.md:199 lists it as a required backend var and .env.example:20 includes it, so a careful operator probably set it — I cannot read the prod .env to confirm. This is therefore a fail-open-on-misconfiguration defect, not a proven live breach. However, for a regulated SA financial marketplace the correct posture is fail-CLOSED, the weak default is committed to the repo, the operator is non-technical and hand-manages env on a self-built VPS (elevated misconfig probability), and a single missing/empty var silently downgrades the entire admin plane to a public shared secret with no signal. That justifies CRITICAL as a launch blocker. Recommendation stands: remove the literal from all 4 files, source from one config provider, and throw at bootstrap if missing/empty/equal-to-default when NODE_ENV==='production'; rotate the secret since it is in git history.

title: markPaid never validates the paid amount against buyerTotal — under/over-payment (or any forged webhook amount) marks the order fully paid
description: Both verifyResult() and handlePeachWebhook() decide success purely on result.isSuccess (the Peach result-code regex) and never compare result.amount to the transaction's expected total (tx.buyerTotal). markPaid (lines 926-957) receives only txId, paymentId, resultCode, listing — it has no amount parameter and performs no amount check before setting paymentStatus='HELD' and listing.status='SOLD'. A Peach authorisation for the wrong (lower) amount, or — combined with the fail-open webhook above — a forged webhook carrying any amount, will fully settle the order. For a regulated marketplace holding buyer funds, accepting a payment without confirming the captured amount equals the amount owed is a money-correctness defect.
evidence: transactions.service.ts:276 `if (result.isSuccess) { await this.markPaid(tx.id, result.paymentId, result.resultCode, tx.listing); }` — result.amount (populated by peach.service.ts:114) is discarded. markPaid signature (line 926) has no amount param.
recommendation: Pass result.amount into markPaid and reject (or flag for manual review) when it does not equal tx.buyerTotal (allowing only currency==='ZAR'). This single check also blunts the forged-webhook vector even before the signature wiring is fixed.

verdict.reasoning:
VERIFIED REAL but the severity rationale leans on the weaker of two vectors. Facts confirmed directly: markPaid (transactions.service.ts:926-931) takes only (txId, paymentId, resultCode, listing) — no amount param. Both callers branch solely on result.isSuccess: verifyResult (line 276-277) and handlePeachWebhook (line 319-320). result.amount IS populated (peach.service.ts:114 from verify, :276 from webhook parse) and is discarded. A grep for buyerTotal across backend/src/payments shows it is used at checkout (line 223 amountZarCents: buyerTotal) and in refunds (479, 1144) but NEVER compared to result.amount in any confirmation path. So the technical core — captured amount is never validated against tx.buyerTotal — is factually correct.

WHERE THE FINDING OVERSTATES: The headline 'under/over-payment via a Peach authorisation for the wrong amount' is largely theoretical. createCheckout sends amountZarCents: buyerTotal to Peach (peach.service.ts:60, txns:223) and Peach charges that amount server-side on a DB (debit) checkout; a buyer cannot make the hosted widget authorise a different amount on their own. So buyer-driven under-payment essentially can't happen through the legitimate flow — it would need a Peach-side bug. With a correctly-signed Peach webhook, Peach is the source of truth for the amount, making the standalone missing-check a defense-in-depth gap, not a live breach.

WHERE IT IS RIGHT AND DANGEROUS: The genuinely exploitable path is the FORGED webhook, which the finding correctly identifies as the compounding vector. verifyWebhookSignature (peach.service.ts:298-302) returns true when PEACH_WEBHOOK_SECRET is unset, and that env var appears nowhere else in the repo (no .env, no config) — i.e. fail-open today. PaymentsWebhookController.peachWebhook (transactions.controller.ts:284-310) is unauthenticated and returns 200. So an attacker who knows a real un-paid Transaction.id can POST {merchantTransactionId, 'result.code':'000.100.110', amount:<anything>} and the order settles to HELD + listing SOLD with zero real payment — and because amount is ignored, the forged amount passes unchecked. That is real money/goods loss. BUT this is driven primarily by the fail-open signature (a distinct, arguably-more-severe finding); the missing amount check is the secondary control that would blunt it. Note also line 301 JSON.stringify(body) will not reproduce Peach's HMAC over raw bytes, so even enabling the secret may break legit webhooks — confirming the webhook-auth area is the larger problem and should be tracked on its own.

CONCLUSION: The defect (no amount validation) is real and worth fixing — for a funds-holding platform you should reject/flag when result.amount !== tx.buyerTotal and currency !== 'ZAR'. But as a STANDALONE finding its impact is gated by the separate webhook-auth issue; with a properly authenticated webhook it is low/medium. HIGH is overstated for this finding in isolation; MEDIUM (defense-in-depth money-correctness control) is the accurate standalone rating. The serious exploitability the description invokes actually belongs to the fail-open webhook finding.

title: Peach defaults to test/sandbox base URL (test.oppwa.com) when PEACH_BASE_URL is unset — payments silently route to sandbox in prod
description: PeachService.baseUrl falls back to the sandbox host: `process.env.PEACH_BASE_URL ?? 'https://test.oppwa.com'`. Every checkout, payment-verify, AVS and refund call uses this baseUrl (lines 73, 87, 100, 177, etc.). If PEACH_BASE_URL is unset/typo'd in prod, all real payments silently go to the Peach test gateway — checkouts 'succeed' against sandbox, real cards are never charged, and verifyPayment queries the test environment. This is the exact class of dangerous silent prod fallback the audit flags (same family as the SMS-localhost bug). isConfigured only checks ENTITY_ID + ACCESS_TOKEN (line 37-39), not the base URL or a mode flag, so nothing catches a missing base URL.
evidence: peach.service.ts:26 `return process.env.PEACH_BASE_URL ?? 'https://test.oppwa.com';` and admin-health.service.ts:95 shows the same sandbox default in the health probe, confirming prod relies on the env var being present.
recommendation: In production require an explicit PEACH_BASE_URL (or a PEACH_MODE=live|test switch) and refuse to start / log a CRITICAL if it resolves to test.oppwa.com while NODE_ENV is production. Mirror the VerifyNow VERIFYNOW_MODE pattern but make 'live' the asserted prod value rather than defaulting to the safe-but-wrong sandbox.

verdict.reasoning: VERIFIED REAL but overstated; corrected to MEDIUM. All factual claims confirmed: peach.service.ts:26 `baseUrl` returns `process.env.PEACH_BASE_URL ?? 'https://test.oppwa.com'`; this baseUrl drives every gateway call — createCheckout (73, 87), verifyPayment (100), AVS verifyBankAccount (177), refundPayment (238). isConfigured (37-39) checks only PEACH_ENTITY_ID + PEACH_ACCESS_TOKEN, never the base URL or a mode flag. main.ts bootstrap (full file read) has NO env validation — no NODE_ENV guard, no assertion, no refuse-to-start. .env.example:64 ships `PEACH_BASE_URL=` empty, so a forgotten/typo'd value silently resolves to the sandbox host. admin-health.service.ts:95 mirrors the same default (corroborating env-var reliance, though that is only the probe). The finding's contrast with VerifyNow is apt: verifynow.service.ts:77-81 deliberately defaults mode to 'sandbox' because for KYC sandbox=safe (no credits burned); for a payment acquirer the safe direction inverts — defaulting to test means real checkouts can succeed against the test gateway while our side marks the order paid and no card is charged. So the unsafe-default-direction + no-fail-fast critique is legitimate. WHY DOWNGRADED FROM HIGH: the dangerous silent-success path requires a specific combination — TEST entity/token credentials present (so isConfigured is true) AND PEACH_BASE_URL unset. A normal prod misconfig (LIVE credentials + missing base URL) will not authenticate against test.oppwa.com (Peach isolates credentials per environment), so it fails loudly via the thrown errors at lines 79-81 / 105-107 rather than silently charging nothing. That self-limiting behavior makes the 'all real payments silently route to sandbox and succeed' framing broader than reality. Genuine config-hardening gap worth fixing (assert an explicit PEACH_BASE_URL / PEACH_MODE=live in production and refuse to start if it resolves to test.oppwa.com under NODE_ENV=production), but the blast radius is narrower than HIGH.

title: KYC (VerifyNow) defaults to mode='sandbox' when VERIFYNOW_MODE is unset — identity checks silently return canned sandbox results in prod
description: VerifyNowService.mode defaults to 'sandbox' (`(process.env.VERIFYNOW_MODE ?? 'sandbox')`), and this mode is sent in every verify request body (verifyIdNumber line 99 sends `mode: this.mode`). Sandbox mode does not hit Home Affairs — it returns free canned data. If VERIFYNOW_MODE is unset or anything other than exactly 'production' in prod, KYC/ID verification passes against fake data, defeating the regulated-platform requirement that a passing KYC means the person's SA ID was really verified. Given the auto-memory note about tying AVS to a real verified identity, a silently-sandboxed KYC undermines the whole seller-trust chain. Nothing asserts the mode at boot.
evidence: verifynow.service.ts:79 `const m = (process.env.VERIFYNOW_MODE ?? 'sandbox').toLowerCase(); return m === 'production' ? 'production' : 'sandbox';`
recommendation: In production assert VERIFYNOW_MODE==='production' at startup (throw or hard-log CRITICAL otherwise). Do not let an unset/typo'd value silently fall back to sandbox; failing closed here is required for KYC integrity.

verdict.reasoning:
VERIFIED REAL. The cited code at backend/src/kyc/verifynow.service.ts:78-81 is exactly as described: mode getter returns 'sandbox' for any value that isn't exactly 'production' (after .toLowerCase()), defaulting to sandbox when VERIFYNOW_MODE is unset. That mode is sent in the body of both verifyIdNumber (line 99) and faceMatch (line 192).

Fail-open is confirmed, not mitigated anywhere:
- main.ts (the real bootstrap) does NO config validation — it just dotenv.config({override:true}) and listens. No Joi schema, no ConfigModule validationSchema, no assert/throw on VERIFYNOW_MODE. Grep across backend/src for VERIFYNOW_MODE returns ONLY verifynow.service.ts:79 — nothing asserts it at boot.
- admin-health.service.ts:115-120 health-checks VerifyNow but only requiresEnv ['VERIFYNOW_API_KEY'] — it never checks the mode, so a sandbox-misconfigured prod still reports healthy.

Worse than the report implies: backend/.env (the file main.ts loads) literally contains VERIFYNOW_MODE=sandbox (line 30), and backend/.env.example (lines 22-25) does NOT document VERIFYNOW_MODE at all — only VERIFYNOW_API_KEY and VERIFYNOW_BASE_URL. So an operator provisioning the VPS from the example would never set it and would silently get sandbox.

Blast radius confirmed via kyc.service.ts: verifyId() writes Home-Affairs firstName/lastName onto User and sets kycStatus PENDING; submitFaceMatch() stamps kycStatus='VERIFIED' + kycVerifiedAt when score>=75 && status==='Approved' (lines 251-264). VERIFIED gates seller payout release (triggerSellerVerification, lines 337-384). In sandbox VerifyNow returns mock data (corroborated by the file's own comments at lines 58-60, the getCreditBalance sandbox-vs-production shapes at lines 263-268, and the admin KYC page text 'Sandbox returns mock data and does not consume credits' at frontend .../kyc/page.tsx:168), so any SA ID number + a self-matching selfie would pass KYC, defeating the regulated requirement that a passing KYC means a real verified SA identity — directly undermining the AVS-to-KYC seller-trust chain noted in auto-memory.

One caveat on certainty of impact: I could not (read-only, and shouldn't) hit the live VerifyNow API to prove sandbox returns a PASS for arbitrary IDs; this is inferred from consistent in-repo documentation, which is strong but not first-hand. Note .toLowerCase() does correctly handle 'Production'/'PRODUCTION', so the only failure values are unset / typos / 'prod' / 'live' — but the shipped .env uses 'sandbox', making the failure likely in practice.

Severity: original HIGH is correct and well-justified. It is a dangerous fail-open default on a compliance-critical, money/payout-gating, legally-regulated firearms KYC path with no boot-time guard and an undocumented env var. It stops short of slam-dunk CRITICAL only because exploitation requires the operator to not set VERIFYNOW_MODE=production (a fail-open misconfiguration risk rather than an unconditional live breach). However, because the repo's own .env ships 'sandbox' and the example omits the var, if production is in fact running with that env, this becomes an active CRITICAL (fake-identity 'verified' sellers => firearms-transfer fraud + FICA/regulatory legal exposure). Recommend the original fix: assert VERIFYNOW_MODE==='production' at startup in prod (throw/exit), and add it to .env.example.

title: Cron health panel monitors a key that is never written and omits 5 crons that ARE written — including the every-minute featuredTick which records nothing
description: The /admin/health 'Cron status' panel (the operator's 'is everything up?' screen) is out of sync with reality in both directions. (1) It lists key 'pending-tickets-sweep' (admin-health.service.ts:273) but NO cron anywhere calls recordCronRun('pending-tickets-sweep') — it will perpetually show 'never', a permanent false alarm. (2) Several real crons that DO call recordCronRun are absent from the monitored list, so they are invisible to the panel: 'subscriber-raffle-draw' (tasks.service.ts:229), 'dispatch-sla' IS listed but 'accept-escalation' (line 338), 'credit-poll' (line 367/406), and 'push-prune' (line 58) are not. (3) Most importantly, featuredTick (tasks.service.ts:99-182) — runs EVERY MINUTE and performs financial featured-auction settlement (closing auctions, releasing sold slots) — has NO recordCronRun call AND no try/catch, so an unhandled rejection silently kills the run and the operator has zero visibility into whether featured settlement is alive.
evidence: admin-health.service.ts:273 monitors `{ key: 'pending-tickets-sweep' ... }` (no matching writer found in backend/src). tasks.service.ts:99 `@Cron(CronExpression.EVERY_MINUTE) async featuredTick()` runs to line 182 with no recordCronRun and no try/catch, unlike every other cron in the file.
recommendation: Make the monitored definitions list match the actual recordCronRun keys: drop or implement 'pending-tickets-sweep', and add featured-tick, subscriber-raffle-draw, accept-escalation, credit-poll, push-prune. Add recordCronRun('featured-tick') plus a try/catch to featuredTick so a thrown error in one slot doesn't abort the whole tick and so staleness is observable.

verdict.reasoning:
Verified every factual claim against the code; all hold.

(1) Permanent false alarm — CONFIRMED. admin-health.service.ts:273 monitors key `pending-tickets-sweep`, but a repo-wide grep for `recordCronRun(` shows the only 12 call sites are all in tasks.service.ts and none uses `pending-tickets-sweep` (keys written: push-prune, offer-expire, auction-end, raffle-draw, subscriber-raffle-draw, raffle-expire, verifynow-balance, shipping-poll, dispatch-sla, accept-escalation, credit-poll x2). cronStatuses() is the ONLY definition list (no second consumer), and the frontend at frontend/app/admin/(protected)/health/page.tsx:259-272 renders c.status as a colored badge, so this row will perpetually show "never" — a standing false alarm. (Note the misleading label too: it says "Pending raffle tickets sweep" yet the actual pending-ticket cleanup is RafflesService, not a tasks cron.)

(2) Blind spots — CONFIRMED. The monitored list (8 keys, lines 266-273) omits 4 crons that DO record: push-prune (line 58), subscriber-raffle-draw (line 229), accept-escalation (line 338), credit-poll (lines 367/406). These run but are invisible on the panel. The finding's list matches exactly.

(3) featuredTick — CONFIRMED. tasks.service.ts:99-182 is @Cron(EVERY_MINUTE) with NO recordCronRun and NO try/catch, unlike the other crons (push-prune, offer-expire, raffle-draw, etc. all wrap try/catch and/or record). Its body awaits featured.closeAuction/expireBindWindow/expireFeatured/openAuction/releaseSoldListing; closeAuction (featured.service.ts:638-713) settles featured-slot auctions (awards winner, opens BIND_WINDOW where the tier-discounted slot fee is later collected). So a persistent throw in one slot aborts the rest of that tick AND there is zero panel visibility. Minor nuance: NestJS does not kill the scheduler on an unhandled rejection — the next minute still fires, so transient errors self-heal; only a persistent bad row stalls settlement. Also note endAuctions (the other EVERY_MINUTE cron) likewise lacks try/catch but DOES record auction-end and IS monitored, so the operator can see auction staleness but not featured-slot staleness — exactly as claimed.

Net: this is a genuine observability defect with both a permanent false positive and blind spots over revenue-bearing crons. Not a security/money-loss/data-loss bug, and failures mostly self-heal, so MEDIUM (not higher) is correct.

title: No global exception filter or error-reporting (no Sentry) on the financial backend — production errors are visible only in pm2/console logs
description: There is no APP_FILTER / @Catch ExceptionFilter and no error-reporting integration (Sentry/captureException) anywhere in backend/src — a repo-wide search for Sentry|ExceptionFilter|APP_FILTER|captureException|@Catch returns nothing. main.ts wires ValidationPipe and CORS but no global error handler. For a platform moving real money (payments, refunds, credit billing on Pudo which is on production mode per memory), unhandled exceptions and 500s are only discoverable by tailing pm2 logs on the Vultr box. There is no alerting on payment/KYC/refund failures, no structured error capture, and the many `void this.prisma...catch(...)` fire-and-forget writes (e.g. transactions.service.ts:907-916) swallow failures into warn logs only.
evidence: Grep for `Sentry|ExceptionFilter|APP_FILTER|captureException|@Catch` across backend/src returned only an unrelated ask-gg comment match. main.ts has no filter registration.
recommendation: Add a global ExceptionFilter that logs structured context (route, user, txId) and, before launch, an error-reporting sink (Sentry or equivalent) at least for the payments/kyc/refund/zoho paths so settlement failures page the operator instead of dying silently in pm2 logs.

verdict.reasoning:
The factual core is correct: a repo-wide grep for Sentry|ExceptionFilter|APP_FILTER|captureException|@Catch returns nothing, app.module.ts (lines 88-93) registers only ThrottlerGuard via APP_GUARD (no APP_FILTER), no package.json declares any error-reporting dependency, and the fire-and-forget void this.prisma...catch(warn) writes exist (transactions.service.ts:907-916). So "no custom global exception filter and no Sentry" is true.

But the finding is materially OVERSTATED in impact and severity:
1. NestJS ships a built-in BaseExceptionFilter that catches every unhandled exception, returns a 500, and logs it — the process does not crash and requests don't hang. The absence of a CUSTOM filter is not a missing safety net; "errors visible only in pm2 logs" is the framework default, not a defect.
2. The finding ignores a real observability layer: admin-health.service.ts actively probes Peach, Pudo, VerifyNow (KYC), Zoho Books, Clerk etc., tracks cron staleness, and surfaces money-sensitive queue depths including "HELD payments past dispatch SLA (24h+)" (lines 305-333). This is pull-based via /admin/health, but it directly covers the payment/KYC/settlement monitoring the finding claims is absent.
3. The money-critical paths do NOT die silently. On a failed Peach refund during sale-reject, transactions.service.ts:482-497 raises an urgent AdminAlert AND throws a user-facing "support has been alerted" error. There is a mature AdminAlert system across payments, KYC (kyc.service.ts:393), dispatch-SLA (dispatch-sla.service.ts:138/176) and duplicate-address detection, plus an operator push channel: notifications.service.ts creditAlert (1994-2037) emails AND SMSes the operator's phone on credit-balance alarms.
4. The Peach webhook (transactions.controller.ts:284-310) returns 200 by design but does not wrap handlePeachWebhook in try/catch, so a throw there yields a 500 → Peach retries (markPaid is guard-checked), and the error lands in the default filter + pm2 log. A genuine but narrow gap, not money lost.

So the genuinely defensible gap is narrower than stated: there is no PUSH-based aggregation/alerting of UNEXPECTED 500s/exceptions (operator must tail pm2 or open the dashboard), and fire-and-forget writes degrade to warn-logs. That is legitimate operational hardening but creates no money-loss, data-loss, or cross-user data-leak path, and the genuinely dangerous failures already alert the operator. For a single-operator pre-launch platform that already has a health dashboard + AdminAlert + email/SMS alerting, this is polish, not a MEDIUM observability hole.

title: Deploy uses 'prisma db push --accept-data-loss' against the production DB on every deploy — destructive and unguarded
description: The documented prod deploy step (CLAUDE.md:76) is `npx prisma db push --accept-data-loss` with the comment that tsvector GENERATED columns get re-created by onModuleInit, followed by a mandatory `npx prisma generate` (line 77, 'stale client = build fails'). `--accept-data-loss` instructs Prisma to apply schema drift WITHOUT confirmation, dropping columns/tables it thinks are unneeded. The project deliberately fights Prisma over GENERATED tsvector columns (schema.prisma:2257-2259, 2357 warn that db push tries to DROP textTsv and Postgres repopulates it). Relying on --accept-data-loss + onModuleInit DDL re-creation as the normal deploy path means any unexpected drift (a column Prisma doesn't know about, a partially-applied schema) is silently destroyed on the next deploy, on the live Vultr Postgres, with no migration history and no review gate. There are no committed migration files (schema.prisma:3 references migrate dev, but the deploy uses db push), so there's no audit trail or rollback.
evidence: CLAUDE.md:76 `npx prisma db push --accept-data-loss  # tsvector GENERATED cols get re-created by onModuleInit`. schema.prisma:2259 'Operational rule: if prisma db push warns about dropping textTsv...' confirms db push routinely proposes destructive drops.
recommendation: Move to versioned migrations (`prisma migrate deploy`) for prod so changes are reviewed, ordered, and reversible. If db push must stay, never pair it with --accept-data-loss on prod unattended — take a DB snapshot immediately before, and review the printed drift. At minimum document a pre-deploy `pg_dump` so an accidental drop is recoverable.

verdict.reasoning:
VERIFIED PARTIALLY REAL but OVERSTATED, with a material factual error.

CONFIRMED facts: CLAUDE.md:76 is verbatim `npx prisma db push --accept-data-loss  # tsvector GENERATED cols get re-created by onModuleInit`. schema.prisma:2259-2263 and 2354-2359 confirm `db push` routinely proposes dropping `textTsv`, with the operational rule to accept it. CLAUDE.md:1436 uses `db push` as the apply step. So the destructive flag is genuinely the documented, unattended prod deploy path with no pre-deploy pg_dump and no review gate — that part is real process risk.

But the finding is wrong/overstated on the two points that drive its severity:

1) FALSE CLAIM "no committed migration files / no audit trail or rollback." There ARE 13 committed migrations in backend/prisma/migrations/ (20260518042140_init through 20260518162012_add_raffles, plus 20260528170000_add_range_estimate and 20260529000000_add_hunt_pdf) with migration_lock.toml. A migration history exists. The deploy doesn't use them, but the claim "no migration history" is false.

2) OVERSTATED data-loss impact. The ONLY drift db push is documented to destroy is the `textTsv` STORED GENERATED columns on ReloadingManualPage and HuntPdfPage. These are derived columns (GENERATED ALWAYS AS (to_tsvector(... coalesce(extractedText,'')...)) STORED). Dropping them loses ZERO source data — the base columns (extractedText/text) survive, and reloading.service.ts:72-80 / hunt-pdf.service.ts re-add the column+GIN index idempotently (ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS) on next boot, with Postgres auto-repopulating the tsvector. So the documented drift is self-healing.

3) Blast radius bounded: core marketplace search runs on Meilisearch (search.service.ts, INDEXES.LISTINGS), NOT Postgres FTS. No money/PII/listings/offers/payments table carries a GENERATED column db push would touch. tsvector only exists on the secondary reloading/hunt-PDF reference surfaces.

Net: the legitimate residual risk is purely latent — `--accept-data-loss` unattended with no mandatory snapshot means a FUTURE unexpected drift (e.g. a hand-added column Prisma doesn't know about) could be silently dropped with no recovery step in the runbook. That is worth hardening (recommend mandatory pg_dump before db push, or prisma migrate deploy since migrations already exist). But the present, demonstrable exposure is effectively nil, and the finding's MEDIUM rests on a factual error (no migrations) plus an overstated data-loss premise. Correct rating is LOW process-hardening, not MEDIUM.

title: BACKEND_URL falls back to http://localhost:3001 for the Peach notificationUrl — a missing var registers a localhost webhook Peach can never reach
description: createCheckout registers the Peach webhook target as `${process.env.BACKEND_URL ?? 'http://localhost:3001'}/api/payments/webhook/peach` (line 70). If BACKEND_URL is unset in prod, every checkout tells Peach to POST payment notifications to http://localhost:3001 — which Peach's servers cannot reach — so the asynchronous webhook confirmation path is silently dead. Payments would then depend entirely on the user landing back on the result page to trigger verify-result; users who close the tab after paying never get their transaction marked paid. This is the same localhost-fallback class as the SMS bug and would degrade silently (no error, just missing webhooks).
evidence: peach.service.ts:70 `'notificationUrl': `${process.env.BACKEND_URL ?? 'http://localhost:3001'}/api/payments/webhook/peach`,`
recommendation: Require BACKEND_URL in production (assert at boot) and remove the localhost fallback, or derive the public base from a single validated config value. Log a startup error if the resolved notificationUrl host is localhost while NODE_ENV is production.

verdict.reasoning: The localhost fallback is real and correctly located: peach.service.ts:70 sets notificationUrl to `${process.env.BACKEND_URL ?? 'http://localhost:3001'}/api/payments/webhook/peach`. A repo-wide grep shows BACKEND_URL is referenced ONLY on this line — it is NOT in backend/.env.example, NOT in CLAUDE.md's canonical env-var list (lines 198-205, which use FRONTEND_URL/PEACH_*), and NOT in any pm2/deploy/shell file. The project's convention for a public base URL is FRONTEND_URL (main.ts:51, transactions.service.ts:219). So "unset in prod" is the likely default, not a corner case, and main.ts has no boot-time assertion, so it would fail silently. The webhook does real work: transactions.controller.ts:308 -> handlePeachWebhook -> markPaid (transactions.service.ts:299-320). I also confirmed there is NO payment-reconciliation cron (scanned all crons in tasks.service.ts; the only PAYMENT_PENDING reference, featuredTick line 106, merely frees featured slots and never polls Peach). So with BACKEND_URL unset, Peach's async webhook is genuinely dead.\n\nHOWEVER the claimed MEDIUM severity is overstated. The finding says payments would "depend entirely on the user landing back on the result page," but that PRIMARY confirmation path does NOT use BACKEND_URL at all: shopperResultUrl is built from FRONTEND_URL (transactions.service.ts:219, controller :84), Peach appends resourcePath to that browser redirect, and frontend/app/checkout/complete/page.tsx:15,24-28 POSTs verify-result -> verifyPayment -> markPaid (both paths idempotent on tx.paidAt). In the normal flow the buyer's browser returns and the payment is confirmed correctly even with BACKEND_URL unset. The webhook is the backstop, not the main path. The real residual impact is limited to buyers who pay then close the tab before the redirect resolves: they stay PAYMENT_PENDING with no automated recovery (manual admin re-verify needed). That is a genuine money-adjacent edge-case worth fixing pre-launch (drop the fallback, add the var to the canonical list, add a PAYMENT_PENDING reconciliation cron), but it is not a broken core flow. Additionally the webhook signature already fails-open with approximate raw-body handling (controller :297-301, peach.service.ts:298-302), so the team already treats it as non-load-bearing scaffolding. Net: real config-fallback bug, correctly located, but blast radius is the closed-tab minority rather than all payments — LOW, not MEDIUM.

title: FRONTEND_URL fallback in checkout uses request Host header (attacker-controllable) for redirect/shopperResultUrl construction
description: In the checkout create handler, frontendUrl falls back to the request-derived host: `process.env.FRONTEND_URL ?? `${req.protocol}://${req.get('host') ?? 'localhost:3000'}``. This value is passed to txService.create and used to build the Peach shopperResultUrl / redirect base. The Host header is client-controllable, so if FRONTEND_URL is unset in prod, an attacker can set Host to an arbitrary domain and influence the post-payment redirect target (open-redirect / phishing of the payment return flow), and a missing var also risks shopperResultUrl pointing at localhost. Most other frontend-URL usages correctly default to https://gungalore.co.za (transactions.service.ts:1121) or to FRONTEND_URL only — this controller is the weak spot because it trusts the inbound Host.
evidence: transactions.controller.ts:83-85 `const frontendUrl = process.env.FRONTEND_URL ?? `${req.protocol}://${req.get('host') ?? 'localhost:3000'}`; return this.txService.create(clerkId, dto, frontendUrl);`
recommendation: Require FRONTEND_URL in prod and drop the Host-header fallback (or replace with the hardcoded https://gungalore.co.za default already used at transactions.service.ts:1121). Never derive a payment redirect base from a client-supplied Host header.

verdict.reasoning:
The technical mechanics in the finding are accurate. transactions.controller.ts:83-84 sets `frontendUrl = process.env.FRONTEND_URL ?? `${req.protocol}://${req.get('host') ?? 'localhost:3000'}``; req.get('host') is the client-supplied Host header. It flows to transactions.service.ts:219 (`resultUrl = `${frontendUrl}/checkout/complete?...``) and :225 (`shopperResultUrl: resultUrl`), and peach.service.ts:48 confirms shopperResultUrl is "where Peach redirects after payment". I also confirmed FRONTEND_URL is genuinely undocumented as a required prod var: it is absent from backend/.env, backend/.env.example, and the authoritative CLAUDE.md var list (lines 198-205), and there is NO `app.set('trust proxy')` anywhere in the backend (verified main.ts and grep).

HOWEVER the MEDIUM/open-redirect-phishing framing is overstated, because the exploit cannot harm any user but the attacker:
1. Self-targeting only. shopperResultUrl is baked into the Peach checkout for the attacker's OWN transaction; only the buyer who initiated that specific checkout is redirected there post-payment. Forging your own Host to redirect your own payment-return to evil.com phishes only yourself. The resultUrl never touches another user's request, session, or stored record — it is per-transaction and consumed by the same actor. verifyResult()/markPaid() do no server-side res.redirect using Host (verified transactions.service.ts:264-320), so there is no cross-user redirect surface.
2. Browsers cannot set the Host header (forbidden header for fetch/XHR); the legitimate frontend (checkout-form.tsx:518-523) always sends the correct Host. Exploitation requires a non-browser client (curl/Postman) acting on the attacker's own authenticated Clerk session or action token — i.e., attacking themselves.
3. Prod likelihood is low: main.ts:51 puts process.env.FRONTEND_URL in the CORS allow-list, so if it were unset in prod the real frontend origin would fail CORS and the site would break — strong evidence it IS set in prod, making the fallback effectively dead code there.

So this is a real config-robustness/hardening gap (undocumented, unguarded reliance on FRONTEND_URL + a Host-header fallback that yields a localhost or wrong-scheme redirect if the var is ever omitted on redeploy), not an open-redirect that can phish other users. The recommended fix (drop the Host fallback; hardcode https://gungalore.co.za as already done at transactions.service.ts:1121) is correct as defense-in-depth. Severity should be LOW, not MEDIUM.
